Manage your subscription Your newsletters Subscriber benefits Sign out Subscribe now Health Pancreatic cancer halted by virus injection in three patients A cancer-killing virus has stopped pancreatic tumours from growing and spreading in three people in an initial safety trial, raising hopes that it may help to beat the deadly condition By Alice Klein 29 May 2026 Facebook Threads X / Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn Reddit Email Print A scanning electron micrograph of pancreatic cancer cells ANNE WESTON, EM STP, THE FRANCIS CRICK INSTITUTE/SCIENCE PHOTO LIBRARY A virus has stopped pancreatic cancer in its tracks in three people in a clinical trial in the US. Further evaluation is needed in larger trials, but the early results are encouraging, especially since only small doses of the virus were administered for initial safety testing. “We only injected one-tenth of the dose we are eventually aiming at, so the efficacy is better than I expected, especially as this is pancreatic cancer,” says Masato Yamamoto at the University of Minnesota, who led the development of the viral treatment. Read more Woman in cancer remission without treatment in highly unusual case Pancreatic cancer is notorious for being the deadliest type of the condition. One reason is that symptoms tend to appear late, when the cancer has already spread and cannot be surgically removed. Once diagnosed, people usually live only around three to six months . Advertisement Another reason is that pancreatic tumours have tough, fibrous exteriors that block chemotherapy drugs from getting in. “They’re hard as hockey pucks,” says Yamamoto. Immunotherapies that boost immune activity against cancer are also ineffective, because pancreatic tumours can hide from the immune system . The first patient in the trial, who had a pancreatic tumour 7 centimetres across, was administered the treatment a year ago, and the other two have been since then. At the time, their tumours hadn’t spread beyond the pancreas. Since being treated, their tumours haven’t grown any further. “They are all still alive and have clinically stable disease,” says Yamamoto, who presented the results at the annual meeting of the American Society of Gene and Cell Therapy in Boston, Massachusetts, earlier this month. Another 15 patients will now be given higher doses to find the optimum level. “I think this is an interesting early signal, but as a pancreatic surgeon, I think it’s important to keep perspective,” says Kai Brown at Royal North Shore Hospital in Sydney. “The history of oncology is littered with promising early signals that vanished by the time rigorous phase III [late-stage] testing was done, so I think these preliminary conference results should probably just be seen as hypothesis-generating at this stage.” He also notes that the trial so far hasn’t included a control group, so it is hard to know whether the cancer-killing virus works better than other treatments or none at all. Free newsletter Sign up to Health Check Sign up to newsletter The virus is an adenovirus that has been genetically engineered to replicate only inside tumours and not healthy tissue. Its replication is specifically activated by an enzyme called cyclooxygenase-2 (COX-2), which is present at much higher levels in cancer cells than in normal ones. After cancer cells become infected with the virus, they burst open and die, releasing more virus that can infect neighbouring cancer cells. In the trial, the virus was injected directly into the patients’ tumours through a thin tube that was guided down a patient’s throat to their pancreas. The tube had an ultrasound probe on the end to allow visualisation of the tumours. The reason the tumours have stopped growing but haven’t become any smaller may be due to the low treatment dose, says Yamamoto. He thinks they may start to shrink as the virus has more time to replicate. As the tumour cells start to break apart and leak their contents, the immune system may also be able to recognise and fight the cancer, says Yamamoto. “The patient’s immune system can realise something is wrong, and then go and attack the tumour,” he says. The hope is that the immune system will also recognise and destroy any tumour cells that have spread to other parts of the body. If so, the treatment could be effective against metastatic pancreatic cancer. mRNA covid vaccines spark immune response that may aid cancer survival An analysis of patient records suggests that mRNA covid-19 vaccines boost the immune response to cancerous tumours when given soon after people start a type of immunotherapy, extending their lives To try to supercharge this natural immune response, Yamamoto and his colleagues are now planning to combine the viral treatment with immunotherapies like checkpoint inhibitors – drugs that block proteins that stop the immune system from attacking the cancer cells – in future clinical trials. Adenoviruses, which cause cold- and flu-like symptoms in their unmodified forms, have a long history of being investigated as potential cancer treatments . In the 1950s, for instance, women with cervical cancer were injected with an unmodified adenovirus in a clinical trial , with partial success. However, it became clear that adenoviruses must be engineered to make them selectively target cancer cells, for safety and efficacy reasons. The only cancer-killing virus that has been approved by the Food and Drug Administration in the US is T-VEC , a genetically modified herpes simplex virus that is injected directly into melanoma tumours, causing the cells to rupture and die. title: Claude solves two open problems in the physics of black holes
body_text: Claude Fable 5.2 solves two open problems in the physics of black holes \ Anthropic Skip to main content News Research Policy Commitments Company Try Claude 01 Introduction Claude solves two open problems in the physics of black holes 01 Introduction 02 A note about Claude’s methods 03 The Hawking-Page transition 04 The modular bootstrap 05 Conclusion Published Nov 17, 2026 Team Science Topics Discovery Agents Reasoning Beneficial Deployments See more... Related articles Science Nov 4, 2026 Investigating vault particles with Claude View more Claude has solved two open problems in theoretical physics. Both concern black holes and the search for a theory of quantum gravity. In the first, it completed a calculation that physicists set up more than 20 years ago, but which had never been solved. Claude’s result showed that a sudden transition associated with the formation of black holes persists even where spacetime no longer has a definite shape. In the second, Claude found the exact limit of the simplest version of a technique used to test candidate theories of quantum gravity. This post explains both findings, first in plain terms and then in more technical detail. The preprints are available here and here . Introduction Modern physics rests on two frameworks: general relativity and quantum mechanics. General relativity describes very large things, like stars; quantum mechanics describes very small things, such as atoms. Both are astonishingly good at predicting how the universe behaves, but they’re mathematically incompatible. Finding a theory that unites them—“quantum gravity”—is one of the field’s biggest goals. Black holes are a natural testing ground, because they’re one of the few areas where both relativity and quantum mechanics matter—they pack immense mass into a very small space. One of the most useful tools for studying quantum gravity is called holographic duality . The real universe has three dimensions of space and one of time, which relativity combines into four-dimensional spacetime. But physicists studying quantum gravity often work with simpler model universes that they can understand in more detail. The basic idea of holographic duality is that some of these theoretical universes can be described in two ways: as a complete universe with gravity and spacetime, and in quantum terms, with no gravity at all, “written” on the universe’s outer boundary. Just as a real hologram encodes a 3D image on a 2D plane, the quantum model encodes all the information of the universe in one dimension fewer (a universe with four dimensions of space, for instance, can be fully described by a quantum theory with three). This lets physicists turn hard questions about gravity into questions about quantum physics, which are sometimes easier to answer. The first problem Claude solved concerns what happens when you heat up one of these theoretical universes. At low temperatures, the universe fills up with a gas of particles. Above a certain temperature, a black hole forms instead. In 1983, Stephen Hawking and Don Page showed that this switch is abrupt: it’s a phase transition, similar to how water suddenly boils at 100°C. But Hawking and Page’s calculation relies on general relativity, which holds only when the universe is vast, compared with the tiny scale at which that description breaks down. As the theoretical universe shrinks toward that smaller scale, spacetime loses any definite shape and becomes blurry, and nobody knows how to do the calculation on the gravity side of the duality. On the quantum side, though, the same situation can be calculated, at least in principle. In 1999, physicists found that there was a phase transition in that regime as well. But they didn’t know whether it was abrupt, like Hawking and Page’s, or smooth. In 2003, a group of physicists set out the calculation that would settle the question , but it was extremely complex and was never completed. Claude did it by running a small research group of copies of itself, in which it worked out almost every piece of the calculation independently and checked its math against known results. It showed that the phase transition is abrupt. The same sudden switch appears at both extremes, suggesting that black hole formation isn’t just a feature of relativity but is actually built into the underlying quantum theory. The second problem concerns a simplified theoretical universe with two dimensions of space instead of three. This universe is straightforward enough to study in detail, but still has black holes and other mysteries similar to those of our own universe. Even in this simpler universe, physicists don’t know how to create a full theory of quantum gravity, so they approach it from the other direction: rather than building a single, correct theory, they try to rule out wrong ones by showing that they are internally inconsistent. This method is called bootstrapping . Since 2009, physicists have used a version of this method to set a ceiling on how heavy the lightest black hole in such a universe could be. Any theory that breaks the ceiling is ruled out, and each lowering of the ceiling narrows the search. Results from numerical calculations hinted at where the best possible ceiling lay, but they couldn’t prove it, and the best proven ceiling was well short of what the numerical results suggested. Claude Fable 5.2 noticed a pattern in the numerical results that physicists had missed and borrowed a method from elsewhere in math and physics to calculate the precise ceiling for the simplest version of this technique and prove that it could not be lowered. It doesn’t identify the correct theory, but it may point physicists in the right direction. Neither result describes our own universe directly, and neither has practical applications, but both contribute to a long-running theoretical effort to understand how quantum mechanics and relativity fit together. In the rest of this post, we explain in more detail what each problem was and what Claude did to solve them. A note about Claude’s methods In August, an Anthropic researcher, Hongbin Chen, was testing Claude’s capabilities as a side project. He asked Claude to draw up a list of interesting open problems in theoretical physics, specifically focusing on black holes and the bootstrap method. Claude came back hours later with 22 candidates, and Hongbin set up separate agents to work on each one; they could read each other’s progress posts and collaborate when working on related problems. The agents ran in the background, with no special setup, for about six weeks. The agents solved the two problems in this post. One was the Hawking-Page phase transition, the question of when a hot gas turns into a black hole. Weeks after one of the agents reached a solution, a physicist, who had independently used Claude to tackle the same problem, shared his result, and a colleague realized that Hongbin’s agent had reached the same answer earlier. The two solutions used different methods, so they were a useful check on each other. The modular bootstrap result came from several agents. The one that was assigned the problem spotted the pattern in the numerical results when surveying the bootstrap literature, and another one—which was working on a mathematically related problem about how tightly spheres can be packed into a high-dimensional space—turned that pattern into a method. It found that this method reproduced a sphere-packing result recently proved by an OpenAI model . Claude then applied the same method to the bootstrap problem, which an earlier Claude agent had tried, and failed, to solve in 61 parallel attempts. Two other agents also independently arrived at the same answer. One half of the final proof, showing that the ceiling can’t be lowered, follows the strategy of the OpenAI proof. In September, the results were formally verified in Lean, a computerized proof checker. Claude then wrote the paper with minimal guidance, and a physicist checked every main result. The Hawking-Page transition To understand the first problem, we need to start with something much more familiar: a walk through New York City. Two equally good routes from Penn Station (A) to the High Line entrance (B). In theory, a quantum particle can take both simultaneously. Imagine that you’re heading from Penn Station to the High Line entrance on West 30th Street and 10th Avenue, and there are two equally good routes. You could walk west along West 33rd Street and turn south, or head south first and then walk west along West 30th Street. Either way, you have to pick one. In the quantum world, though, that’s not true: a particle can take both routes simultaneously. This is most clearly demonstrated in the famous double-slit experiment. In this test, you fire particles, one at a time, at a barrier cut with two narrow slits, and record where, on a screen behind it, each one lands. Each particle lands at a particular point on the screen, as a particle should. But as you fire more of them, they build up a pattern of stripes that would only be possible if each one had passed through both slits, like a wave. The double-slit experiment. When electrons are fired one at a time from a source (A) toward a barrier with two slits, each lands at a single point on the screen. The hits build up a pattern of stripes that is only possible if each one passed through both slits. To predict what a quantum particle will do more generally, physicists have to add up every path it could possibly take, known as its possible histories . Not every history counts equally; some contribute far more to the sum than others. It’s an extravagant and mysterious way to describe how a single particle behaves, but it’s also one of the most successful ideas in physics. This approach, known as the “sum over histories,” is well established for particles and anything made of them. But what about gravity? Einstein showed that gravity is a consequence of curved spacetime: objects with mass bend space and time around them, and we feel that bending as gravity. In a quantum theory of gravity, therefore, what gets summed over is the shape of spacetime itself, rather than just the paths of particles moving through it. To make predictions in a quantum theory of gravity, we would have to add up every shape that the universe could possibly take, and nobody yet knows how to do that. Much of modern quantum gravity research is an attempt to work it out. Hawking and Page found a case where this sum is simple enough to handle but still interesting. To explain Hawking and Page’s work, we need to imagine a different kind of universe, called anti-de Sitter spacetime. Imagine you’re standing in a giant bowl. No matter how hard you throw an object, it will always roll back to the place you threw it from. Our universe isn’t like that. The difference comes down to a quantity called the cosmological constant , which describes the energy of empty space. In our universe, this energy is positive, which makes space expand ever faster. In anti-de Sitter spacetime, the energy is negative, so everything is pulled back to where it started. Hawking and Page chose this universe for their calculation because of how it behaves when it heats up: the bowl keeps heat in so it can stay at a steady temperature. At any given temperature, two histories matter far more than all the others. Here, a “history” means an entire version of the universe: a particular shape of spacetime, along with everything in it. In one, the bowl is filled with an ordinary gas of particles—including gravitons, the particles believed to carry gravity. In the other, it contains a black hole. Whichever contributes more to the sum is, in effect, what we would observe—it “wins.” At low temperatures, the gas history wins, and the universe is full of gas; at high temperatures, the black-hole history wins, and the universe contains a black hole. At one particular temperature—which physicists now call the Hawking-Page temperature—the universe switches abruptly from one to the other. This is the phase transition. Which history wins depends on temperature. Below the Hawking-Page temperature (black line), the universe is filled with a gas of particles, including gravitons; above it, the universe contains a black hole. It’s a rare case where we can see two very different shapes of spacetime competing in the sum over histories, and can say which one wins. This is where the holographic principle enters the story. In the 1970s, Jacob Bekenstein and Hawking found that the amount of information a black hole can hold is proportional to its surface area, not to its volume. That’s very different from ordinary matter, where every bit of volume holds roughly the same amount of information. In the early 1990s, Gerard ’t Hooft and Leonard Susskind proposed that this idea applies to gravity in general—that everything inside a region of space can be fully described by the information on its boundary, just as a flat hologram can display a three-dimensional image. In 1997, Juan Maldacena formalized the idea further. Gravity inside the anti-de Sitter bowl, he argued, is equivalent to an ordinary quantum theory of particles, with no gravity at all, existing on the rim of the bowl (the universe’s outer boundary). These are the gravity side and the quantum side of the duality we described in the introduction—they’re two languages for describing the same underlying reality. In the case Claude studied, the quantum theory on the rim is called N=4 super Yang-Mills theory. It’s related to the theories that describe how particles interact in the real universe, but it has extra symmetries that make it much easier for physicists to work with. (Claude has worked with this theory before, calculating how particles interact within it to a new level of precision .) Since the gravity side predicts two histories competing with each other, the obvious question is: does N=4 super Yang-Mills theory (the quantum side) show the same thing? For now, physicists can analyze this theory in detail only when its particles barely interact with each other, a condition known as weak coupling . This is the opposite end of the spectrum from where Hawking and Page’s gravitational calculation works. Weak coupling on the quantum side corresponds to the small, blurry universe on the gravity side. So there was no guarantee that any of Hawking and Page’s findings would hold there. Remarkably, they do. Bo Sundborg in 1999, and after him Ofer Aharony, Joseph Marsano, Shiraz Minwalla, Kyriakos Papadodimas, and Mark Van Raamsdonk, showed that even at weak coupling, the theory on the rim goes through a transition as it heats up. This is its counterpart of the switch from gas to black hole inside the bowl. But it was still unknown whether this transition is abrupt, like Hawking and Page’s, or smooth and gradual. When particles barely interact, physicists have to calculate how they behave one step at a time. They start with a simplified version of the theory in which particles don’t interact at all. Then they add a series of corrections, each more precise and harder to compute than the last. Physicists call these steps loops . In 2003, Aharony and his colleagues realized that whether the phase transition was an abrupt jump, as Hawking and Page predicted, or gradual, hinged on a single number that appeared only three loops in. Computing that number involves many thousands of terms, known as diagrams—far too many to work through by hand. In 2005, the same group completed the calculation for a simpler cousin of the theory and found an abrupt transition. But the version for N=4 super Yang-Mills, more than 10 times larger, was never completed. The scale of the computational problem, while daunting, wasn’t the only obstacle to completing the calculation. There was a conceptual issue, as well: naively adding up all the parts of the calculation gives an infinite answer, and those infinities have to be tamed carefully to extract a meaningful result. To solve the problem, Claude ran a small research group of agents, all copies of itself. Almost every piece of the calculation was done twice, by agents acting independently. For extra consistency checks, parts of the calculation could also be compared to previous results in the literature. The result Claude found is an abrupt jump as the temperature rises, exactly analogous to what Hawking and Page had found using the sum over spacetime histories. The emerging picture is very simple: the transition is abrupt at both weak and strong coupling—the blurry and the smooth ends, in the gravity description. The most natural possibility is that it stays abrupt everywhere in between. This is a beautiful outcome. It shows that a calculation using the sum over histories in gravity qualitatively matches the behavior of an ordinary quantum theory with no gravity at all. Many open questions remain. The abrupt transition Claude found is very much like the one we see whenever we boil water. One interesting feature of abrupt transitions is that the losing side of the competition can survive for a while: for instance, water can be superheated above 100°C without boiling, as you could see for yourself if you were to put a cup of extremely pure water in the microwave. (But please don’t do this; it’s dangerous, and Anthropic would rather not be responsible for an epidemic of scalded readers.) Something similar happens here. Above the Hawking-Page temperature, the hot gas of gravitons and other particles can survive for a long time in a superheated state. But at a higher temperature it can no longer survive: this is another transition, the Hagedorn transition, which is a characteristic signature of string theory. On the gravity side, that transition has many interesting properties of its own, and it would be valuable to check in detail whether they also appear in N=4 super Yang-Mills theory. Another open question concerns the other possible histories of spacetime. Hawking and Page considered three: one in which their model universe is filled with gas, one that contains a large black hole, and one containing a smaller black hole that never comes to dominate the sum over histories. In principle, there are many more possible histories. As far as anyone knows, none of them ever dominates. But given certain changes to the starting conditions—if the universe is set spinning, for instance, or given a fixed amount of energy or charge—then some of these histories do take over. Working out exactly which ones win, and when, is an interesting problem for the future. The modular bootstrap As we saw earlier, one useful model universe has just two dimensions of space and one of time: it’s called “3D gravity” because it describes gravity in three spacetime dimensions. According to the principle of holographic duality, 3D gravity inside the anti-de Sitter bowl is equivalent to an ordinary quantum theory living on the bowl’s rim. As a model, 3D gravity is much simpler than the real thing, but it still allows for black holes and many of the same mysteries. It provides a useful laboratory for studying the sum over spacetime histories. It’s also a good place to test the idea that spacetime isn’t a basic ingredient of the universe, but emerges from something deeper. In general relativity, black holes look smooth. But in quantum gravity, if you zoom in to the smallest scales—the Planck length, around 10 -35 meters, where quantum effects on gravity become impossible to ignore—black holes are made of an enormous number of tiny, individual building blocks. Physicists believe the same is true in our own, four-dimensional universe, but the 3D version is much easier to analyze with holographic duality. Claude’s results build on a method called the bootstrap, a general strategy for solving quantum theories. Counterintuitively, the strategy doesn’t try to solve a theory directly. For 3D gravity, that isn’t even possible, because nobody knows how to define the theory precisely. Instead, the bootstrap rules theories out by showing that they contradict themselves. Physicists scan over all possible quantum theories and try to eliminate them one by one. Remarkably, in many cases this method makes it possible to pinpoint a single quantum theory and calculate precisely how it behaves. The requirements of relativity and quantum mechanics are so demanding, and so delicately balanced, that together they rule out every alternative. In 2012, the bootstrap was used to solve a quantum field theory called the 3D critical Ising model , a simple model of magnetism that also describes water at the point where liquid and vapor become indistinguishable. Since then, it has been applied to many different quantum systems. In 2009, Simeon Hellerman introduced a technique called the modular bootstrap , which applies the bootstrap method to 3D gravity. Its goal is to rule out inconsistent theories of quantum gravity in three spacetime dimensions. By combining it with other bootstrap methods, physicists hope to eventually eliminate every inconsistent theory. Whatever is left must be consistent. There could be no consistent theories, or just one, or whole families of them. Any of these outcomes would be interesting, because it would help us understand what spacetime looks like at the Planck scale in this simplified universe, and give us hints about the Planck scale in our own. Here’s how the modular bootstrap works. 3D gravity in anti-de Sitter spacetime has a quantity called the central charge (c), which roughly counts how many microscopic building blocks the universe is made of. When general relativity holds, c is very large, because large black holes contain an enormous number of building blocks. A second quantity, M₁, is the mass of the lightest black hole. To run the bootstrap, physicists scan over every possible theory, with every possible value of c and M₁, and look for inconsistencies. To understand how that search works, we need to go back to the sum over spacetime histories. In 3D gravity, that means adding up different 3D shapes of spacetime. They can be simple, like a ball, or more complicated, like the donut and two-holed donut in the figure below. The spacetime is the inside of the shape—the dough inside the donut. Its surface, like the rim of the bowl in the earlier section, is where the quantum theory is “written,” in one fewer dimension. Three possible shapes of spacetime in 3D gravity: a ball, a donut (or torus), and a two-holed donut. The spacetime is the inside of each shape, and the quantum theory is “written” on its surface. The modular bootstrap starts with a spacetime shaped like an ordinary, one-holed donut, or torus . There are two different ways to interpret this shape, depending on which direction we call “time” and which we call “space.” In the first, the long direction around the hole is time and the other, shorter loop, around the tube, is space. In the second, they’re swapped: the long loop is space and the shorter loop is time. Two ways to interpret the same donut-shaped spacetime. (left) Time runs the long way around the hole, and space is represented by the shorter loop; (right) space runs the long way around, and time is represented by the shorter loop. In calculations like these, the length of the time loop sets the temperature: the shorter the loop, the hotter the universe. So swapping the two loops trades a cold universe for a hot one. The two interpretations correspond to the two competing histories that Hawking and Page studied. In 3D gravity there are no gravitons, but there is a transition similar to the one that Claude analyzed in N=4 super Yang-Mills theory. Now we come to the crucial step. In relativity, space and time are on an equal footing. So it can’t matter which loop we label space and which we label time. As far as relativity is concerned, the two interpretations are equivalent, and the physics must be the same for every possible experiment. Quantum mechanics, however, treats time differently from space. To calculate anything, you pick a direction to call time and track how the system evolves along it. So, when we calculate observable quantities in quantum gravity, the two interpretations of the donut lead to calculations that look very different. But in relativity, it doesn’t matter which loop is called time, so the two calculations have to give exactly the same answer. If we knew the theory of 3D quantum gravity, we could do both calculations and confirm that they match. We don’t, but with the bootstrap method, that isn’t a problem. Physicists scan over the possible values of c (the number of building blocks) and M₁ (the mass of the lightest black hole). For each pair of values, they try to prove that the theory would be inconsistent—that the two calculations on the donut couldn’t possibly give the same answer. This involves searching for a special mathematical object called a bootstrap functional. If physicists find one, then the theory is inconsistent, and those values are ruled out. The hope, supported by the bootstrap’s successes elsewhere, is that combining this approach with other bootstrap methods will eventually rule out most possible theories of 3D quantum gravity. The theories left standing would be the only ones consistent with both gravity and quantum mechanics. Physicists could then use them to explore some of the biggest questions in quantum gravity: is there only one theory? Does it rely on string theory, or are there alternatives? What are black holes made of at the microscopic level, and how do we sum over spacetime histories? This strategy can work in principle, but it’s very difficult in practice, because bootstrap functionals are hard to find. What matters for quantum gravity is what happens when c is large—but the larger c gets, the harder the search becomes. In the original paper on the modular bootstrap, Hellerman proved that in any consistent theory of 3D gravity, M₁ can be no larger than c/6, up to small corrections. Theories with a heavier lightest black hole can’t possibly be consistent with both gravity and quantum mechanics. The goal of the modular bootstrap is to push this ceiling as low as possible, pinning down how heavy the lightest black hole can be. Physicists write the ceiling as M₁ ≤ c/Λ. A lower ceiling means a larger number Λ. The results below, including Claude’s, concern the simplest and most-studied version of the method, which ignores how the black holes spin. Over the past 15 years, physicists have worked to lower the ceiling and pin down the theory as tightly as possible. There are two ways to do this. One is analytical—building a bootstrap functional by hand, with pen-and-paper mathematics. The other is numerical—using computers to search for functionals and optimize them. The results of these numerical calculations suggested that the modular bootstrap could push the ceiling down to about c/9.1. But these calculations get harder as c grows, so they couldn’t settle the question. On the analytical side, Tom Hartman, Dalimil Mazáč, and Leonardo Rastelli proved a ceiling of c/8.5, but because this was higher than the numerical results had suggested, this clearly wasn’t the best the modular bootstrap could do. Since then, just how tightly the modular bootstrap can constrain quantum gravity has remained an open question. Claude set about solving the problem by running numerical experiments and reproducing results from the literature. In doing so, it noticed a pattern that physicists had so far missed, involving the way the numerical ceiling shifted slightly as c grew. Based on that pattern, Claude developed a hypothesis about the behavior of the bootstrap functional, using a mathematical tool called a spectral curve . Spectral curves are well known in other areas of mathematics and physics, but had never been applied to this problem. Claude found the spectral curve that governs the modular bootstrap at large values of c. It then used it to prove that the lightest black hole in 3D quantum gravity can be no heavier than c/Λ, where Λ is given by an exact formula and is approximately 9.1266. It also proved that this ceiling is optimal: it’s the lowest this version of the modular bootstrap can ever go. Claude delivered the solution across four research notes, which it later merged into a single paper. This is one of the first times the bootstrap has been used to derive an exact result in the regime of quantum gravity where black holes matter. It also shows that this version of the method can’t, on its own, push the ceiling down to c/12, the mass at which black holes first appear; that will take other ingredients. Although it doesn’t pin down the theory of quantum gravity in three dimensions by itself, it provides a starting point and helps to narrow the search. Conclusion These two results show Claude doing two very different kinds of research. The first is a known calculation that physicists had set aside for two decades, because the work was too long and error-prone to complete by hand. The second required a new idea: spotting a pattern others had missed and bringing in a mathematical tool from another area of physics. Both were carried out largely autonomously. Neither result settles the question of quantum gravity, or even comes close to doing so, but each pushes physics forward in a longstanding area of research. Read the black hole phase transition paper here , and the modular bootstrap paper here . title: Garage Door Spam
body_text: Garage Door Spam – Harrison Was Here Harrison Was Here About Posts RSS Harrison Photography Garage Door Spam 16 Nov, 2026 In the beginning, my garage door opener worked fine. When the door opened or closed, I would get a notification. If I'm away from home and the door opens, something weird is going down. The "myQ" app generally worked although it was encrusted with ads: I continued using it because I trusted that notifications were meaningful... ...until recently (October 2026): This is un-fucking-acceptable. As in, absolutely fucking not. The manufacturer (Chamberlain) cut off third-party access to its APIs (via myQ) in late 2023. In response, I purchased a pair of ratgdo32 devices to opt out of the bullshit. ratgdo is a WiFi control board for your garage door opener that works over your local network using ESP Home or HomeKit The device is a ~$62 board from ratcloud llc running open-source firmware that wires to the opener's existing terminals and speaks LiftMaster's Security+ 2.0 protocol locally. These were easy enough to hook up. I won't reproduce the instructions here. The bundle included six black wires, an auxiliary harness I didn’t need. My router hands each board a fixed address at 192.168.0.192 and 192.168.0.245. Apple's HomeKit just worked and I'm able to control them with voice commands: “Hey Siri, open Door 1” The devices have their own web interface: When I was growing up, my father wired a mercury switch onto our garage door that lit up a light in the hallway when we'd left the garage door open. This was a valuable signal that helped our family avoid accidentally leaving the door open overnight. Since the ratgdo32 has a JSON status endpoint, I was able to rebuild Dad's solution in software with Slack: The script runs at night checking for an open door: */10 21 -23,0-5 * * * garage-watch The repo maintainer made my day when I submitted a tiny pull request : "Simple and useful. Happy to merge this. Thank you." Both boards are now reachable over my Tailscale network, so my monitoring software can load /healthcheck. This required a custom route: /Applications/Tailscale.app/Contents/MacOS/Tailscale set \ --advertise-routes = 192 .168.0.192/32,192.168.0.245/32 After approving the route, my monitoring software can verify the hardware is working. Everything runs locally with no cloud, and notifications now say who opened the door which myQ never did. To anyone at Chamberlain responsible for myQ, I offer my sincerest Fuck You. title: UK government forced to admit it issued Apple a secret encryption order
body_text: UK Government Forced to Admit It Issued Apple a Secret Encryption Order Home Field Notes Sightings About Contact Donate Fellow Anorak Search Sign in Subscribe Field Notes UK Government Forced to Admit It Issued Apple a Secret Encryption Order The Investigatory Powers Tribunal has rejected the UK government’s attempt to keep its order secret, marking a significant victory for transparency. MacAnorak 19 Nov 2026 5 min Share There's something pretty extraordinary about a government being able to demand changes to the security of devices used by millions of people, prevent a company that makes those devices from discussing those demands, and then refuse to even acknowledge that the demands exist at all. That has been the sordid situation surrounding the UK governement's ongoing dispute with Apple over encrypted iCloud data. Up until today, the UK government's position has essentially been that it would neither confirm nor deny whether it issued Apple with a Technical Capability Notice (TCN). These are secret orders issued under Section 253 of the Investigatory Powers Act 2016 , which gives the UK government powers to require technology companies to make changes to their services to facilitate the exercise of investigatory powers. Today, the Investigatory Powers Tribunal has ruled that the UK government must acknowledge that it issued Apple with such a notice . This is a big deal. Whilst it doesn't mean we suddenly know everything the UK government wants Apple to do, the government's attempt to keep even the existence of the order secret has now suffered a major defeat. I covered the background to this extensively in my piece, Two-Tier Encryption in the UK . The story goes back to February 2025 when the Washington Post exposed that the government had ordered Apple to provide ‘backdoor’ access to encrypted iCloud data, belonging not just to users in the UK, but around the world. The order was reportedly issued in January 2025 under the Investigatory Powers Act — the centrepiece of the UK’s modern surveillance law. Rather than weaken its security provisions, Apple took the quite extraordinary step of withdrawing Advanced Data Protection (ADP) from new UK users. ADP is an optional feature that extends end-to-end encryption to additional categories of iCloud data — when enabled, even Apple can't decrypt the protected information. [1] Apple subsequently made clear that it would not build a backdoor or a master key into any of its products or services . They stated this without publicly referencing the Technical Capability Notice, as they were forbidden from doing so. The original order's scope extended beyond British users — it potentially implicated the encrypted data of Apple's customers all around the world, including the United States. Following months of diplomatic wrangling involving the Trump administration, the UK government withdrew that original notice , but that wasn't the end of it. The UK government issued a second Technical Capability Notice , this time reportedly restricted to British users. Apple's original legal challenge was subsequently dismissed following with the withdrawal of the first notice, so the company launched a fresh legal challenge in 2026 . The difficulty for the UK government has always been that the existence of the original order was already widely reported. The Washington Post had published its exposé, and many other news outlets subsequently reported on it. The UK government nevertheless maintained its position of neither confirming nor denying the existence of individual TCNs. At a hearing at the Investigatory Powers Tribunal on 17 September this year, lawyers representing civil rights organisations Liberty and Privacy International challenged that position. Ben Jaffey KC, representing the organisations, argued that the UK government's insistence on maintaining secrecy had become increasingly difficult to justify. Jaffey compared the secrecy order to the “emperor’s new clothes… and brings the administration of justice into disrepute” . The existence of the order was already public knowledge and continuing to pretend otherwise was obstructing the proper consideration of the legal challenge. The UK government disagreed, arguing that abandoning its neither-confirm-nor-deny policy could damage national security by assisting hostile actors in building a picture of which companies were subject to such notices. Today the tribunal rejected that argument. As Reuters reports , the Tribunal concluded: “The respondent has not established that it would be damaging to national security to reveal in these proceedings, as is the case, that the respondent has given Apple a Technical Capability Notice.” The Tribunal hasn't ruled that the underlying order was unlawful; it hasn't made a determination whether the UK government can legitimately require Apple to make changes to its encryption systems; it hasn't disclosed the precise technical requirements of the notice. But the government has lost an important argument about keeping the proceedings secret. In my Two-Tier Encryption in the UK piece, I used the idea of “Alice and Bill”, two fictional people living in the UK, both using identical iPhones and both paying for iCloud, to illustrate a fundamental problem that had arisen from the dispute between Apple and the UK government. Alice had enabled Advanced Data Protection before Apple withdrew the feature for new UK users , Bill hadn't. Alice continued to benefit from Apple's strongest available iCloud encryption protections, Bill couldn't even enable them. The result was a peculiar situation in which two customers using the same service had materially different levels of protection. Because Apple withdrew ADP for new UK users in February 2025, existing users who had already enabled the feature have not since been required to turn it off — Apple’s security documentation says its servers can’t modify the ADP setting, or roll it back on a user’s behalf. This has created a ‘two-tier’ system of protection based on when somebody enabled a particular security feature. Our iCloud accounts contain a lot of private information — photos, documents, backups, other material that most of us reasonably expect to remain fully private. Encryption exists so that the service provider shouldn't have the ability to access that information. If a government can compel a technology company to undermine its own protections, the consequences deserve considerably more scrutiny than secret exchanges between officials and lawyers. Today's ruling makes scrutiny more possible. The Investigatory Powers Act doesn't only exist to regulate Apple's relationship with the UK government. Its provisions establish powers that can potentially be applied to other communications and technology providers. What happens when these powers are used against another company? What happens when the next notice concerns a different service or a different encryption system, or a different category of personal information? How would customers even know about it anyway? That's one of the most troubling aspects of the TCN regime - the secrecy . Companies receiving TCNs can be legally prohibited from disclosing that they have received them. The UK government’s position, of course, is that these powers are necessary to support lawful investigations and protect public safety. Liberty and Privacy International have thankfully been challenging the lawfulness, necessity and secrecy of this regime. They argue it lacks adequate safeguards and threatens fundamental rights. Apple is pursuing its own legal challenge. These cases are now proceeding alongside one another with a substantive hearing expected sometime in 2027. Today's decision doesn't resolve the wider questions, but it does remove one obstacle to examining the dispute in public. Apple has consistently argued that it will not build ‘backdoors’ into its products. The UK government, meanwhile, has relied on powers that allow it to issue orders to technology companies in secret. For now, the legal process has at least established that the government issued this particular order, but my guess is that we're still some distance from fully understanding what it actually wants Apple to do, and whether it has the legal authority to demand it. I will continue to follow this one very closely indeed. Advanced Data Protection is not synonymous with all iCloud data encryption. Apple already encrypts various categories of iCloud information without ADP, but some of those categories remain accessible to Apple and can potentially be provided in response to valid legal demands. ADP changes that arrangement by extending end-to-end encryption to additional categories of data. ↩︎ Read next A Wolf at the Door: Apple Is Rethinking Mac Permissions for the Age of AI Agents Following the furore surrounding Meta’s Muse and the appetite of AI agents for access to our personal data, Apple promised to tighten macOS privacy controls. Now we know what it’s planning. MacAnorak 18 Nov 2026 The MacBook Pro’s OLED PWM Problem: When a ‘Better’ Display Becomes Worse to Use Apple has made a spectacular display. But spectacular isn’t the same as comfortable, and the people discovering that distinction deserve to be heard. MacAnorak 14 Nov 2026 Some M5 Macs Are Struggling With High-Refresh-Rate Displays. Is Apple’s Graphics Pipeline Broken? What began as a scrolling problem with Apple’s Studio Display XDR is now being reported across multiple M5 Macs and external displays. Users report that their M6 machines don’t suffer from the same problems. MacAnorak 08 Nov 2026 Subscribe to MacAnorak Become a Fellow Anorak and get my Field Notes directly delivered to your inbox. title: An Oregon library ditched Dewey Decimal and got people excited about books again
Making 8-page foldable zines from a single A4 sheet in the browser
body_text: Paper, folds, and what’s new in fanzines.app – Wilson Tovar (krthr) Wilson Tovar (krthr) home • blog • poesía • photography • say hi 👋 Paper, folds, and what’s new in fanzines.app 19 Nov, 2026 A few months ago, I wrote about how I started giving away zines to my friends, my family, and people at work. If you've never made one, the fold is simple. Take a single A4 sheet of paper, fold it in half three times, open it back up, and cut along the center crease with scissors. Fold the sheet into a cross and close it, and you have an 8-page booklet with no staples or glue. I fill mine with whatever I feel like printing: photos, poems, or notes. Why fanzines.app exists The part I never liked was laying out the flat sheet on the computer before printing. Because the A4 paper folds back on itself, the pages sit in a strange order and the top row has to be upside down: ┌─────────┬─────────┬─────────┬─────────┐ │ 6 │ 5 │ 4 │ 3 │ ← upside down (180°) ├─────────┼─────────┼─────────┼─────────┤ │ Back │ Cover │ 1 │ 2 │ ← right-side up └─────────┴─────────┴─────────┴─────────┘ I got tired of rotating pictures and double-checking columns in Photoshop every time I wanted to print a new zine, so I built fanzines.app . In the browser, you lay out each page right-side up with photos and text. When you export, the app places all 8 panels onto the A4 grid with the top row rotated 180 degrees and generates a 300 DPI PDF. Everything stays local in the browser; no photos are uploaded to a server. Over the last few days, I rebuilt the editor around the things that kept getting in my way when I sat down to make a zine. Fixing how pages are paired In the first version, the sidebar listed the 8 pages in a plain two-column grid. It paired the Front Cover with Page 1, Page 2 with Page 3, Page 4 with Page 5, and Page 6 with the Back Cover. It looked tidy on screen, but it didn't match the physical booklet. When you hold a folded zine, the front cover sits alone on the right. Open it and Page 1 faces Page 2 across the fold, then 3 faces 4, 5 faces 6, and the back cover ends up alone on the left. The sidebar now groups the page thumbnails into those real spreads, in reading order. I also added a Spread view on the canvas. While you're editing Page 1, Page 2 sits beside it at lower opacity so you can check how the two facing pages sit together before printing. Clicking the dimmed page switches straight to editing it. Smaller changes that make the editor less fussy When I make a photo zine, I usually start with a folder of 8 photos already picked out. Now you can drag the whole batch onto the editor window, and the sidebar highlights which pages will take each photo in reading order before you drop them. I changed the side panel too. Early on, clicking a photo opened four coordinate inputs ( X , Y , Width , Height ). I rarely needed to type coordinates; mostly I wanted a photo to fill the page, fit inside the margins, or sit centered. Fill, Fit, and Center now sit at the top of the inspector and in a small toolbar above the selection. The exact fields are still in a collapsible section at the bottom, now in millimeters (for the 74.25 × 105 mm folded panel) and points for text. Before downloading the PDF, a Review step shows the full unfolded A4 sheet with toggles for cut/fold lines and a 5 mm safe margin. Most home printers clip a few millimeters around the edge of an A4 sheet, so the safe margin scales the layout to about 95% to keep the covers intact. A couple of other additions: the editor now works on phone screens (one page at a time with a thumbnail strip along the bottom), and the site is available in English as well as Spanish . Changing the language keeps your current pages. Thanks for reading, Wil You can create your own zine in English or Spanish at fanzines.app #tech #zines Toast this post   Subscribe to my blog via email or RSS feed . Powered by Bear ʕ•ᴥ•ʔ

title: What's New in PHP 8.6
body_text: PHP: PHP 8.6 Release Announcement Downloads Documentation Get Involved Help English Русский 简体中文 Nederlands Français Italiano Brazilian Portuguese 日本語 Search docs PHP 8.6.0 Released! Getting Started Introduction A simple tutorial Language Reference Basic syntax Types Variables Constants Expressions Operators Control Structures Functions Classes and Objects Namespaces Enumerations Error Handling Fibers Generators Attributes References Explained Predefined Variables Predefined Exceptions Predefined Interfaces and Classes Predefined Attributes Context options and parameters Supported Protocols and Wrappers Security Introduction General considerations Installed as CGI binary Installed as an Apache module Session Security Filesystem Security Database Security Error Reporting User Submitted Data Hiding PHP Keeping Current Features HTTP authentication with PHP Cookies Sessions Handling file uploads Using remote files Connection handling Persistent Database Connections Command line usage Garbage Collection DTrace Dynamic Tracing Function Reference Affecting PHP's Behaviour Audio Formats Manipulation Authentication Services Command Line Specific Extensions Compression and Archive Extensions Cryptography Extensions Database Extensions Date and Time Related Extensions File System Related Extensions Human Language and Character Encoding Support Image Processing and Generation Mail Related Extensions Mathematical Extensions Non-Text MIME Output Process Control Extensions Other Basic Extensions Other Services Search Engine Extensions Server Specific Extensions Session Extensions Text Processing Variable and Type Related Extensions Web Services Windows Only Extensions XML Manipulation GUI Extensions Keyboard Shortcuts ? This help j Next menu item k Previous menu item g p Previous man page g n Next man page G Scroll to bottom g g Scroll to top g h Goto homepage g s Goto search (current page) / Focus search box Released November 19, 2026 Faster, Safer, More Powerful. PHP 8.6 is a major update of the PHP language , with new features including Partial Function Application , a new Duration class, a Polling API , and a new clamp() function What's new in 8.6 Upgrade to PHP 8.6 Key Features in PHP 8.6 More expressive code , stronger types , and scalable I/O . Partial Function Application Allows some of a function's arguments to be provided in advance, returning a Closure that accepts the rest. New \Time\Duration Class The Duration class represents elapsed time as measured by a stopwatch. Polling API Scalable I/O multiplexing using epoll, kqueue, and other native mechanisms, available to event loop libraries like ReactPHP and AMPHP. New clamp() Function Ensures that a given value (numeric or otherwise) falls within a specified range. New SortDirection Enum A standard, type-safe way to express sort order that can be shared across libraries. Readonly Property Defaults Allows readonly properties to declare default values, so fixed values no longer have to be assigned in the constructor. Partial Function Application Allows some of a function's arguments to be provided in advance, using ? and ... placeholders for the rest. The result is a Closure, and the function is only called once the remaining arguments are passed to it. PHP 8.5 and older $versions = [ '8.4' , '8.5' , '8.6' , '8.7' , '9.0' ]; $supportsPfa = array_filter ( $versions , fn ( $version ) => version_compare ( $version , '8.6' , '>=' ), ); PHP 8.6 NEW RFC ↗ Doc ↗ $versions = [ '8.4' , '8.5' , '8.6' , '8.7' , '9.0' ]; $supportsPfa = array_filter ( $versions , version_compare (?, '8.6' , '>=' ), ); New \Time\Duration Class The Duration class represents elapsed time as measured by a stopwatch. Its representation is independent of any time and timezone and can represent a range of more than 250 years with nanosecond precision. This makes it well-suited to represent timeouts or benchmark timings in an expressive way. PHP 8.5 and older /** * All delays are in microseconds. */ function backoff ( int $baseDelay , int $step , int $attempt , ): void { $delay = $baseDelay + ( $step * ( 2 ** $attempt )); // Wait at most 30 seconds. usleep ( min ( $delay , 30_000_000 )); } // 1 second base delay, plus 100 milliseconds // doubling with each attempt. backoff ( 1_000_000 , 100_000 , $attempt ); PHP 8.6 NEW RFC ↗ Doc ↗ use Time\Duration ; function backoff ( Duration $baseDelay , Duration $step , int $attempt , ): void { $delay = $baseDelay -> add ( $step -> multiplyBy ( 2 ** $attempt )); // Durations are comparable, so min() works directly. $delay = min ( $delay , Duration :: fromSeconds ( 30 )); time_nanosleep ( $delay -> seconds , $delay -> nanoseconds ); } backoff ( Duration :: fromSeconds ( 1 ), Duration :: fromMilliseconds ( 100 ), $attempt , ); // Preconfigure the delays using Partial Function Application. $waitBeforeRetry = backoff ( Duration :: fromSeconds ( 1 ), Duration :: fromMilliseconds ( 100 ), attempt : ?, ); $waitBeforeRetry ( $attempt ); Polling API The new Io\Poll API efficiently monitors many streams at once using the best mechanism available on each platform (epoll, kqueue, event ports, or WSAPoll), without the scalability limits of stream_select() . It is designed as a common foundation that event loop libraries such as ReactPHP and AMPHP can build on. PHP 8.5 and older $server = stream_socket_server ( 'tcp://0.0.0.0:8080' ); $clients = []; while ( true ) { $read = [ $server , ... $clients ]; $write = $except = null ; // Based on select(), which typically can't handle // more than 1024 connections stream_select ( $read , $write , $except , null ); foreach ( $read as $stream ) { if ( $stream === $server ) { $clients [] = stream_socket_accept ( $server ); continue; } $data = fread ( $stream , 8192 ); if ( $data === '' || $data === false ) { $key = array_search ( $stream , $clients , true ); unset( $clients [ $key ]); fclose ( $stream ); } else { fwrite ( $stream , $data ); } } } PHP 8.6 NEW RFC ↗ use Io\Poll \{ Context , Event }; $server = stream_socket_server ( 'tcp://0.0.0.0:8080' ); // Automatically uses epoll, kqueue, event ports, or WSAPoll $poll = new Context (); $poll -> add (new StreamPollHandle ( $server ), [ Event :: Read ]); while ( true ) { foreach ( $poll -> wait () as $watcher ) { $stream = $watcher -> getHandle ()-> getStream (); if ( $stream === $server ) { $client = stream_socket_accept ( $server ); $poll -> add ( new StreamPollHandle ( $client ), [ Event :: Read ], ); continue; } $data = fread ( $stream , 8192 ); if ( $data === '' || $data === false ) { $watcher -> remove (); fclose ( $stream ); } else { fwrite ( $stream , $data ); } } } Stream Error Handling Stream operations can now be configured to throw a StreamException or to fail silently instead of emitting warnings. Errors are reported as structured StreamError objects with a StreamErrorCode enum case, the wrapper name, and the affected path or URL, and can also be retrieved later with stream_last_errors() or passed to a custom error handler. PHP 8.5 and older $config = @ file_get_contents ( '/etc/app/config.json' ); if ( $config === false ) { // Only an unstructured message string is available $error = error_get_last (); log_error ( $error [ 'message' ]); } PHP 8.6 NEW RFC ↗ Doc ↗ $context = stream_context_create ([ 'stream' => [ 'error_mode' => StreamErrorMode :: Exception , ], ]); try { $config = file_get_contents ( '/etc/app/config.json' , context : $context , ); } catch ( StreamException $e ) { foreach ( $e -> getErrors () as $error ) { // $error->code is a StreamErrorCode enum case log_error ( $error -> code -> name , $error -> message , $error -> wrapperName , ); } } New clamp() Function Ensures that a given value (numeric or otherwise) falls within a specified range. Otherwise, the nearest boundary value is returned. PHP 8.5 and older var_dump ( max ( 0 , min (- 10 , 100 ))); // int(0) var_dump ( max ( 0 , min ( 50 , 100 ))); // int(50) var_dump ( max ( 0 , min ( 110 , 100 ))); // int(100) PHP 8.6 NEW RFC ↗ Doc ↗ var_dump ( clamp (- 10 , 0 , 100 )); // int(0) var_dump ( clamp ( 50 , 0 , 100 )); // int(50) var_dump ( clamp ( 110 , 0 , 100 )); // int(100) // Any comparable value works with clamp(). This // includes the new Duration class. var_dump ( clamp ( \Time\Duration :: fromSeconds ( 30 ), min : \Time\Duration :: fromMinutes ( 1 ), max : \Time\Duration :: fromMinutes ( 10 ), )-> seconds ); // int(60) New SortDirection Enum The SortDirection enum provides a shared, type-safe way to express sort order with its Ascending and Descending cases. Previously, every library had to define its own way of representing sort direction, resulting in a mix of incompatible integers, strings, booleans, and custom enums. Since SortDirection is built into PHP, libraries can accept it in their public APIs without needing adapter code. Learn more about this feature in The PHP Foundation’s blog . PHP 8.5 and older class QueryBuilder { private array $orderBy = []; public function orderBy ( string $column , int $direction = SORT_ASC , ): static { $this -> orderBy [] = $column . ' ' . match ( $direction ) { SORT_ASC => 'ASC' , SORT_DESC => 'DESC' , }; return $this ; } } $qb -> orderBy ( 'name' , SORT_DESC ); $qb -> orderBy ( 'name' , SORT_STRING ); // Accepted by the signature, then fails inside the method: // UnhandledMatchError: Unhandled match case 2 PHP 8.6 NEW RFC ↗ Doc ↗ class QueryBuilder { private array $orderBy = []; public function orderBy ( string $column , SortDirection $direction = SortDirection :: Ascending , ): static { $this -> orderBy [] = $column . ' ' . match ( $direction ) { SortDirection :: Ascending => 'ASC' , SortDirection :: Descending => 'DESC' , }; return $this ; } } $qb -> orderBy ( 'name' , SortDirection :: Descending ); $qb -> orderBy ( 'name' , SORT_STRING ); // TypeError: QueryBuilder::orderBy(): Argument #2 ($direction) // must be of type SortDirection, int given DocComments for Function Parameters Function and method parameters can now have their own DocComments, which are available via the new ReflectionParameter::getDocComment() method. This allows each parameter to be documented right next to its declaration, without repeating its name and type in a @param tag. PHP 8.5 and older class DB { /** * Returns up to $limit items matching the $query. * * @param string $query Terms to search * @param int $limit Maximum number of results */ public function search ( string $query , int $limit = 10 ): array { return []; } } // Parameter descriptions can only be extracted // by parsing the function's DocComment. PHP 8.6 NEW RFC ↗ class DB { /** * Returns up to $limit items matching the $query. */ public function search ( /** Terms to search */ string $query , /** Maximum number of results */ int $limit = 10 , ): array { return []; } } var_dump ( new ReflectionParameter ([ DB ::class, 'search' ], 'query' ) -> getDocComment (), ); // string(22) "/** Terms to search */" New ReflectionProperty::isReadable() and ReflectionProperty::isWritable() Methods With readonly properties, asymmetric visibility, and property hooks, checking whether a property is public is no longer enough to know whether it can be read or written. The new methods answer this directly for a given scope, and optionally for a specific object, taking into account visibility, initialization state, hooks, and magic methods. PHP 8.6 NEW RFC ↗ Doc ↗ class NewsEntry { public string $title = 'PHP 8.6 released!' ; public private(set) string $slug = 'php-86-released' ; } $entry = new NewsEntry (); foreach ([ 'title' , 'slug' ] as $item ) { $property = new ReflectionProperty ( NewsEntry ::class, $item ); printf ( "%s: isReadable=%s isWritable=%s\n" , $item , $property -> isReadable ( null , $entry ) ? 'yes' : 'no' , $property -> isWritable ( null , $entry ) ? 'yes' : 'no' , ); } // title: isReadable=yes isWritable=yes // slug: isReadable=yes isWritable=no Readonly Property Defaults Instance readonly properties, including those in readonly classes, can now declare a default value. This makes it simple to implement get-only interface properties with fixed values, which previously required assigning them in a constructor. The default counts as the property's initialization, so the constructor cannot overwrite it. PHP 8.5 and older interface Rule { public string $parser { get ; } } final readonly class SlugRule implements Rule { public string $parser ; public function __construct () { $this -> parser = SlugParser ::class; } } PHP 8.6 NEW RFC ↗ Doc ↗ interface Rule { public string $parser { get ; } } final readonly class SlugRule implements Rule { public string $parser = SlugParser ::class; } Additional Features and Improvements The #[\Override] attribute can now be applied to class constants and enum cases. Enums can now implement the __debugInfo() magic method. Properties of objects stored in constants can now be modified directly, e.g. Config::DEFAULTS->timeout = 30 . New Uri\Rfc3986\UriBuilder and Uri\WhatWg\UrlBuilder classes build URIs from their components, along with new methods for detecting URI and host types and a Uri\WhatWg\url_percent_encode() function. The Sodium extension adds post-quantum key encapsulation (X-Wing and ML-KEM-768), IP address encryption, and the SHAKE and TurboSHAKE extendable-output functions. TLS streams now support session resumption, external pre-shared keys, and TLS 1.3 early data (0-RTT). New mysqli::quote_string() method escapes a string and wraps it in quotes, matching PDO::quote() . pack() and unpack() now accept the < and > endianness modifiers on integer and float format codes. JSON error messages now include the location of the error in the input. The new error_include_args INI setting consistently includes function arguments in error messages. New grapheme_strrev() function reverses strings by grapheme cluster, and the new IntlNumberRangeFormatter class formats ranges of numbers. New ZipArchive::openString() and ZipArchive::closeString() methods work with in-memory archives. Performance improvements include compiling array_map() with first-class callable or partial application callbacks into loops, faster printf() calls, caching of stateless closures, and faster JSON encoding. Deprecations and Backward Compatibility Breaks Using return inside a finally block is now deprecated, as it silently discards exceptions and overrides values returned from the try or catch block. Returning a value from __construct() or __destruct() is now deprecated, as is making them generators. Declaring a nullable return type for __debugInfo() is also deprecated. Using let or is as the name of a class, function, or constant is now deprecated. Using _ as a constant name, namespace as a class constant name, or readonly as a function name is also deprecated. The mbstring regular expression functions such as mb_ereg() and mb_split() have been deprecated, as the underlying Oniguruma library is no longer maintained. PCRE functions with the u modifier can be used instead. The is_double() , is_long() , is_integer() , and doubleval() aliases have been deprecated. Use is_float() , is_int() , and floatval() instead. spl_object_hash() has been deprecated in favor of spl_object_id() , and spl_classes() in favor of ReflectionExtension::getClassNames() . Passing an object where an array is expected to array_walk() , array_walk_recursive() , http_build_query() , mb_convert_variables() , and compression functions and filters is now deprecated. Use get_object_vars() to convert the object first. strcoll() and the SORT_LOCALE_STRING sort flag have been deprecated. Use the Collator class from the intl extension instead. Passing a third argument to define() is now deprecated, as is calling is_a() or is_subclass_of() with a class name string when $allow_string is false . Using more than 16 filters in a php://filter URL without setting the filter.max_filter_count context option is now deprecated. Sessions are now more secure by default: session.use_strict_mode and session.cookie_httponly are enabled, and session.cookie_samesite is set to Lax . Custom session handlers that do not implement both create_sid() and validateId() are now deprecated. The metaphone() , mysqli_get_charset() , and mysqli_stmt_init() functions are now deprecated, along with the CSV methods of SplFileObject and the sorting, flag, and serialization methods of ArrayIterator . trim() , ltrim() , and rtrim() now also strip form feed ( \f ) characters by default. fclose() , file_put_contents() , and copy() now return false when flushing or closing the stream fails, instead of silently ignoring the failure. Many functions now throw a ValueError for out-of-range values, invalid flags, or strings containing NUL bytes, instead of silently truncating or ignoring them. Better syntax, improved performance and type safety. Upgrade to PHP 8.6 The full list of changes is recorded in the ChangeLog . Please consult the migration guide for a detailed list of new features and backward-incompatible changes. PHP is developed and maintained by a global community of contributors. The PHP Foundation helps fund this work. If PHP is part of your business or projects, consider sponsoring the Foundation. title: Do not buy RAM, compress
body_text: Do not buy RAM, compress! | Therry van Neerven Home Services Contact Blog en Do not buy RAM, compress! 19 Nov, 2026 AI has changed a lot. We do more work in parallel. This increases the memory demand on our workstations. Also, memory is expensive and often not extendable. So buying more RAM is not an easy option. Recently I was running out of memory, I found my solution in zram , a solution to compress memory. Memory compression is not new. If you have a Windows or Mac device you are already using it. Also, many Android smartphones utilize the technique of using compression to put more data into the RAM. Unfortunately not all Linux environments have RAM compression enabled by default. Fedora, Pop!_OS do, but Ubuntu doesn’t. Amazon Linux only enables zram on smaller virtual machines. Most other distributions do not have it enabled. Compressing memory does come with small, but not really noticeable, downsides. It takes a little bit more from your CPU and adds latency to some processes. What you gain is gigantic amounts of extra capacity. It is not uncommon to see compression ratios up to 1:4. I remember that in the early days of writing SaaS software we would often need double the size of the machines when we added more features to our monolithic app. Often the CPUs were under little stress, so we could have avoided upgrading if we had enabled RAM compression. This could have cut our Cloud spend in half! How it looks in practice I opened a lot of websites in Firefox. So many, it would almost fully take all system memory. (I have 32GB with some reserved for the graphics) for u in nos.nl nu.nl telegraaf.nl ad.nl volkskrant.nl nrc.nl rtl.nl tweakers.net buienradar.nl ns.nl npo.nl \ bbc.com/news edition.cnn.com theguardian.com nytimes.com reuters.com apnews.com aljazeera.com dw.com spiegel.de lemonde.fr washingtonpost.com bloomberg.com \ theverge.com arstechnica.com techcrunch.com wired.com engadget.com phoronix.com lwn.net news.ycombinator.com tomshardware.com \ github.com/torvalds/linux github.com/microsoft/vscode github.com/rust-lang/rust stackoverflow.com/questions gitlab.com developer.mozilla.org docs.python.org kernel.org ubuntu.com huggingface.co \ youtube.com "youtube.com/results?search_query=linux" "youtube.com/results?search_query=music" "youtube.com/results?search_query=documentary" twitch.tv vimeo.com dailymotion.com soundcloud.com open.spotify.com \ reddit.com reddit.com/r/linux reddit.com/r/worldnews reddit.com/r/pics reddit.com/r/technology x.com instagram.com linkedin.com pinterest.com tumblr.com imgur.com 9gag.com medium.com quora.com \ bol.com coolblue.nl marktplaats.nl amazon.nl amazon.com ebay.com aliexpress.com ikea.com/nl/nl zalando.nl etsy.com mediamarkt.nl ah.nl \ google.com/maps openstreetmap.org booking.com airbnb.com tripadvisor.com klm.nl schiphol.nl \ en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linux en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amsterdam en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II nl.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nederland \ imdb.com rottentomatoes.com archive.org nationalgeographic.com nasa.gov flickr.com/explore espn.com weather.com \ canva.com figma.com notion.so trello.com office.com dropbox.com wikihow.com ; do firefox --new-tab "https:// $u " >/dev/null 2 > & 1 ; sleep 1 done If we look at the running apps, then we see it should not fit. In the memory usage we see that some demand was placed into the zram swap space. In the terminal we can check how much memory is used, and we can calculate the compression ratio. 5.7G of data in 1.7G of RAM. That’s a compression ratio of 1:3.35. Getting started Compressing RAM is something which helps to get you more out of your own hardware, but also out of your cloud environment. Do more with less. The Arch Linux wiki has a good article on how to get started . Looking forward to hear about your experiences. Get in touch Looking to hire a software engineer or technical leader for your project?
