title: Pete warden on local AI, open models, voice interfaces, the future of hardware
body_text: Why AI Wants to Be Local - The Data Exchange Skip to content The Data Exchange Bluesky Linkedin RSS YouTube Reddit 🥇 One of the Top 0.5% most popular podcasts. Menu Home About Subscribe Contact Archive Gradient Flow Why AI Wants to Be Local Ben Lorica November 19, 2026 November 19, 2026 Uncategorized Post navigation Previous Pete Warden on Local AI, Open Models, Voice Interfaces, and the Future of Hardware. Subscribe: Apple • Spotify • Overcast • Pocket Casts • YouTube • AntennaPod • Podcast Addict • Amazon • RSS . Pete Warden , co-creator of Moonshine Voice and a longtime deep learning engineer, joins me to discuss why AI increasingly wants to run locally rather than in the cloud. We explore the rapid progress of open-weight models, what it takes to run AI on laptops and in browsers, and how low-latency speech models could make voice a more natural interface. We also discuss specialized versus end-to-end models, the economics of local AI, and emerging hardware approaches that could challenge today’s GPU-centric infrastructure. [This episode originally aired on Generative AI in the Real World , a podcast series I’m hosting for O’Reilly.] Subscribe to the Gradient Flow Newsletter Interview highlights – key sections from the video version: Local AI Is More Capable Than Most People Realize Open Models, Quantization, and Running LLMs on Laptops Can Local AI Replace Cloud Models for Knowledge Work? Privacy, Personal AI, and Models Built Into Operating Systems Voice as a Computing Interface Beyond Siri and Alexa Why Latency Matters for Voice AI and User Experience How Local AI Changes the Economics of Applications Designing Voice Interfaces for Failure and Human Feedback Compound AI Versus End-to-End Speech Models Multimodal Models Versus Specialized Speech Models Running AI Models Directly in the Browser Why AI Wants to Be Local and Why Enterprises Need Control Apple, NVIDIA, and Rethinking GPUs for AI Inference High-Bandwidth Flash and the Future of AI Hardware Jump to transcript Related content : A video version of this conversation is available on our YouTube channel . Hacker News thread for this episode The local AI question I had backwards I changed my mind about world models Previewing the Debate Over Frontier AI Regulation Your Model Is Not Your Moat Richard Ho → Inside OpenAI’s First Chip Joel Hron → Why Build Your Own AI Model When Frontier Models Already Exist? Pete Warden → TinyML, Sensor-Driven AI, and Advances in Large Language Models Support our work by subscribing to our newsletter📩 Transcript Below is a polished and edited transcript . Ben Lorica. All right. Today we have an old friend, Pete Warden of Useful Sensors, and their main website is actually at moonshine.ai. If you go to the website, you’ll see that they’re very much about voice on-device, and we will definitely talk to Pete about all things speech and all things edge computing. But I do want to take advantage of Pete being one of the OG deep learning engineers to get his sense of what’s going on these days. And with that, Pete, welcome back to the podcast. Pete Warden. Thanks for having me, Ben. Ben Lorica. All right. So I would say, Pete, I don’t know if this is a fair characterization, but one of the main thrusts of your work is the whole idea that local AI does not have to be compromised. In fact, it’s something that people should take more seriously. As I mentioned, we’ll definitely talk about your work on speech models on-device. But broadly speaking, Pete, for our audience that doesn’t really follow local models, where are we for someone who wants to run a model on a laptop, not a phone, just a laptop? What’s the state of ease of use? I guess one of the obstacles is that it’s always easier to use a cloud API, right? So where are we in terms of the tooling around local AI? Pete Warden. Yeah. So at the moment, it’s like many open-source projects. Every year is going to be the year of the Linux desktop. I think there’s always going to be a bit of a lag in usability for the average user with this stuff, but I think there’s an even bigger lag in marketing because it’s very hard to make money off local models. That means the big companies like Anthropic and OpenAI, and even the big tech companies generally, aren’t going to push that. If you give them a choice between a SaaS service that you can actually make money on and this other thing where you’re not even going to know that people are using it because they’re not contacting your service, every company is going to go for the one that has an easy subscription revenue model. That means you have a massive amount of marketing around all of these tools that are basically a little text box on a website. And so it means that most people have never heard of these local models. Now, if you use something like Ollama, which is probably the most well-known, I think people will be pleasantly surprised by how straightforward it is to use and by the quality of the models. I saw some news recently that Anthropic is actually a bit concerned because people are turning to more specialized models versus always going for the most sprawling, expensive model that’s available. Local models are actually doing very well in the benchmarks. They continue to be only a few months behind the capabilities of the big commercial Anthropic and OpenAI models. But I also believe that local models have gotten to the point where they can do the things that people want to use them for. What I’m really hoping is that it’s one of those situations, for those of us old enough to remember the dot-com boom, when people were paying thousands of dollars for SPARC servers or using Microsoft IIS and paying massive amounts of money because web servers were seen as such an arcane thing. Then, of course, Apache, Nginx, and all of these alternatives, once people actually had time to look around and the alternatives had a little bit of time to improve, just wiped the floor with the commercial alternatives. I don’t know if we’re going to quite get there, but that’s the pattern I’m seeing. Ben Lorica. Yeah, my sense is that open models, whatever your definition of open is, mainly open weights, I guess, will ultimately prevail. It just seems like that makes a lot more sense to me. As you mentioned, in the early days of Linux versus Solaris, or even Postgres and MySQL versus Oracle, it was far from clear that these open-source projects would ever get to the point of us having to take them seriously. But ultimately, I think they’re such important parts of the stack that the open alternatives are what people will opt for. Speaking of which, Pete, you mentioned Ollama, right? And obviously, there are other alternatives. Let’s say, for the sake of argument, that they are in fact easy to install and use. As far as the models are concerned, you have things like Gemma, I suppose, and other small models, right? What kind of hardware does someone need to have in order to run these models so that they don’t have to wait 20 minutes for each prompt? Pete Warden. So a lot of it comes down to your model choice. Ben Lorica. Yeah. Pete Warden. You can get very capable models that are like 9 billion parameters these days. Especially if you look around at the Qwen family of models, they tend to be doing very well, though there are a bunch of other alternatives. Ben Lorica. But translate that, Pete. To someone with a normal laptop, is 9 billion big or small? Pete Warden. So the key thing is whether you can fit that into your graphics card’s memory. With weight quantization, 9 billion, if it was eight bits, is like nine gigabytes. A lot of decent midrange laptops that are shipping now have more than that. But using Q4, and there are all sorts of schemes, you can actually get that down into a four-gigabyte graphics card, and that’s widely available. There are a lot of even older laptops that have that amount of GPU memory, VRAM, in them. So really, the hardware barriers are a lot lower than people think. And the other piece of good news is that all of the hardware manufacturers are looking at this. They’re slightly hobbled by the DRAM craziness, the price increases. But if you look at the new M5 Studio from Apple, they have a configuration that’s 256 gigabytes of system memory. Apple does a great job of actually making that available to the accelerators that they build into all of their Macs now, too. And with that, you’re looking at something like a model with hundreds of billions of parameters that you can actually run at a decent speed. Once you get up into those numbers, you’re really looking at something where it can be hard to tell if you’re using Claude or if you’re using an open-weights model at that point. They have different characteristics, but one isn’t clearly worse than the other. Ben Lorica. So as I mentioned, we’ll definitely dive deep into voice and speech in a second here. But sticking with this notion of local models, obviously privacy and IP security are arguments for it. Do you think, if we look ahead, let’s say 12 to 24 months, these local models are going to be capable enough that people doing knowledge work in an enterprise might even consider them here and there? For example, someone who travels a lot is on an airplane, not connected to the internet, and needs to keep writing a document or generating images or even coding, vibe coding, on a laptop. Do you think we’ll get to the point where, with these local models, you essentially feel like you’re not compromising when you’re doing your knowledge work? Pete Warden. I think you can actually get to that point right now, and I know that’s a fairly bold statement. Ben Lorica. But when you say you, does that mean Pete Warden, who’s going to compile all of these? We want normal people. We want civilians, Pete. Pete Warden. I think the biggest barriers are usability. If you look at the benchmarks, it really is no longer a question of model quality. Ben Lorica. Model quality. Pete Warden. Yeah, a question of model quality. There are still things around the edges where you might prefer some of the commercial online models, but it’s not clear-cut. And people are finding that some of the models actually work better, especially if you’re dealing with things like, I don’t want to call it censorship because I feel like that’s a loaded term, but a lot of commercial models have restrictions. They may be intended to prevent a bad use case, but pretty often they can also trip you up even if you’re trying to do something benign. I know a lot of people who work in cybersecurity, for example, who are white hats, but they’re having to work with a lot of stuff where they’re asking questions about malicious actions. With the commercial models, you’re going to keep tripping over the restrictions and the guardrails that are built in with good intentions, but they can really impact your work. Ben Lorica. Right, right, right. By the way, Pete, the model is one component, but then there are the things surrounding the model, the so-called harness, or even context, memory, knowledge. You can imagine someone, and this is actually something I’ve thought about. You know how people are starting to use these LLMs as therapists or friends, right? Pete Warden. Yes. Ben Lorica. Then if you’re going to do that, why not do that on a local model? Why do it on something connected to the cloud? I guess one argument against it is that if you do it locally, you’re responsible for model upgrades and things like that, right? Whereas if you use one of these digital or AI therapist services, they take care of all your history and all of this. Do you think it will become easier for consumers to use local models that are essentially something they trust 100% because they own it? Pete Warden. Yeah, I mean, these should be part of the OS. At this point, it’s really an operating system capability that should be available to apps, and I feel like Apple is moving in this direction. Ben Lorica. I see. Yeah, that makes a lot of sense. Pete Warden. Yeah, they’re getting the hardware capabilities. The other thing I would say is that local doesn’t have to mean on your laptop. Especially as an enterprise user, you can host on-prem or even spin up a cloud instance that your enterprise has control over, run these models there, and have the same experience. One thing I do want to emphasize is that people are finally having to pay something approaching the real cost of running these models through Anthropic and OpenAI, and hosting locally or hosting on-prem can cost a lot less, too. Ben Lorica. Although if you look at their consumer offerings, it’s still insanely cheap, right? So $20 a month. I mean, you probably blow through that in a day. Pete Warden. Yeah. Especially on the enterprise side, there are a bunch of options that don’t require high-end NVIDIA GPUs. You still need those for training, but for inference, for just running models, as an enterprise, you might already have the capacity lying around. Ben Lorica. So another important aspect of what you’ve been doing is getting people excited about voice and speech, right? This notion that speech could become a basic computing primitive. It doesn’t necessarily have to feel like some remote service. I still remember you demonstrating to me this voice transcription service in a loud coffee shop near Precita Park. Pete Warden. Yes. Right. Yeah. Ben Lorica. This was several years ago. The accuracy of this thing was insane, and it was running not even on a laptop. I think it was just running on a Raspberry Pi. Pete Warden. That’s right. Yeah. Ben Lorica. And so talk to us about the state of voice as an actual interface, similar to a mouse or a keyboard. Where are we? Pete Warden. I think a lot of people are skeptical of voice because they’ve used Siri and Alexa, and it’s a very stilted way of communicating. But the question I often ask people when I’m having a conversation about this stuff and I encounter that resistance is, when you’re sitting on the couch and you’re trying to decide what TV show to watch with your significant other next to you, do you text them or do you talk to them? Ben Lorica. Right. Pete Warden. Apart from a few Gen Z people, almost everybody says talk to them. And so following on from that, it’s like, okay, well, it’s not that people don’t like voice interfaces. It’s that people don’t like bad voice interfaces. So the problem becomes an engineering and user experience problem of how do we make voice interfaces that are pleasant and efficient to use? I think once we do that, voice can really take its place as maybe even a more frequent input medium than the keyboard or touchscreen. Ben Lorica. Yeah, because I think the general impression people have is that voice and speech are much less deterministic than a keyboard or a touchscreen, right? Although people now interact with their LLMs and misspell things right and left, and it doesn’t seem to matter. But the impression people have is that there’ll be problems with accents, background noise, phrasing, and so on and so forth. So where are we in terms of all of these things? Pete Warden. We have solutions available to most of those problems, or at least big improvements. But because there’s no commercial incentive to pull them all together, it really hasn’t hit the mainstream yet. I feel like we’re still dealing with interfaces that are from the previous generation. They haven’t taken on board the LLM era fully, and they’re still suffering from a lot of those problems you listed. And that’s why I think open source can be a really strong lever. Ben Lorica. So as you’ve been trying to solve a lot of these interface problems, what are some of the lessons that you’ve learned? In fact, maybe some of them might even apply to people who are not working with voice but are just building AI applications. I think one of the things you mentioned to me years ago is that with voice, you don’t have to wait until someone has finished talking to start doing work, right? So what are some of these interface lessons? Pete Warden. I think latency is a massive deal. That is something you just don’t get with cloud-based voice interfaces. You’re usually waiting at least a couple of seconds, and that’s long enough for people to wonder if they were actually heard. Ben Lorica. Yeah, it’s like being on a Zoom call or phone call with someone, and then there’s a pause. Pete Warden. Yeah, and they’re just sitting there. It feels like the other person is just sitting there, ignoring you. We know from general user experience research that you really want to be in that 200-millisecond or lower range to feel responsive. I often ask people to imagine that you press a key on the keyboard and it takes two seconds for the key to show up in the window. That would be very awkward. Ben Lorica. By the way, this is something that people who work with LLMs also have to deal with, but on the output side, right? They want to make sure that the response is not too long. Otherwise, people get impatient, right? Pete Warden. Yeah, absolutely. And I do want to mention another thing, which I think might be helpful to people thinking about local AI in general as well. When you’re no longer paying per token, when you’re no longer having to pay to use a voice interface, the way you can use these things, the world of possibilities, becomes so much wider. If you imagine that every app developer had to pay a few cents every time somebody touched an icon on the touchscreen in their app, you would design apps very differently, and a lot of apps wouldn’t exist because of that tax. So once LLMs are built into the OS and just generally available with no cost, and the same with voice, that is not just an incremental change going from a cent to zero. That massively increases the number of viable things that you can use those for. Ben Lorica. So I imagine, Pete, this is one thing where you’ve done a lot of work, which is basically designing for failure, right? Because in voice, a lot of things can go wrong. What are some of the lessons there in terms of designing your applications with failure in mind? Pete Warden. One of my favorite examples of designing for failure is the use of snippets in Google Search. Google Search, from the beginning, knew they couldn’t always get the number one result right. There’s a reason you didn’t just hit “I’m Feeling Lucky.” Ben Lorica. Yeah, exactly. “I’m Feeling Lucky.” Pete Warden. What was genius about their approach was that they actually let you browse, just scan with your eyes. They hoped to get the right result in the top three most of the time, and then you actually narrow it down by looking at the snippets, which tell you enough to click on the right one. And the same thing for voice. The more you can actually read the body language of somebody, as we’re talking, you’re nodding a little bit to indicate what’s happening. Ben Lorica. Wait a minute, I’m only voice, so you can’t see me. Pete Warden. No, I can see. Ben Lorica. No, no, but in general, right? In general. Pete Warden. Well, that’s actually a whole other part of this that I haven’t mentioned. I think having a little camera that’s completely local-only will be a massive part of this. But even without a camera, if you hear supportive noises, or if you start giving a response and somebody reacts, all of those things that we recognize as people, we respond to them and ask more questions versus assuming that we picked the right thing. So really trying to understand all of those cues that we use as people. Some of them are verbal, some of them are body language and visual, but really having them all understood locally. And ensuring that all of those recordings never get recorded, because you can verify that locally. You don’t know what happens to audio and video once you send it up to the cloud. It’s impossible to audit, basically. With local stuff, you can audit. So I’m hoping that opens up the chance to use cameras without increasing the risk to users around privacy. Ben Lorica. So there are the people who work on speech models, and there’s been a lot of work in that area. In fact, one thing that I think is vastly underappreciated is that people talk about deep learning having an ImageNet moment, but actually the first impressive deep learning models were in speech, before ImageNet, right? So there are people working on speech models. They’ve even talked about end-to-end models, but obviously we have LLMs. For the people who don’t follow this closely, Pete, what’s the relationship between the LLMs and the speech models, or do people not use LLMs? Do they just use speech models? Pete Warden. There’s been a massive debate, a split between what I think of as LLM maximalists, who expect everything to be an end-to-end model. Ben Lorica. “Machines of Loving Grace.” Pete Warden. Yes, exactly. And I see usually Anthropic, OpenAI, the big AI companies. Ben Lorica. Or, you know, the hype machine has to be fed, right? Pete Warden. Well, the hype machine has to be fed, and specifically, if the future is end-to-end models, then only the people with the most money can actually build and train them. Now, I’m very strongly in what Berkeley calls the compound AI camp, where you actually build your applications out of multiple models, each of which has a specialized task. So there, instead of having a model that takes speech in and outputs speech audio, you actually have a model that takes speech audio in, converts it to text, feeds that into an LLM, and the LLM then outputs text, which is converted into speech. Now, every time you convert the audio into text, you actually lose a bunch of expressiveness. It’s like a bottleneck of information. You can’t tell how somebody’s asking it, whether they’re asking it with a particular intonation and all of this other stuff. Ben Lorica. Can’t you, as you’re doing that translation, add metadata? Pete Warden. You kind of can, but the whole point of compound AI is that you can take models from different sources and plug them together. So you need some kind of common language, and at the moment, the only thing that all LLMs speak is text input and text output. But the advantages are that you can actually train all of the models independently. With a speech end-to-end model, if you have a new accent, then if it’s a true end-to-end model, you have to do a whole bunch of training. If you have a new input accent, if you have new output voices or new capabilities, if it’s a true end-to-end model, then you’re having to train the whole thing. If it’s not actually, if end-to-end is just a marketing term, then you can train individual components, individual modules separately. But then you’re always agreeing on some settled interface data, like some schema, some language. Even if it’s not text, even if it’s an embedding, you still have to have those fixed points. So yeah, I see end-to-end as much more of a marketing term and something to justify the insane amounts of money that are flowing into these companies. Ben Lorica. Pete, what about, for our listeners who’ve heard of the term multimodal, right? Gemini is supposed to be multimodal. And coincidentally, I just spoke to someone who works in the visual reasoning and understanding space, and they said actually Gemini is quite poor in terms of understanding video. So what is the state of these multimodal models for your domain, speech? Pete Warden. They’re actually often pretty good. Qwen, 1.7 billion, I think it is, actually does a better job than Whisper, a significantly better job on some languages like Mandarin. And the same goes for Gemma. The trouble is that, as general-purpose models, one of the failure cases with Gemma is that you upload audio of some speech, it transcribes it, but it then gets confused by the content of that speech and thinks you’re asking it a question, say, if there was a question in the transcribed speech. So it’s one of these things where you’re trying to use a Swiss Army knife, and it’s a lot easier to use an actual wood saw versus the thing that can do everything and has a little saw attachment with it. So that’s another drawback of the end-to-end models. Ben Lorica. By the way, obviously you’re the king on this topic. General-purpose models are dead on arrival on the edge, right? Pete Warden. I mean, right now, only… Ben Lorica. For the types of, I mean, some of the really small pieces of hardware that you work on. Pete Warden. One of the things I recently did was get a full voice interface where you could connect to Wi-Fi, set the password, and all of this sort of stuff, running on a Raspberry Pi Pico microcontroller that only has 500 kilobytes of RAM. Now, there, you’re never going to have a general-purpose model that’s going to work well for you. But as always… Ben Lorica. And by the way, one of the things that you’ve also worked on, which is interesting, and which I don’t see a lot of people working on, is taking the browser more seriously, right? So tell us, what’s the motivation behind that, and what has been the reception? Pete Warden. Yeah, so it’s tricky because I sometimes think of “We’ve done X, but in the browser” as Hacker News bait, because that always gets a lot of attention as a novelty. But it’s often hard to find practical uses for a lot of these things. With the voice capabilities, with voice input and voice output, what I’ve seen is that it makes it part of the browser operating system, or feel like part of the browser operating system. And once you’re able to transcribe fast and accurately in the browser, it’s a way for people to easily start experimenting with this stuff, and there aren’t any costs for this at the moment. I’ve tried to put a few examples. If you go to Moonshine AI… Ben Lorica. But the whole notion of using the browser as a point of inference, right? You can imagine other models doing that too, not just yours, which focuses on speech. You can imagine text, I mean, browser inference for text kinds of applications, right? Pete Warden. Well, if you’re running Chrome, you’ve already got a very capable model installed. You’ve got a 4-billion-parameter model. I actually did a blog post last year showing how you could just go through Chrome settings and start using it as a chatbot, just typing in the window and getting responses. I think that’s an example of the models becoming part of the operating system, because Chrome is essentially an operating system that sits on top of other operating systems. You can already access that built-in LLM, I think now from any website. It used to be just extensions, but now I think any website can access that from JavaScript. And again, we’re still figuring out what the best use cases are for that. But once it becomes free and you can rely on it being everywhere, I really feel like it’s an iPhone moment for a lot of these new LLM technologies. Ben Lorica. Or even what you mentioned earlier, which is for people on a laptop, it’ll be part of the OS somehow, right? So looking ahead, Pete, and again, for our listeners, you can follow Pete’s work at Moonshot AI. Moonshine. Ah, Moonshine. Moonshine.ai. And a lot of the work is open source, and you can take advantage of that. So looking ahead, Pete, 12 to 24 months. I hate to put you on the spot. Where are we in terms of, I guess, local or edge models, number one, and number two, just the state of open models in general? Pete Warden. Yeah, and I’m always terrible at predictions. Ben Lorica. But one thing Pete is super good at, for our listeners, is knowing what to work on. So that’s an indication. Just tell us what you’re working on. Pete Warden. Yes. So what I see from being deep in the technical side, most of what I end up working on is because I’ve been working on something, and it becomes blindingly obvious that the only reasonable technical solution is X, and so of course I want to work on X. And what I see, and what I’ve seen for the last few years, is the gravitational pull of running this stuff locally or on-prem, or however you want to call it. I often say, “AI wants to be local.” If you think about something like Google Search, you need massive databases, you need armies of servers, you need all of this stuff. If you look at what Claude and ChatGPT are doing, you can run that entirely on one laptop with no internet connectivity. So the shape of these models is perfect for running locally, unlike almost everything else we’ve seen over the last couple of decades, where the cloud has made more sense. So what I expect is all of these pressures: cost for enterprises especially, worries about privacy, worries about capabilities going away, worries about changes. If you built an application on top of a particular version of Claude, even if you’re using the same version in the dropdown, what’s actually happening behind the scenes can change from day to day. So if you want stability, you actually need to host your own, at least in your own cloud infrastructure, if not locally on users’ laptops. And I can keep going on and on. Ben Lorica. Yeah. And then the other thing, too, is I think a lot of enterprises are recognizing that the moat, or their moat, is really not the model. It’s that compounding loop around the model, right? As you use the model more, you learn more and things like that. So why in the world would you send that to a commercial proprietary model? Pete Warden. And why not do fine-tuning on your own model? Ben Lorica. Yeah, I mean, with that data. Pete Warden. Yeah, exactly. Ben Lorica. And then, as you point out, you actually control your timing and roadmap as well, because you have the model and you know when it’s safe to replace that model with something else. No one is going to replace that model underneath you, right? Pete Warden. Nobody’s going to start charging 10 times as much overnight. Ben Lorica. Right, right, right. And then also, even if they keep the cost the same, they may weaken the model for some reason, right? Pete Warden. Yep. Yeah, and it could even be pressure from outside. Ben Lorica. So by the way, one last question for you, Pete, because obviously you work in a space where you really care about hardware, right? Right now, we’re in a world where Jensen Huang seems to own everything. So what’s your prediction about the state of AI hardware? Are we going to get more diversification? Is AMD going to up its game, or what’s going on in hardware in general? Pete Warden. So watch Apple. And disclaimer, I worked at Apple for five years in the 2000s. My wife worked there for 13 years. But if you look at what they’re doing, they’re getting lots of RAM, increasing the RAM speed so that you can actually run models much faster, and they have their own inference-only accelerators. I think with those three, you don’t need a GPU. Ben Lorica. So you just run everything on a CPU? Pete Warden. Well, run everything on a different kind of accelerator. Ben Lorica. Oh, okay. That’s not a… Pete Warden. GPU. Ben Lorica. I see. I see. So CPU… Pete Warden. Could actually be pretty fast. Obviously, the… Ben Lorica. The NVIDIA answer is why we have all the HBM, high-bandwidth memory, on the GPU, right? Pete Warden. And I like to think of GPUs as being designed for large batches and training. I like to think of a GPU as trying to use an oil tanker to go and do your shopping. They’re fantastic for these large training jobs, but they’re complete overkill for inference. Inference has a very different shape to the workload that it places on hardware. Ben Lorica. One thing that I’ve started to pay attention to lately, and it’s very, very early, is high-bandwidth flash. Pete Warden. Absolutely. Ben Lorica. Right. So what’s your take? Pete Warden. So that’s another example. I see the massive amount of money that NVIDIA is pulling in, and that also has its own gravitational pull on all of these hardware companies, where they’re looking from a technical side. I don’t have any special insights. I’ve just worked with these things. I know what the workloads look like. Other people are looking at those too, and they’re like, “Oh, I see. We have to stream all of the weights. All of the weights have to be processed for every token.” So if you have something, even if you’re running on the CPU, if you have something that’s got high enough bandwidth to pull the 27 billion weights in a fraction of a second, then the rest of it is fairly easy in terms of actually doing the processing. It’s very much memory-bound, usually. So it’s been awesome seeing high-bandwidth flash, what Apple is doing, increasing the bandwidth on regular RAM. I think we’re going to see a lot of really imaginative solutions now that people understand what the workload looks like. Ben Lorica. Yeah, and with that, thank you, Pete. And again, the website is moonshine.ai. title: Everything you need to survive and rebuild society
body_text: Lastbook — Everything you need to survive and rebuild society. Skip to content Lastbook Open source ↗ Lastbook Everything you need to survive and rebuild society. Free, local, offline and private. It’s for Mac, Windows and Linux computers, not iPhone, iPad or Android. Open lastbook.org on your computer. Download for Mac 28.6 MB · Apple M1 or newer · macOS 14+ Download for Windows 105 MB · Windows 10 or 11, 64-bit Download for Linux Ubuntu 24.04 or 26.04 · Intel/AMD 64-bit Open source. Built by the community. Build with us on GitHub ☆ 748 stars ↗ Free, local, private. AI Free. Local. Private. Gemma 4 26B A4B Maps Free. Local. Private. 258,000+ searchable places W Water + Medical F Fire stations ⌂ Shelters Videos Free. Local. Private. 2,324 videos First aid & health Wounds, illness and emergency care. Safe drinking water Find, filter, treat and store water. Food & preservation Grow, prepare and preserve your food. Critical repairs Tools, equipment and shelter repairs. Power & energy Generators, solar and electrical basics. Emergency preparedness Plan for outages, disasters and evacuation. Lastbook is open source. Help us improve it. Improve the app Code, design and accessibility. Grow the library Recommend resources and help review guides. Try it. Tell us. Report bugs and share what you need. Questions Will it run on my computer? On a Mac, you need Apple Silicon (M1 or newer) and macOS 14 Sonoma or newer. Intel Macs are not supported. To check: Apple menu > About This Mac . Chip should say Apple M1 or later (M2, M3 and so on), and macOS should be 14 or higher. On Windows, you need Windows 10 or 11, 64-bit. To check: Settings > System > About . System type should say 64-bit. Lastbook doesn’t run on phones or tablets. How much space do I need? Choose Small (7.7 GB), Medium (67.5 GB), or All (about 388 GB). Local AI adds about 17 GB. Your selected state map and address index add more, with sizes shown in setup. Mac setup checks free space before downloading. Does it need the internet? Internet is needed to download the app, library and optional AI. Once setup finishes, reading, maps, videos and AI work offline. What is Chat? Chat uses the optional local Gemma model to answer questions from your library and link to its sources. It is available in the Mac, Windows and Linux apps. Is the medical information checked? It comes from published guides, such as Hesperian, the World Health Organization and the Red Cross. Lastbook itself is not clinically reviewed, and it doesn’t replace trained care. In an emergency, call 911 if you can. Is there a bigger library? Yes. Small (7.7 GB) and Medium (67.5 GB) are available. All (about 388 GB) is also available. Mac setup shows the available choices. Something else? Email hello@lastbook.org . Set it up now, while you have internet and power. Then it’s ready when you need it. Free for Mac, Windows and Linux. Download for Mac Download for Windows Download for Linux Mac 1.1.13 · 28.6 MB · Windows 1.1.13 · 105 MB · Linux 1.1.13 · 30.0 MB Buying guide Practical gear for first aid, water, food and repairs. title: Distributed, high-performance blob storage on SQLite
body_text: Distributed, high-performance blob storage on SQLite - Zerodha Tech Blog Home Blog Projects Stack Distributed, high-performance blob storage on SQLite 19 Nov 2026 Sarat Chandra Software Engineer TLDR; We built Blobasaur, a sharded, distributed, lightweight blob storage server on top of SQLite to solve our high-throughput blob read/write usecase. JSON blobs varying from a few KBs to MBs are now written and read thousands of times per second on commodity hardware while maintaining single-digit millisecond latency. On Kite , our trading platform with ~20 million customers, users are able to customize their investment and trading screens heavily. They save multi-chart layouts, financial indicator templates, vector drawings, and various kinds of arbitrary UI preferences. In addition, we offer a Terminal mode that allows users to design their own workspaces by dragging, dropping, and customizing widgets. Under the hood, our backend services store these user preferences and metadata as opaque blobs (mostly JSON) ranging from a few kilobytes to several megabytes. Many years ago, we stored such blobs in CouchDB, which turned out to be ill-suited for the kind of throughput we were starting to see. We then moved to SSDB ( ssdb ), a C++ disk-backed store that speaks the Redis protocol. This made it very easy to integrate as well. SSDB solved our immediate performance problems and ran reliably in production for several years. Over time, two problems forced us to look for a replacement: SSDB became unmaintained, which was an obvious operational risk. It is written in C++, which is not a part of our stack or expertise, so forking and maintaining was also not viable. Scaling and size limits. SSDB is not a distributed system and can only run on a single node. This imposes significant future scaling challenges, including at one point forcing us to cap blob sizes at 1 MB because latency degrades on larger payloads. As we added features like the Terminal mode and onboarded more internal services, we needed a robust solution. Our criteria were: A key-value blob store with a simple API. Designed for multi-megabyte blob read/write ops and high throughput. We sustain loads of thousands to tens of thousands of requests per second reading and writing arbitrary blobs. These are unpredictable and bursty thanks to the volatility in stock markets. Horizontally scalable, distributed. Disk-space efficiency / compression. Easily maintainable and highly economical. So we investigated FOSS databases optimized for high-throughput blob storage and looked at the following: ScyllaDB: We already run ScyllaDB for high-throughput workloads, but in our tests, it turned out to be suboptimal for large blobs. Significantly lower throughput and higher resource usage. We specifically want multi-megabyte blobs. Tombstones from frequent overwrites and TTL expiries require careful tuning in ScyllaDB. PostgreSQL: We already have considerable experience with Postgres in our stack and experimented with storing blobs as BYTEA columns, but it turned out to be severely suboptimal again for the use case in terms of performance and disk-space efficiency. YugabyteDB: Has blob storage as one of the options, but is not primarily designed or optimized for it. Also, a large system with too many features. RocksDB: Had the right primitives, but again, not architected for high throughput multi-MB blob writes. Ceph: Severe operational complexity and resource requirements. We didn’t even get to trying it out. SeaweedFS: This was the closest candidate. However, there were a few blockers. Our use case is overwrite-heavy (a user changing their workspace) over the same key, and SeaweedFS keeps appending before compaction, which can cause disk usage to grow uncontrollably. Blobs have their own IDs, which then have to be mapped against user keys in a separate DB, adding another layer. It doesn’t support TTL per blob. Also, reasonably complex setup with many parts. S3 and MinIO: Object storage has high per-request latency for small blobs, high request costs under write-heavy workloads (writes are 50% of our traffic), and coarse lifecycle TTLs instead of exact key expiry. Not to mention, S3 would incur significant costs given thousands of ops per second and tens of millions of ops per day. Raw filesystem (one file per blob): Putting blobs directly on disk meant implementing atomic writes and write batching, managing large numbers of files and directories, good old atomic read/write disk performance and inode headaches, and maintaining a separate metadata index for TTLs. Not to mention, orchestrating this over AWS storage volumes. Around this time, we were toying with SQLite for another project and were marveling at its 35% Faster Than The Filesystem claim. We also happen to have a query cache system that creates millions of tables every day in a Postgres instance, which pushes the database to its limits quite successfully. Putting two and two together, we thought, why not build a system on top of SQLite to store millions of blobs and see what happens? So we ended up building Blobasaur , an open source sharded blob server written in Rust that speaks the Redis protocol and uses SQLite as its storage engine. It is a single binary application that is high performance, and super simple to deploy and maintain. It is in production at Zerodha and it has successfully replaced SSDB. What we needed We had several Go and Python services already talking to SSDB via the Redis protocol, with more waiting to onboard. We wanted the new solution to meet these requirements: Redis protocol compatibility (if possible at all): Every existing client already used standard Redis libraries ( GET , SET , HGET , HSET , DEL , EXPIRE ). If we could get a system that could be a drop-in replacement, that would allow us to leave existing services untouched and reduce risk significantly. Low latency across payload sizes: It needed to serve both 2 KB settings blobs and 5 MB chart layouts with single-digit millisecond latency. Built-in compression: Almost all our payloads are repetitive JSON, which compresses well. Simple CRUD with TTLs: We didn’t need complex data structures, server-side scripting, or secondary queries. We just needed key-value and hash CRUD with key expiry. Multi-node partitioning: We needed to split data across multiple machines so a single node wasn’t a bottleneck. Relaxed durability is acceptable: This store holds non-critical UI and workspace preferences, and not critical financial data. If a sudden power loss drops recent writes, a user might lose a recent chart layout tweak, which is annoying, but it never affects trading. This was a good performance trade-off for our use case. Why SQLite (and Rust) We had a few options for the storage. The obvious one is the raw filesystem, with one file per blob. But with that, we’d need to invent everything ourselves: Atomic writes and batching. TTL cleanup, which needs secondary indexes or walking the directories. Dealing with fd limits. Managing metadata separately from the raw data. SQLite pretty much gave us everything that the raw filesystem lacked. For small blobs, SQLite is up to 35% faster than raw filesystem I/O. While raw files start to beat SQLite above ~100 KiB, we compress blobs before writing them. And thankfully, 99% of our compressed values sit well below 100 KiB. Using SQLite also meant inheriting a battle-tested storage engine with ACID transactions, crash recovery, and standard tooling. Any shard on disk can be inspected with the standard sqlite3 CLI or queried with plain SQL for analytics, etc. While most of our backend stack is written in Go, we wrote Blobasaur in Rust. Go’s standard SQLite driver requires CGo, which complicates static builds, pins OS threads during C calls under high concurrency, and adds garbage-collection pressure when allocating and compressing multi-megabyte buffers. With Rust ( sqlx , rusqlite , and tokio ), we call SQLite’s C API directly with predictable memory usage and ship a single static binary. Architecture Splitting data into shards In WAL (Write-Ahead Logging) mode, a single SQLite database allows concurrent readers, but still permits only one writer at a time. Since writes make up roughly 50% of our production traffic, a single SQLite file per node would bottleneck quickly. To get write concurrency on a single machine, Blobasaur splits data across multiple SQLite database files on disk, called shards: Consistent hashing: Each key maps to one shard via multi-probe consistent hashing. Per-shard writer with group commit: Each shard has a dedicated writer task fed by a bounded queue. Instead of committing one key at a time, the writer drains a batch of pending writes from the queue and executes them inside a single BEGIN IMMEDIATE ... COMMIT transaction. This amortizes transaction and WAL overhead across concurrent clients. Concurrent readers: Reads go directly to a per-shard pool of read-only SQLite connections and can run concurrently with the writer. How much does sharding help? We benchmarked 1 shard against 16 shards using a load generator opening 64 concurrent connections. Each request used a 64 KiB JSON blob payload (close to our production average), which zstd compresses roughly 9x. All runs used 100,000 keys, synchronous writes, and batch_size = 50 , with the data directory on tmpfs to isolate SQLite locking and CPU overhead from disk variance. Both setups received the same total resources: 1,600 MB of SQLite page cache and 64 total read connections. Workload 1 shard 16 shards HSET only 7,740 ops/s, p99 10.7 ms 25,324 ops/s, p99 8.3 ms 50% HSET , 50% HGET 14,227 ops/s, p99 10.5 ms 29,538 ops/s, p99 8.5 ms HGET only 67,128 ops/s, p99 2.1 ms 70,884 ops/s, p99 2.3 ms With 16 shards, write throughput increases 3.3x and median write latency drops from 8.2 ms to 2.1 ms. Read throughput stays nearly identical because SQLite WAL mode already serves concurrent readers without contention. At 25,324 HSET operations per second, each carrying a 64 KiB payload, Blobasaur processes roughly 1.66 GB/s of uncompressed JSON through zstd. Both the server and load generator ran on the same 16-core laptop, sharing its CPU resources. Schema Our services use both plain keys ( SET / GET ) and Redis hashes ( HSET / HGET ) to group blobs by service or feature (for example, HSET prefs userID <json> ). Inside each shard, plain keys live in a blobs table: CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS blobs ( key TEXT PRIMARY KEY , data BLOB , created_at INTEGER NOT NULL , updated_at INTEGER NOT NULL , expires_at INTEGER , version INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0 ); CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS idx_expires_at ON blobs(expires_at) WHERE expires_at IS NOT NULL ; SET writes to blobs . HSET writes to a table for its namespace, blobs_<namespace> , with the same columns. For example, HSET prefs user42 ... stores user42 in blobs_prefs . Expiry is stored in expires_at on the same row. Read queries filter out expired rows at read time ( expires_at IS NULL OR expires_at > ? ), while a background worker reaps expired rows asynchronously. Because the index on expires_at is a partial index ( WHERE expires_at IS NOT NULL ), rows without a TTL take up no space in the expiry index. Compression Blobasaur supports zstd, lz4, gzip, and brotli compression before writing to SQLite. We run zstd in production. Here is the compression ratio across one hour of production HSET traffic: HSET payload Sent by the client Stored in SQLite Reduction Average 63.6 KiB 5.5 KiB about 11x p99 935 KiB 59.3 KiB about 16x With SQLite’s default 4 KiB pages, shrinking a 63.6 KiB payload to 5.5 KiB reduces its storage footprint from roughly 16 pages to roughly 2, before accounting for row and index overhead. Fewer pages holding blob data means less pressure on the page cache and less data to write through the WAL and into the database. Durability Because we don’t require strict durability for our specific use case of UI preferences, shards run in WAL mode with PRAGMA synchronous = NORMAL . SQLite does not fsync on every transaction commit. An OS crash or power loss can lose recent committed transactions that have not yet been synced to durable storage, while preserving database consistency. For workloads that want even lower write latency, Blobasaur also supports an optional async_write mode that acknowledges writes as soon as they enter the shard’s memory queue, before the SQLite batch commits. Scaling across machines To scale beyond a single server, Blobasaur implements the Redis Cluster protocol, making it compatible with standard cluster-aware Redis clients. Like Redis Cluster, the keyspace is divided into 16384 hash slots using CRC16 . Each Blobasaur node owns a configured range of slots, and nodes discover each other via gossip. If a client sends a key to the wrong node, the node responds with a MOVED redirect pointing to the owner node. This gives Blobasaur two-level routing: Cluster level: CRC16(key) % 16384 selects the machine. Node level: Multi-probe consistent hashing selects the SQLite shard on that machine. There are some limitations right now. At present, slot assignment is static in config. Live slot rebalancing between running nodes and automatic failover are not implemented yet. Changing the number of shards We chose multi-probe consistent hashing so resharding a node only has to move minimal data, without needing virtual nodes. With naive hash % num_shards , increasing from 4 to 5 shards moves ~80% of keys. With consistent hashing, only ~20% of keys move (the share belonging to the new shard). Resharding is currently an offline operation via the built-in CLI: Stop the server. Run blobasaur shard migrate 4 5 --verify . Update num_shards in config.toml and start the server. The migration tool moves keys whose target shard changed. With --verify , it checks that keys are in the expected shards and reports post-migration row counts. Moving off SSDB We rolled out Blobasaur in a phased deployment strategy: New workloads first: When we launched Kite Terminal mode, we pointed its workspace storage directly at Blobasaur. Dual-write and backfill: For existing workloads like chart preferences, we updated the services to dual-write to both SSDB and Blobasaur while running a background migration for historical keys. Reads went to Blobasaur first and fell back to SSDB on a cache miss or error. Cutover: On the client side, the only code change was switching from a single-node Redis client to a Redis Cluster client with the three Blobasaur node IPs. After running dual-writes for a month with zero discrepancies, we turned off SSDB. What we learned along the way Deleting rows doesn’t shrink SQLite files Early on, we noticed disk usage only grew, even after millions of keys expired or were deleted. By default, SQLite keeps freed pages on an internal freelist for future writes rather than returning space to the OS. To fix this, we enabled PRAGMA auto_vacuum = INCREMENTAL across every shard and added a blobasaur shard vacuum subcommand to reclaim unused freelist pages within a set allocation (128 MB default). Since shrinking the actual database file in WAL mode requires a checkpoint, Blobasaur runs PRAGMA wal_checkpoint(TRUNCATE) right after executing an incremental vacuum. Async writes have to be visible to every read When async_write is enabled, a write returns OK while still sitting in the shard’s memory queue waiting for the next batch commit. To preserve read-your-writes consistency, queued writes are also placed in an in-memory pending map that reads check before querying SQLite. During testing, we hit edge cases where certain read and existence-check paths bypassed this pending map or didn’t account for deletes. For example, a DEL followed immediately by a GET could return the old value from SQLite because the queued DEL hadn’t committed yet. We fixed this by storing explicit tombstones in the pending map and routing every read ( GET , HGET , EXISTS , TTL ) through it first. Expiry cleanup has to share the writer In production, our p99 write latency normally sat below 5 ms, but we occasionally saw spikes to 30 to 50 ms. We traced the spikes to the background TTL cleanup task. Initially, the cleanup worker opened its own write connection and ran a single large DELETE statement for all expired rows. That large DELETE contended with the shard’s main writer for SQLite’s single write lock, stalling normal client batches. We fixed this in two ways: routing cleanup batches through the shard’s existing writer connection so they take turns cleanly with client writes, and bounding each pass with cleanup_chunk_size (1,000 rows by default). Since expired rows are already filtered out at read time, spreading physical deletion across smaller chunks eliminated the latency spikes without affecting correctness. In production Our current Blobasaur deployment runs as a three-node (4 vCPU, 8 GB RAM) cluster. Over a full trading session (09:00 to 15:30), p99 latency across all commands stays around 2 ms on every node, and p50 sits between 250 and 550 µs. Broken down by command, HSET p99 sits around 2 ms, HGET p99 around 1.4 ms, and HDEL p99 mostly under 1 ms. Blobasaur is open source under the AGPLv3 license and available on GitHub @iamd3vil/blobasaur . Find other projects from the Zerodha.tech hacker collective at 4th Cross Labs . rust databases Zerodha © 2026 All rights reserved.

title: Unauthenticated remote code execution in Nginx
body_text: Unauthenticated Remote Code Execution in NGINX: CVE-2026-123633 and CVE-2026-123007 | Wiz Blog Wiz Platform Solutions Pricing Resources Customers Company Sign in Under attack? Get a demo Blog Unauthenticated Remote Code Execution in NGINX: CVE-2026-123633 and CVE-2026-123007 Two critical HTTP/2 flaws can allow attackers to compromise NGINX servers, putting the websites, APIs, and sensitive data they handle at risk. Watch the Threat Briefing Webinar Nir Ohfeld , Tomer Schwartz November 18, 2026 | Executive Summary Wiz Research, Ikotas Labs, Metnir, Rapid7, and Xint independently uncovered two critical remote code execution vulnerabilities in NGINX, software used to receive and route traffic to production applications and APIs. NGINX is a common default for the front door of modern web architectures, where it handles HTTPS and routes incoming traffic to the right application or API. As the world's most widely used open-source web server , it powers more than 225 million websites . Successful exploitation could let attackers take control of affected NGINX servers, steal sensitive data, tamper with websites, or disrupt services. The vulnerabilities, tracked as CVE-2026-123633 and CVE-2026-123007, are both rated Critical, with a CVSS 4.0 score of 9.2. The flaws are in NGINX itself. Websites and APIs can be exposed even when their own application code is secure. Both vulnerabilities require HTTP/2 to be enabled on the affected NGINX server. Additional conditions are described below. CVE-2026-123007 affects versions dating back to NGINX 1.9.5 in 2015. We reported our findings to F5, the company behind NGINX, and collaborated with its security team on remediation and coordinated disclosure. Organizations should identify affected deployments and apply the security updates when released. We recommend updating affected NGINX deployments to the latest release which includes multiple security fixes. Responsible disclosure timeline October 21, 2026: Wiz reports the HTTP/2 use-after-free vulnerability, later assigned CVE-2026-123633, to F5, including confirmed remote code execution with an ASLR bypass and a proposed fix. F5 confirms that another research team had previously reported the same vulnerability. November 10, 2026: F5 supplies a patch for CVE-2026-123633 for review. November 16, 2026 : Wiz reports the second HTTP/2 vulnerability, later assigned CVE-2026-123007, to F5. November 17, 2026 : F5 confirms that the second report matches CVE-2026-123007 and is included in the planned November 18 security release. November 18, 2026: F5 security release and coordinated public disclosure. Overview Wiz Research, Ikotas Labs, Metnir, Rapid7, and Xint independently uncovered CVE-2026-123633 and CVE-2026-123007, two critical unauthenticated remote code execution vulnerabilities in NGINX, and reported them to F5, the company behind NGINX. Successful exploitation can compromise the server running NGINX, allowing attackers to execute code, steal sensitive data, tamper with websites, or disrupt services. NGINX often handles traffic for several applications, so a single affected deployment can put multiple services at risk. The flaws are in NGINX itself and can affect websites even when their own application code is secure. Both vulnerabilities require HTTP/2 to be enabled on the affected NGINX server. Our testing of CVE-2026-123007 demonstrated code execution on NGINX serving ordinary static files, without a backend application or third-party modules. Wiz Research used Wiz Atlas , the harness powering Wiz’s AI Code scanning solution , to discover both vulnerabilities. Our researchers used Gemini 4 Carbon and ChatGPT 5.6 Sol to validate the impact of both vulnerabilities, confirming that each could allow an unauthenticated attacker to execute code on the server. We reported our findings to F5 and worked with its security team on remediation and coordinated disclosure. The integer underflow vulnerability dates back to NGINX 1.9.5 in 2015, meaning it had been hiding in the code for more than a decade. The use-after-free vulnerability had been there for nearly six years. Like the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities we reported last month and Java4Shell , disclosed yesterday by Calif, these are memory-safety flaws that have historically been extremely difficult to discover and exploit. Finding them often requires tracing subtle interactions between memory operations and multiple code paths. For years, that complexity itself created a practical barrier. AI is fundamentally dissolving that barrier. As AI models get better at following those interactions, both researchers and attackers can uncover longstanding flaws in software that powers the internet and modern applications. The fact that multiple independent research teams uncovered the same vulnerabilities in both PHP and NGINX, after they had remained in the code for years, makes this shift particularly striking. And as AI capabilities advance, each new generation of models may uncover even more complex vulnerabilities that were previously beyond practical reach. Complexity can no longer be relied upon as a barrier to discovery or exploitation. This changes not only which vulnerabilities can be found, but how quickly longstanding risks can become real threats. Over time, finding and fixing these flaws can harden the software we all depend on. In the near term, faster discovery and a shorter window between disclosure and exploitation add to an already demanding workload for security teams. Turning a published fix into protection in production still takes substantial manual work, from validating patches to coordinating rollouts with service owners. We recommend focusing on how quickly you can reduce exposure in production. Identify deployments running the affected version and configuration, prioritize those an attacker can reach, and apply mitigations while patches are tested and rolled out. In this post, we explain the vulnerabilities and their impact, and provide mitigation and detection guidance. Organizations should identify affected deployments and apply the security updates as soon as they are available. If upgrading is not immediately possible, temporarily disable HTTP/2. What is NGINX? NGINX is the world's most widely used open-source web server , powering more than 225 million websites . It is commonly used as a reverse proxy in front of websites and APIs. In this role, NGINX accepts incoming requests, forwards them to the appropriate application server based on its configuration, and returns the response to the user. NGINX can also serve web content directly and act as a load balancer , distributing traffic across multiple servers. A single NGINX deployment can serve several applications, making it a shared entry point for the websites and APIs behind it. The Vulnerabilities Both vulnerabilities are memory-safety issues in how NGINX handles HTTP/2 traffic. In CVE-2026-123633, a connection's memory is freed while a request still needs it, creating a use-after-free. In CVE-2026-123007, incorrect flow-control accounting leads to an invalid memory copy. Each can lead to unauthenticated remote code execution on the NGINX server. Tracking ID The bug What an attacker can achieve CVE-2026-123633 HTTP/2 connection use-after-free Execute arbitrary code on the NGINX server without authentication. CVE-2026-123007 HTTP/2 send_window integer underflow Execute arbitrary code on the NGINX server without authentication. Both vulnerabilities require HTTP/2 to be enabled, but their additional requirements differ. CVE-2026-123633 affects reverse-proxy processing when available connection slots run low. CVE-2026-123007 can also affect NGINX serving content directly, as demonstrated in our testing over HTTPS on 64-bit systems. Typical memory safety mitigations such as ASLR do not protect against these issues, as attackers can use either vulnerabilities for memory read access prior to code execution. Impact On affected NGINX versions with HTTP/2 enabled, these vulnerabilities can allow an unauthenticated attacker to execute arbitrary code on the server. The flaws are in NGINX itself. Exploitation does not depend on a bug in the website or API behind it, so applications with secure code can still be exposed. For CVE-2026-123007, we demonstrated remote code execution on a server serving ordinary static files, without a backend application or third-party module. An attacker could use this access to run commands, steal sensitive data, tamper with websites, or disrupt services. Because one NGINX deployment can serve several applications, the impact could extend across multiple websites and APIs. Illustrative deployment: an attacker exploits NGINX to run code on the server, putting the applications and data it serves at risk. Coordinated disclosure We reported both vulnerabilities to F5 and collaborated with its security team on remediation and coordinated disclosure. We also shared proposed fixes. Ikotas Labs, Metnir, Rapid7, and Xint also independently discovered and reported these issues to F5. We thank the F5 and NGINX teams for their work on the fixes. Vulnerabilities Addressed in the Release F5's security release addresses several other vulnerabilities in NGINX. Below is a summary of these additional CVEs, as well as the two critical HTTP/2 remote code execution flaws detailed in this post (captured in the first two rows of the table): CVE Description Impact CVSS Affected Versions CVE-2026-123007 Memory corruption in HTTP/2 flow control Exploitable in default configurations with HTTP/2 enabled 9.2 1.9.5-1.31.8 CVE-2026-123633 UAF in HTTP/2 Exploitable configured with HTTP/2 as a proxy server 9.2 1.19.7-1.31.8 CVE-2026-121810 UAF in HTTP/3 Exploitable configured with HTTP/3 as a proxy server 9.2 1.25.0-1.31.8 CVE-2026-123634 UAF during response processing in DNS resolver RCE when attacker controls upstream host name 9.2 0.6.18-1.31.8 CVE-2026-113425 UAF in mail proxy module RCE when configured as a mail server proxy with auth_http 9.2 0.5.33-1.31.8 CVE-2026-118899 Infinite loop while reading client request body Potential denial-of-service when server supports TLS 1.3 8.7 1.13.0-1.31.8 CVE-2026-120993 NULL pointer dereference Denial-of-service when configured with proxy_protocol v2 6.9 1.31.4-1.31.8 CVE-2026-125283 Buffer overflow when using alias with try_files Theoretical RCE in uncommon nginx.conf configuration 6.9 0.9.6-1.31.8 CVE-2026-123640 Insufficient validation in stream ssl_preread SSRF-like access when configured with ssl_preread 6.9 1.15.2-1.31.8 CVE-2026-120967 Client certificate bypass Client certificate bypass in specific SNI configurations 6.3 1.25.5-1.31.8 Mitigation and detection Identify affected NGINX deployments with HTTP/2 enabled and upgrade to a release that fixes both vulnerabilities as soon as it is available. Product CVE and first affected version or branch Fixed releases NGINX OSS CVE-2026-123633: 1.19.7 1.30.7 stable; 1.31.9 mainline NGINX Plus CVE-2026-123633: R33; 37.0.0 37.0.7.1; 37.2.0.1 NGINX OSS CVE-2026-123007: 1.9.5 1.30.7 stable; 1.31.9 mainline NGINX Plus CVE-2026-123007: R33; 37.0.0 37.0.8.1; 37.3.0.1 If you cannot upgrade immediately, temporarily disable HTTP/2 on affected NGINX instances: Set http2 off; in affected server blocks on NGINX 1.25.1 or later, and remove the http2 parameter from any listen directives . Test application compatibility, reload NGINX , and confirm the old workers have exited. Re-enable HTTP/2 after upgrading. Investigate unexpected NGINX worker crashes or commands launched by NGINX; these are general warning signs, not confirmed indicators of these vulnerabilities. Technical deep dive CVE-2026-123633: An active connection marked as reusable NGINX keeps a list of connections that it can close when it needs room for new ones. An HTTP/2 connection can join this list when it has no active requests, but must leave it when a request starts. We start by sending only part of a HEADERS frame, which carries an HTTP/2 request's headers. With no active request streams, ngx_http_v2_handle_connection() marks the connection as reusable while waiting for the rest: ngx_reusable_connection(c, 1); if (h2c->state.incomplete) { return; } When we send the rest of the frame, ngx_http_v2_create_stream() creates a request stream and increments h2c->processing . However, it does not remove the connection from the reusable list. We now have a request being processed on a connection that NGINX still considers safe to close. Triggering the use-after-free Next, we need NGINX to close this connection while the request is still running. Forwarding the request to an application server can trigger this. Opening an upstream connection calls ngx_get_connection() . When free connection slots run low, ngx_drain_connections() selects reusable connections to close. Our HTTP/2 connection is still on that list, so NGINX can select it while processing its own request. Before closing it, NGINX tries to send a GOAWAY frame to notify the client. Even creating this frame can fail, for example, if NGINX has reached its internal frame limit for the connection and has no frame available for reuse. In that case, the error path closes the connection and frees the memory associated with it. Processing then resumes in the original request, which still uses that memory. We have reached the use-after-free. From use-after-free to remote code execution The freed memory can now be reused for other data. The request-processing code still follows its old pointers, treating the new contents as the original request or connection. This use-after-free can lead to unauthenticated remote code execution on the NGINX server. CVE-2026-123007: HTTP/2 send_window integer underflow Returning credit for unsent data HTTP/2 allows several requests, called streams, to share one connection. Flow control limits how much response data NGINX can send before the client is ready to receive more. NGINX tracks the connection's remaining allowance in a counter called h2c->send_window . When NGINX queues response data, it subtracts that data's size from the counter before sending it. If a stream is canceled while its data is still queued, ngx_http_v2_filter_cleanup() removes the unsent data and returns the unused allowance: h2c->send_window += window; This refund does not check HTTP/2's maximum allowed window. If the client has already increased the allowance while data was waiting to be sent, the refund can push the counter above that maximum. NGINX is now tracking a value the rest of its HTTP/2 code assumes cannot occur. A bounds check that no longer works The next problem is in ngx_http_v2_state_window_update() , which checks whether an increase would exceed the limit: if (window > NGX_HTTP_V2_MAX_WINDOW - h2c->send_window) The check subtracts the current allowance from the maximum to calculate how much room remains. But the refund has already pushed the allowance past that maximum. Because the calculation uses an unsigned integer, which cannot represent a negative number, the subtraction wraps around and underflows to a very large positive value. The check now treats an invalid counter as though it has plenty of room left and allows further increases. From an invalid length to remote code execution The invalid counter eventually reaches ngx_http_v2_send_chain() , where it is converted to the signed integer type off_t to calculate how much data to send. A sufficiently large value becomes negative. That negative length then reaches the code that describes a portion of a response buffer, leaving its end pointer before its start pointer. When the TLS send path in ngx_ssl_send_chain() processes this malformed buffer, further signed and unsigned conversions turn the invalid length into an out-of-bounds memory copy. An attacker can use this to disclose memory, corrupt the heap, and lead to unauthenticated remote code execution on the NGINX server. We confirmed remote code execution with an ASLR bypass on official NGINX 1.31.7 and 1.31.8 builds. The tested path used HTTP/2 over TLS on 64-bit systems serving response data from memory. Ordinary static files can reach this path through standard TLS processing, without a backend application or third-party module. Exploitation To confirm these vulnerabilities, Wiz Research built proof-of-concept exploits and managed to run them in multiple lab settings against servers running common NGINX configurations we’ve seen in customer environments. In the interest of customer protection, we will not be releasing these exploits at this time. Like other memory-safety issues, such vulnerabilities are difficult to exploit remotely and require the attacker to disclose memory addresses, groom and shape the heap correctly, and handle different NGINX versions, builds, and configurations. In reality, attackers may not need to target every single configuration, and we have seen in PHP2Shell that widespread attacks initially start against packaged products where many customers use the exact same build and configuration. Motivated attackers may tailor exploits for specific targets. Any exploit assumes the attacker is able to communicate directly with the affected NGINX server. CDNs and WAFs that terminate HTTP/2 may mitigate parts of the exploit by not reflecting the exact payload back to the underlying NGINX server. This depends on implementation. Specifically, CVE-2026-123007 requires the attacker to send a large number of WINDOW_UPDATE records to increase it to an arbitrary value. Detection rules covering long standing HTTP/2 connections sending large amounts of data may hint at an attack associated with this vulnerability. CVE-2026-123633 has different exploitation constraints and is more likely to be exploited when NGINX is configured in proxy configuration. How Can Wiz Help? Wiz customers can use the pre-built query and advisory in the Wiz Threat Center to search for vulnerable instances in their environment. Conclusion With NGINX handling traffic for critical websites and applications, the impact of flaws in its core extends far beyond a single service. This research is another example of AI uncovering critical vulnerabilities in widely deployed infrastructure. The flaws were already there; AI helped us find them. As we saw with PHP2Shell , AI is changing the economics of vulnerability research. The same capabilities that help defenders uncover flaws can also help attackers investigate them. Software that has been used and reviewed for years still needs to be examined as these tools improve. The opportunity is to make this work routine: finding vulnerabilities in the software organizations depend on and working with maintainers to fix them. Our collaboration with F5 brings that approach to NGINX, helping protect the applications and services behind it. Stay in touch Hi there! We are Nir Ohfeld and Tomer Schwartz from the Wiz Research Team ( @wiz_io ). We are a group of veteran white-hat hackers with a single goal: to make the cloud a safer place for everyone. We focus on finding new attack vectors in cloud software and uncovering isolation issues in the systems organizations depend on. We would love to hear from you on X or at research@wiz.io .
