title: SSD prices may begin to decline in the latter half of 2027
body_text: When Will Hard Drive Prices Come Down? The 2026-2028 Outlook | DriveVault DriveVault Features Pricing Changelog Blog FAQ Download on the App Store Storage Market When Will Hard Drive Prices Come Down? The Honest 2026-2028 Outlook Published September 17, 2026 • 11 min read • Forecasts and price data checked September 2026 Photo: Sandisk on Unsplash . It is the question we get asked more than any other right now, and it is the most searched phrase that brings people to this blog. So here is the straight answer: SSD prices should start to ease in the second half of 2027. Hard drives will take longer, probably into 2028, because the factories that make them have already sold that output. That is not a guess. It comes from the analysts who track memory contract prices every quarter, and from what Seagate and Western Digital told their own investors this summer. Below we lay out the evidence, explain why spinning drives and SSDs are running on different clocks, and give you a realistic timeline with the signals to watch. We have been following this since the start. Our April explainer on the storage price surge covered why prices took off. This article is the follow-up everyone keeps asking for: when does it end? While you wait, the cheapest terabyte is the one you already own. DriveVault scans each of your external drives once and keeps a searchable catalogue of everything on them, so you can see free space, spot duplicate project folders and find old files without plugging anything in. For a lot of people that audit pushes the next drive purchase back by months, which is exactly what you want when prices are at a record. Waiting for prices to fall? Use what you have first. DriveVault catalogues every drive you own so you can search them offline, find free space and spot duplicates before you buy. Download Free The short answer SSDs and flash Second half of 2027 NAND supply is forecast to catch up with demand from mid-2027. Expect a gradual slide, not a crash. Hard drives 2028 at the earliest Capacity is contracted into 2028 and no new factories are planned. Relief comes via bigger drives, slowly. The Short Version Prices are still rising, just more slowly. A year into the crisis, hard drives cost 134% more than in September 2025 and SSDs 129% more, in ComputerBase's tracking. SSDs should turn first. TrendForce expects the NAND shortage to end in the second half of 2027. Hard drives are booked up. Seagate has most of its data centre capacity allocated into 2028, and neither it nor Western Digital is building new factories. 2024 prices are not coming back soon. Contracts now include pricing, and AI demand is still growing. Need storage for work? Buy it. Buying speculatively? Wait, and favour SSDs, which should get cheaper first. Where Prices Stand in September 2026 Before looking forward, it helps to be honest about where we are. The German tech site ComputerBase has priced the same dozen popular drives every month since mid-September 2025, which makes its tracker one of the cleanest before-and-after records of this crisis. Its one-year check, published today , shows hard drives averaging 134% above their pre-crisis prices, up from 129% a month earlier. SSDs are 129% higher, up from 126%. Both are new records. Drive Sept 2025 Sept 2026 Change Seagate IronWolf 4TB (HDD) €94 €195 +108% WD Red Plus 8TB (HDD) €170 €349 +105% Toshiba MG09 18TB (HDD) €288 €858 +198% Seagate BarraCuda 24TB (HDD) €308 €804 +161% Kingston NV3 1TB (SSD) €50 €144 +189% Samsung 990 Pro 4TB (SSD) €285 €609 +114% Source: ComputerBase price check , 16 September 2026. German retail prices, excluding eBay and Amazon Marketplace sellers. The pattern in that table matters. The biggest hard drives, the 18TB to 24TB models that data centres also buy, have risen fastest. The smaller desktop drives most creatives actually use have "only" doubled. If you are shopping for a budget external drive , you are feeling the mild end of this. The one encouraging detail: the monthly increases have shrunk to a few percentage points. Prices are still climbing, but the curve is flattening. That is usually the first stage before a market turns. Why Hard Drives and SSDs Will Recover at Different Times Most coverage lumps "storage prices" together. That hides the most useful part of the answer, because hard drives and SSDs are made by different companies, in different factories, and sold in different ways. SSDs follow the chip market SSDs are built from NAND flash chips made by Samsung, SK hynix, Kioxia, Micron, Sandisk and YMTC. Those chips are priced quarter by quarter in contract negotiations, and some trade on a spot market that moves weekly. When supply catches up, SSD prices can respond within a couple of quarters. They went up fast. They can come down reasonably fast too. Hard drives follow multi-year contracts Hard drives come from essentially two companies, Seagate and Western Digital, with Toshiba a distant third. Almost all of their output now goes to cloud providers on long-term agreements. Those agreements lock in volume and, crucially, price for years at a time. That is why hard drive prices rose later and more steadily than SSDs, and it is why they will be slower to fall. Portable SSDs are built on the same NAND flash that AI servers consume, so they are tied to the chip cycle. Photo: Samsung Memory on Unsplash . The SSD Timeline: What the Analysts Say TrendForce is the most widely cited memory pricing firm, and its forecasts have been the best guide through this cycle. Here is how its view has shifted during 2026. At the start of the year, it was forecasting NAND contract prices rising 33 to 38% in a single quarter , with client SSDs rising at least 40% as suppliers moved capacity to data centre drives. By July the tone had changed. Its third-quarter survey forecast a much smaller 10 to 15% rise for NAND , and said plainly that PC and smartphone makers had hit the limit of what they could afford to pay. Then came the forecast that actually answers the question. In its July NAND update, TrendForce said the market would run a 4 to 5% supply deficit through 2026, then move back into balance in the second half of 2027 . The reasons it gives are ordinary ones: manufacturers squeezing more bits out of existing fabs, steady output growth, and consumer demand staying weak because everything costs so much. It expects notebook shipments to fall around 10% this year and shrink again in 2027. New supply is also arriving from China. YMTC reached around 14% of global NAND shipments in the second quarter and has told investors it wants to be the world's largest NAND maker by the end of 2027, backed by a planned $4.9 billion share listing. Even if it falls short of that target, that much extra flash entering the market is exactly the kind of pressure that pushes SSD prices down. Balance is not the same as cheap. TrendForce also warns that memory contract prices will remain broadly elevated in 2027 , with cloud providers' spending projected to rise another 50% next year. And it flags that a breakthrough in agentic AI could soak up the extra supply. A market in balance means prices stop rising and start drifting down. It does not mean a return to 2024. You may also have seen SK hynix's chief executive say that 2027 will be the worst supply year in the industry's history . That sounds like it contradicts TrendForce, but it mostly does not. His comments are about memory overall, and the worst of the squeeze is in DRAM and the high-bandwidth memory used in AI accelerators. TrendForce itself now describes a diverging market in 2027 : DRAM staying tight while NAND eases. That is good news for SSDs and less good news for RAM, which is part of why Macs keep getting more expensive, as we covered in our piece on Apple's price rises . The Hard Drive Timeline: Booked Into 2028 For spinning drives, the most reliable evidence is what the two big manufacturers said on their earnings calls this summer. It is not encouraging for anyone hoping for a quick drop. Seagate reported its fiscal year results on 28 July , with a record 52.7% gross margin. On the call , management said data centres now take around 90% of the capacity it ships, and that the vast majority of its high-capacity drive output is now allocated into calendar 2028. Seagate also told investors it has contracts setting both product configuration and pricing for the whole of 2027, and that it is not adding drive manufacturing capacity . Its plan is to cram more data onto each disk instead. Western Digital tells the same story. Its fourth-quarter revenue rose 44% year on year , while the amount of storage it shipped rose only 22%. The gap is price. According to analysis of the earnings call , the company's average price per terabyte rose by a high-teens percentage, and its long-term agreements run through 2027 with two major customers and through 2028 with one, with price terms attached. Put simply: the companies are sold out, they are making record margins, their contracts fix prices into 2028, and they have chosen not to build more factories. None of those conditions produce falling retail prices. So where does hard drive relief come from? Density. Seagate's HAMR (heat-assisted magnetic recording) drives already make up around 40% of its data centre capacity shipments , and Western Digital plans full-scale HAMR production in 2027 . As the cloud giants move to 36TB, 40TB and larger drives, the cost per terabyte falls for everyone, and older production lines can eventually be freed up for the consumer and mid-capacity drives you and I buy. That is a slow, grinding process. It points to prices levelling off through 2027 and easing from 2028, rather than a sudden correction. Tip: if you need big-capacity archive storage today, our guide to high-capacity external drives from 16TB to 44TB compares the options on value as well as speed. A Realistic Timeline Pulling all of that together, here is our best reading of how the next two years should play out. Treat it as a forecast, not a promise. Every forecast in this cycle so far has been revised at least once. Rest of 2026 Still rising, but slowly Small monthly increases for both hard drives and SSDs. Black Friday may bring a handful of genuine deals on specific SSDs, but no broad drop. The NAND market stays in deficit. First half of 2027 The plateau SSD contract prices flatten as new flash supply builds. Hard drive prices hold at their peak under long-term contracts. DRAM remains very tight, so Macs and PCs stay expensive. Second half of 2027 SSDs start to ease NAND supply and demand move into balance. Portable and internal SSD prices begin a gradual decline, with the largest capacities, which rose most, likely to fall most. Hard drives stay broadly flat. 2028 onwards Hard drives follow As current contracts roll off and HAMR drives dominate data centres, hard drive cost per terabyte should improve. Prices should settle meaningfully below today's levels, but probably above 2024's. What Could Change the Timeline It could come sooner if AI infrastructure spending cools, Chinese NAND output ramps faster than expected, or consumer demand stays so weak that manufacturers start discounting to move stock. Module makers are already sitting on higher inventories because shoppers have stopped buying, which is the kind of pressure that eventually breaks prices. It could come later if agentic AI takes off and data centres start storing far more data per user, if more manufacturers follow Micron's Crucial brand out of the consumer market, or if trade restrictions tighten on Chinese memory makers. Signals worth watching A flat or falling quarter in TrendForce's NAND contract survey. That would be the first since the crisis began, and the clearest sign SSD relief is on its way. ComputerBase's monthly price check going negative for SSDs or hard drives. It publishes mid-month and is a good public scoreboard. New SSD launches at the same or lower prices than the models they replace. The recent Samsung P9 and P7 did the opposite. Seagate or Western Digital mentioning pricing pressure or customers delaying orders. So far, both say demand visibility is improving. The drives you already own are the cheapest storage you will have for the next two years. Photo: Samsung Memory on Unsplash . Should You Buy Now or Wait? That depends entirely on why you need the storage. Here is how we would think about it. You need storage for paid work this year Buy now Waiting has no clear end date, and a lost booking costs more than the price premium. Buy what the job needs, not more. Our 4TB drive roundup and rugged 4TB SSD guide focus on value at today's prices. Your backups are incomplete Buy now A failed drive with no second copy is far more expensive than any price spike, especially when a replacement costs double. A basic spinning drive is still the cheapest way to hold a second copy. Just make sure the backup is actually complete. Our guide to verifying a backup drive shows how. You want a fast SSD upgrade that can wait Wait if you can SSDs are the category most likely to get cheaper first. If your current setup works, holding off until the second half of 2027 is a reasonable bet. You are accepting the risk that prices plateau rather than fall. You are stockpiling "just in case" Don't Buying spare capacity at record prices, to sit empty on a shelf, is the worst trade in this market. You would be paying the peak for storage you might not need until prices have eased. Before You Buy Anything, Audit What You Have The most useful thing you can do while prices are this high is find out exactly what is on the drives you already own. Most creatives with a few years of work behind them have a drawer of drives, a few with duplicate project folders, and at least one nobody is quite sure about. DriveVault turns that pile into a catalogue you can search in seconds, even when the drives are unplugged. See real free space across every drive before assuming you need a new one. Find duplicate folders across drives with drive comparison , and reclaim the space safely. Confirm a backup is complete before you wipe and reuse the original drive. Search files on unplugged drives , so shelved archives stay useful. Here is how offline search works . Share the catalogue with your team so nobody buys a drive to hold footage that already exists. See sharing drive catalogues . If you want a system for keeping it that way, our guide to organising multiple external drives covers naming, folder templates and archiving. Every terabyte you recover now is one you do not have to buy at 2026 prices. Frequently Asked Questions When will hard drive prices come down? Probably not before 2028 in any meaningful way. Seagate says the vast majority of its data centre hard drive capacity is already allocated into calendar 2028, and Western Digital has long-term agreements with price terms running through 2027 and 2028. Neither company is adding factory capacity. Relief is more likely to come from higher-capacity HAMR drives lowering the cost per terabyte than from a sudden price cut. When will SSD prices come down? TrendForce expects the NAND flash market to stay in a 4 to 5 percent supply deficit through 2026 and to move back into balance in the second half of 2027. That makes late 2027 the earliest realistic window for SSD prices to start falling, with gradual easing rather than a sharp drop. Will hard drive and SSD prices go back to 2024 levels? Not within the next two years on current evidence. Manufacturers have signed multi-year contracts that include pricing, and AI data centres now account for most of their output. Prices should ease from their peak, but planning around a return to 2024 prices is not supported by any current forecast. Should I buy a hard drive now or wait? If you need the storage for paid work or your backups are incomplete, buy now, because waiting for hard drive prices has no clear end date. If you are buying extra capacity speculatively, SSDs are the category most likely to get cheaper first, from the second half of 2027. Either way, audit the drives you already own first, since duplicated files often free up more space than people expect. Why are hard drives so expensive in 2026? AI data centres are buying almost all of the high-capacity drives Seagate and Western Digital can build, under long-term contracts. Data centres now take around 90 percent of Seagate's shipped capacity. With consumer products a small slice of their business and no new factories planned, retail prices have more than doubled since September 2025 in ComputerBase's tracking. The Bottom Line Storage prices will come down. Just not yet, and not evenly. SSDs are on track to turn first, from the second half of 2027, as new flash supply catches up and consumer demand stays weak. Hard drives are locked into contracts that run into 2028, and their recovery will be slower and quieter, carried by bigger drives rather than price cuts. The practical move for the next year is simple. Buy what you genuinely need, skip the stockpile, and get every usable terabyte out of the drives already on your desk. We will update this article as the forecasts change. Get more from the drives you already own. software engineering, knowledge work, and science workflows. Koray Kavukcuoglu SVP, Google DeepMind and Chief AI Architect, Google Share x.com Facebook LinkedIn Mail Copy link In this article Gemini 4 Neon is available Delivers across enterprise, analytical, and scientific work Built for production-ready code Brings efficiency and control to production-grade workflows Built for fast, low cost, frontier-level cyber defense Designed for safe, dependable execution Built for deeper analysis Start building with Gemini 4 Neon today Today, we’re introducing Gemini 4 Neon — bringing frontier-level intelligence with fast end-to-end task completion across complex software engineering, knowledge work, and science workflows. Neon ranks ahead of comparable models and #3 overall with a score of 61 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at its xhigh thinking level, landing just behind larger, slower models. On the Vals Index , Neon ranks #2 and lands on the Pareto frontier. Beyond just pushing on raw model capability, we’re continuing to make our models better to work with, Neon ranks #2 on steerability (adapting cleanly to mid-task user corrections) on the new Agent Arena Index . Neon also excels at multi-step instruction following and builds on our ongoing progress to curb fabrication, recording our lowest fabrication rate yet in internal Google Antigravity testing. The model is priced at $3 per million input tokens ($0.15 per million cached input tokens, a 95% discount) and $15 per million output tokens, with a 1 million-token context window. Gemini 4 Neon is rolling out today in the Gemini API in Google AI Studio , Gemini for business (via API and model dropdown), for paid Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers in Google Antigravity , and for Pro and Ultra subscribers in the Gemini app . Delivers across enterprise, analytical, and scientific work Enterprise work lives in spreadsheets, PDFs, charts, audio, and video. Neon can synthesize across all of these inputs in a single 1 million-token context window and turns inputs into structured deliverables. Independent evaluations rank Neon as one of the top models and on benchmarks like the Vals Index , it ranks #2 (70.9%), and reaches #1 on both the Legal Research Bench and Tax Agent Bench . Neon also shows strong wins across categories on Surge AI , ranking #1 on most benchmarks across finance, accounting, spreadsheet modeling, and complex constraint following. It also scores 73.5% on Chartography for reading dense professional charts and performs on par with leading models on Agents' Last Exam v1.1 (75.8%). It achieves #1 overall on both Zapier’s AutomationBench (56.3%) and Andon Labs' Vending-Bench 2 ($16,843), a long-horizon simulation of running a business. Finally, it debuts #2 globally with a score of 1336 on Arena's new Agent Arena Index across 4,200+ real-world agent sessions. On scientific and mathematical reasoning, spanning quantitative analysis, mathematics, and technical research problems, Neon is best in class on Terminal-Bench Science (70.5%), RiemannBench (84.0%), and HLE-Diamond (71.3%). Built for production-ready code Engineered for long-running agent workflows, Neon sustains performance through complex, tool-heavy tasks end-to-end — whether running standalone or acting as a fast, high-judgment Orchestrator directing parallel Hydrogen subagents in Google Antigravity. It cuts down on redundant file reads, shares progress as it works, and handles context compaction reliably in long sessions. Across core developer and researcher workflows, Neon achieves frontier performance and is competitive with the leading models in its class, ranking #1 overall on the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index (58.6), with a score of 65.2% on Terminal-Bench 4.1 and 46.2% (at its default high setting) on FrontierCode 2.0 . For production-ready code, Neon handles multi-file debugging and refactoring across repositories with targeted, surgical edits. On SWE-sweep, it already leads on the mini-SWE harness (12.8%) and more than triples to a state-of-the-art 39.0% in Google Antigravity showing what the Antigravity harness unlocks. Driving Blender MCP in Google Antigravity, Gemini 4 Neon used /swarm to build a photorealistic 3D lab bench visualizing the model names with elemental accuracy pairing Bunsen flames for Gemini 4 Carbon and Gemini 4 Hydrogen with high-voltage gas discharge tubes for Gemini 4 Argon and Neon. In Google Antigravity, Gemini 4 Neon wrote a first-person WebGL2 freeride ski simulator from scratch on real Mont Blanc and Chamonix elevation terrain — combining 10,200 lines of custom shaders, 120 Hz ski physics across six alpine lines, dynamic carved tracks, slab avalanches, and spatial Web Audio with zero pre-made assets. Using /swarm in Google Antigravity, Gemini 4 Neon pulled archival photos to recreate Alan Turing’s 1936 study at King’s College, Cambridge in interactive 3D — from King’s Chapel outside to Room X.8 inside, complete with a working Universal Turing Machine running on his desk. In Google Antigravity, a Gemini 4 Neon agent swarm turned a single image into a 100,000-cell Google Sheet with zero embedded images and zero Apps Script — using over 500,000 live spreadsheet formulas to run edge detection, map 3D depth, and relight the scene across six interactive modes. Brings efficiency and control to production-grade workflows We’re refining thinking levels with each new model release to give teams finer control and a smoother progression from one tier to the next. Neon’s four levels scale steadily, letting teams dial intelligence and token spend to what each workload needs. Neon delivers high performance at a lower cost per task across third-party benchmarks. At its default high thinking level, it pairs a high Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index score with a 32% lower cost per task than Carbon. It also sits on the Pareto frontier on both the Vals index and Agent Arena at high, with roughly 50% to 80% lower cost per task than top competing frontier models. xhigh thinking adds deeper, multi-step reasoning for the hardest engineering, analytical, and scientific workloads. Neon shows its highest intelligence score here, while still costing 36%+ less per task than competing models at their highest setting. Built for fast, low cost, frontier-level cyber defense As agentic coding scales, generating secure code from the start is critical. Gemini 4 Neon produces more secure code than Carbon across all easy, medium, and hard challenges on AutoBaxBench , achieving state-of-the-art on the hard tier (76%). Securing systems also means proactively finding flaws before attackers do. Penetration testing has served as a cornerstone of enterprise cybersecurity. On WebExploitBench v1.2 , Neon is state-of-the-art (51.26%) at half the cost of competing large models. To fortify existing code, Neon for cyber delivers frontier-level performance across the code hardening lifecycle — vulnerability finding, validating, and patching — all while being faster and more cost efficient than large frontier models. Finding code vulnerabilities: Neon achieves state-of-the-art performance on SEC-bench Pro (90.5%), while costing roughly half as much per challenge. Validating risk through exploitation: To prioritize which vulnerabilities to remediate, defenders rely on models to check which vulnerabilities are exploitable. On ExploitGym, it achieves frontier-level performance using half the tokens of Carbon. Patching vulnerabilities: Fixing the root cause of vulnerabilities is a critical step in the cybersecurity defense lifecycle. Neon reaches 70.7% on Collinear’s CWE-bench v2 , driving a 3.4% uplift over Carbon. Gemini 4 Neon for cyber is rolling out to trusted defenders in the coming days as part of the Fairwind Program . Designed for safe, dependable execution Gemini 4 Neon builds on improvements from our Gemini 4 safety and security stack — maintaining Gemini 4 Carbon-level protections against severe misuse and prompt injection while advancing further on model alignment and agentic behavior. For a model meant to carry demanding, long-running work in production, we concentrated on: Mitigating frontier misuse safety risks: Because Neon brings frontier-level capabilities to a faster, lower-cost model, we paired it with strong real-time safeguards against cyber and biosecurity misuse comparable to our Carbon protections, while declining far less legitimate work in these areas, refusing for instance just 1.98% of tasks on Terminal-Bench 4.0 and 0% on Terminal-Bench-Science. Advancing alignment and disciplined model behavior: In internal coding use, alert rates from our chain-of-thought and action misalignment monitor remained below the already low baselines set by Carbon, suggesting improved alignment propensity for Neon — and that same monitor is deployed to protect Neon across external surfaces. Neon is trained to complete multi-step work without cutting corners, fabricating results, or overstepping user boundaries — continuing to improve the balance between following through on requests and staying within scope. It matched Carbon with 0.0% cheating on Terminal-Bench 4.0 and took shortcuts on just 2.45% of tasks on our coding cheating evaluation (the lowest rate of any Gemini 4 model). It also achieved a 0.09% misaligned action rate on our agentic safety suite and a 99.2% pass rate on our agent honesty evaluation. On our agentic behavior evaluation, Neon builds on Carbon’s strong baseline by further reducing under-service by 43%–56% and overreach by 15%–35% across different effort levels. Protecting users from indirect prompt injection attacks: On Gray Swan's IPI benchmark, Neon is more resilient than other models in its class when malicious instructions are planted in the web pages, emails, documents, or code it accesses. We found that with real-time safeguards at its highest thinking level, Neon resisted every attack within this Gray Swan benchmark, matching the 0.0% attack success rate reached only by other Gemini models. For more details, see the Gemini 4 Neon model card . Built for deeper analysis In the Gemini app, Gemini 4 Neon excels at work that requires frontier-level reasoning and fast responses. Higher-quality writing and knowledge work: Neon writes clearly, with well-structured responses and a natural, direct tone. It reads uploads like spreadsheets, PDFs, and photos more precisely, turns dense material into helpful reports and summaries, and pulls in relevant details from Google apps like Gmail and Docs. Reliable research and analysis: Neon frequently incorporates details from sources across the web to keep responses current for fast-moving topics like comparing pricing across vendors before a major purchase or pulling together a complex brief with the latest market data. Faster help for tougher tasks: Tasks in Gemini can now run on Neon, working through complex, multi-step jobs more quickly and efficiently than with larger models. Get more done while stretching usage limits further when handing off tedious to-dos, like analyzing billing statements to spot why a utility charge spiked or cross-checking multiple receipts and documents to negotiate a refund. Where Neon sits in the Gemini 4 family Neon is built for complex coding, analytical reasoning, and production-grade enterprise workflows. While Carbon tackles your hardest, long-horizon projects and Hydrogen handles fast everyday execution, Neon balances depth and efficiency. Neon delivers frontier-level reasoning for complex, high-frequency workflows faster and more cost efficiently. Start building with Gemini 4 Neon today Gemini 4 Neon begins rolling out today: For developers: Build with the Gemini API paid tier in Google AI Studio and Android Studio , if you’re a paid Google AI Pro or Ultra subscriber, you can try Neon in Google Antigravity and all Pro and Ultra subscribers can try it in AI Studio. For enterprises: Use Gemini 4 Neon in Gemini for business (via the API or model drop-down) and Google Antigravity. For consumers: If you’re a Google AI Pro or Ultra subscriber, you can select Gemini 4 Neon from the model drop-down in the Gemini app . title: Ruby2ßhell: Pre-authentication RCE on stock Rails
body_text: Ruby2Shell (CVE-2026-132825) | Veria Labs Blog Sign in Get a demo ruby2Ãhell Ruby2Shell is a one-byte heap overflow to remote code execution in Ruby's string case conversion. Reachable without authentication in the default configuration of common Ruby web frameworks and self-hosted software. Severity Critical Fixed in 3.3.14, 3.4.13, 4.0.10 Access needed Network, no authentication CVE CVE-2026-132825 GHSA-34m4-m9fh-gqp5 Affected software Ruby versions Ruby series Affected Fixed in 4.0 4.0.0 to 4.0.9 4.0.10 3.4 3.4.0 to 3.4.12 3.4.13 3.3 3.3.0 to 3.3.13 3.3.14 3.2 and older All releases back to 2.4.0 EOL Frameworks The bug is reachable from the following frameworks in their default configuration . Other frameworks are not exposed by default, but application code that upcases strings received in a legacy encoding may also be vulnerable. Framework Status on an affected Ruby Rails Affected Sinatra (classic style) Affected Other frameworks and plain Rack Not exposed by default Self-hosted software These products bundle their own Ruby, so the fix has to come from the vendor. Products marked Vulnerable have no fixed release yet: every current version is vulnerable. Software Affected versions Fixed in Status GitLab 19.6.0 and earlier None Vulnerable GitHub Enterprise Server 3.22.5 and earlier None Vulnerable Chatwoot 4.20.0 and earlier None Vulnerable Mastodon 4.7.5 and earlier 4.7.6 , 4.6.12 , 4.5.22 , 4.4.29 Patched OpenProject 17.9.7 and earlier 17.9.8 , 17.8.3 Patched Discourse base image Before 2.0.20261119-0203 2.0.20261119-0203 Patched Updated 20 November 2026 at 03:28 UTC . Remediation Your deployment Upgrade Ruby to a fixed release: 3.3.14 , 3.4.13 or 4.0.10 . Self-hosted software Install the vendor's fixed release. See Self-hosted software for fixed versions of popular products. Technical details Root cause Most of Ruby's single-byte encodings have no capital Ã . Upcasing it writes two bytes, SS , but the loop only bounds-checks one ( to < to_end ). 1 while ( * pp < end && to < to_end) { /* room for one byte */ 2 code = * ( * pp) ++ ; 3 if (code == SHARP_s) { 4 if (flags & ONIGENC_CASE_UPCASE) { 5 * to ++ = 'S' ; /* first byte */ 6 code = 'S' ; 7 } 8 /* ... */ 9 } 10 /* ... */ 11 * to ++ = code; /* second byte, unchecked */ 12 } The output buffer is allocated as the input length plus 20 bytes. Each Ã adds one byte to the output, so an input with 21 of them overflows the buffer by one byte. The same loop is in several ISO-8859 and Windows-125x encodings and has been there since Ruby 2.4.0. It is reached by upcase , swapcase , downcase(:fold) and casecmp? . UTF-8 strings take a different code path and are not affected. Fixed upstream in ruby/ruby@d582f8f . Primitive A one-byte heap overflow. The byte written is S ( 0x53 ) when upcasing or s ( 0x73 ) when case-folding, and it lands directly after the output buffer. The attacker controls the size of the buffer through the input length. Copying the result out of the buffer then reads one byte out of bounds. Proof of concept We'll be publishing a proof of concept demonstrating remote code execution on stock Rails on 25 November 2026 , or later if major vendors have not shipped a fix by then. Credits Veria Labs found this vulnerability independently and was the first to demonstrate remote code execution. The Ruby security advisory also credits Stephan Lipp (Ada Logics) and Anthropic with reporting the underlying primitive. Additional discoverers include Moritz Sanft in collaboration with OpenAI. title: Fuck Your AI Safeguards
body_text: Fuck your AI safeguards | ./techtipsy Skip to content ./techtipsy Posts Categories The Archive RSS Fuck your AI safeguards 2026-11-19 engineering , ramblings While refrigerators were getting hacked in Estonia, I half-seriously took a project I’m working on and asked Claude Code if there are any low-hanging fruit regarding security that we could improve. It found one issue that was easy to fix, simple oversight with a one line fix, so I just went along with it. Then it got stopped because of bullshit “AI safeguards”. Oh no, how dare I , the senior product engineer with my product that I provably have control over, try to fix and prevent security issues and ensure compliance with local laws and regulations? “Oh but you can just apply to get an exemption from them here bla bla fucking blah ” Have you READ the requirements? First of all, you will have to wait for multiple business days to get a response. You forfeit any data retention exemptions, so hope you don’t have any IP to protect! Oh, and oh so please give us your fucking ID or passport! We won’t leak it later, promise! WHAT. And you may just get fucked anyway and not get approval. Approval to appropriately protect your own service! This wasn’t the first time I ran into this issue. As maddening as it sounds, I try to keep up with the security landscape and to apply appropriate mitigations because leaking sensitive information is a big fucking no-no and I can’t let that happen. If there’s a popular exploit out there that applies for our technical stack, I need to know if the public proof-of-concept snippets can be adapted and used maliciously against my services. But no, Claude will tell you to fuck off and use an older model that still will try to stop you from applying adequate protection. You know who don’t need to ask for approval? Criminals. They just go and use the models that don’t have safeguards in place. Abliterated open weights models don’t care. Bad actors reach their goals with or without your “safe” models. You can use a knife to cut up some food, or seriously hurt someone. Yet I don’t get asked to put in an application with my government-provided ID to buy one. Why is this tool so special? Predictably, the only way to actually make our own service more secure ended up involving the use of EU-hosted open weights models, such as GLM 5.3, that actually complied with our intentions, proved that the issue is there, and then helped fix and verify that the issue is now resolved, for good. Congratulations, Anthropic, you’ve made the world an unsafer place. Or maybe that was your plan all along to get regulators to react and build that moat for you right before your IPO to fend off competitors? Either way, I’m just incredibly frustrated. Big AI labs use the same tools without restrictions to make the security landscape a fucking mess, and then they go and prohibit others from using the same tools to protect themselves from the threats they just created. Fucking asshats. 1 and that’s my swear word quota hit for the year.  ↩︎ Subscribe for more tech tips! Subscribe to new posts via the RSS feed. Not sure what RSS is, or how to get started? title: 15M web servers on one VM – smoltcp, DPDK, AF_XDP
body_text:
15 million web servers on one VM - smoltcp, DPDK, AF_XDP Â· kapteko Skip to content kapteko Articles About me 15 million web servers on one VM - smoltcp, DPDK, AF_XDP Nov 18, 2026 Put a web server online and everyone starts trying to hack it. Why? A basic rule of economics. Short supply, big demand - there arenât enough web servers for everyone. Letâs run a web server for every human on the planet, all 8 billion of them. I couldnât get funding, so weâre bootstrapping. The goal is to run 15 million web servers on one VM with 10GB of RAM and 1 CPU core. If we succeed, Iâll find some RAM from old microwaves around the house and weâll scale it up so everyone can have their own web server. Demand will drop to zero and cybersecurity will be solved once and for all. Web server Instead of vibe coding it all, letâs use an ancient technique called learning . First of all, what is a web server? There are a few essential syscalls. listen - syscall, asks kernel to listen for connections on a socket accept - syscall, accepts a connection on a socket recv - receives data from a socket send - sends data close - closes What is a syscall? A function that is executed by the OS kernel. Whatever fancy language or library you use for HTTP, it all comes down to those syscalls (well, yes, but actually no). Letâs use C to make it all explicit. We start listening, then read from the socket in a loop and always reply with OK . int main ( void ) { // We use port 0 which makes OS return any available port int server = socket ( AF_INET , SOCK_STREAM , 0 ); if ( listen ( server , 128 ) < 0 ) return 1 ; const char reply [] = "HTTP/1.0 200 OK 
 Content-Length: 2 

 OK" ; for ( int client ; ( client = accept ( server , NULL , NULL )) >= 0 ;) { if ( recv ( client , NULL , 4096 , MSG_TRUNC ) > 0 ) send ( client , reply , sizeof reply - 1 , MSG_NOSIGNAL ); close ( client ); } } It couldnât be simpler: listen on a socket, accept a connection, read the data, send a reply, close the client connection, and repeat. It gives us around 65k RPS. Now that weâve learned everything, letâs finish the article and call it a day: $ for i in $( seq 1 15_000_000 ); do echo $i ; ./server &; done ... ... 28232 program exited with error 1 Hm, why did listen fail? Ah, weâve run out of ports! Weâre using port=0 , so the kernel picks an available port from ip_local_port_range . $ sysctl net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range = 32768 60999 Why are so many ports skipped? Historically, port 0 was created for outbound connections. When you call connect('example.com', 80) , Linux connects to the remote server (the sending part) and then allocates a random port on the host from ip_local_port_range to receive data (the receiving part). There are a few reasons the default range is small. Port 0 is special. You cannot listen on it (actually, you can - https://acid.vegas/blog/the-port-that-does-not-exist/ ). Ports 1-1024 require root. Ports 1024-32768 are skipped to keep dynamically allocated ports from conflicting with existing apps. You donât want to call connect('example.com') and end up allocating port 3306 to receive incoming data. mysql cannot start because you have example.com open in your Firefox would make for a confusing UX. Ports 60999 - 65535 are excluded for historical reasons dating back to IP Masquerading. Nothing prevents us from overriding the range and using 1-65535 , but thatâs still a bit short of 15 million. A UDP server and a TCP server can use the same port, so we can double that to 128k. We could run a proxy in front to forward requests to the right process (virtual hosting, yay), but these are all ancient techniques - in the AI era, whenever you have a software problem, you just throw money at the hardware. Letâs simply connect 15M/32k=450 new network cards to the server. The 65k limit comes from the TCP standard. A port is a u16 , so even if we hack the kernel with find '*.c' -exec sed -i 's/u16/u32/' \; to support bigger port numbers, normal clients still wouldnât be able to connect. Each listening server is identified by a (protocol, IP, port) tuple. That explains how we can use the same port for UDP and TCP. It also means we can use a bunch of different IPs for our web servers. If we connect 450 network cards to the server, weâll get 450 unique IP addresses and be able to listen on 15 million unique addresses! UPD. Iâve heard from readers that the network card is the ONLY hardware component that didnât get 100 times more expensive in the last year. Canât we avoid ruining that too and solve this in software? Letâs use a beautiful technology called AnyIP , which lets us listen on a whole subnet. Many VPS and dedicated server providers routinely give you a whole TCPv6 subnet. We can simply run sudo ip -6 route add local 2001:db8:1234:5678::/64 dev lo to get 18 quintillion addresses (plus or minus one) to listen on. You can do the same for IPv4 - acquiring a subnet with 15M addresses would cost around $250 million, so adjust the command for your environment. Weâll change our server to pick the nth IP from our range: // Read IP index from CLI, shift base IP by it int i = read_cli_param ( argv [ 1 ]); const uint32_t base_ip = 0x 0a400001 ; // ex. 10.64.0.1 addr.sin_addr.s_addr = htonl ( first_ip + i ); // shift, ex. 10.64.0.2 And now we can finally finish the article. $ for i in $( seq 1 15_000_000 ); do echo $i ; ./server $i &; done ... ... Out of memory Hm, one server consumes 1.5MB of RAM, so running that many would takeâ¦ 20TB of RAM, which is a few bytes more than our 10GB budget. Runtime By pure coincidence (what are the odds?), I explained in Running 10 million Codex CLIs on one server - LFI processes why running millions of processes creates too much overhead. The answer is to run them all in one process inside a custom runtime, much as V8 can run millions of guests in a single process. In Userland Linux scheduler in Rust , I showed how to build a specialised userland scheduler and switch between tasks with the absolute minimum amount of RAM per task. TLDR: Weâre using LFI for sandboxing. It gives us memory isolation and replaces all syscalls with calls to our host handler, which lets us implement I/O however we like. To schedule multiple guests, we load them all into our main processâs memory and make the CPU constantly switch between guests - we become our own micro OS. Since we need to save every byte and CPU cycle we can, weâre doomed to build another specialised runtime. Letâs get started. How much is 10GB divided by 15M, exactly? Ten Great Britains divided by 15 million gives around half of kilo britain. Not much. If we run all our guests in our runtime, our custom scheduler needs to switch between them. Whatâs the absolute minimum state we need to preserve for each guest? We can ignore server initialisation and assume switches only happen within the main loop. Letâs take another look at the loop. for ( int client ; ( client = accept ( server , NULL , NULL )) >= 0 ;) { if ( recv ( client , NULL , 4096 , MSG_TRUNC ) > 0 ) send ( client , reply , sizeof reply - 1 , MSG_NOSIGNAL ); close ( client ); } This code has only two state variables, server and client . Both are simple file descriptors. If our scheduler had to suspend a guest at any syscall point in this loop, weâd need to save the following state: struct Context { pc : u64 , // Instruction address to return to fd_server : i32 , // server file descriptor fd_client : i32 , // client file descriptor } We only need 16 bytes per guest, so to run 15M guests in our runtime and be able to suspend them and switch between them, we would need 220MB of RAM. Weâre playing it safe here - we donât need the full u64 or i32 , and with bit packing, we could probably get down to 8 bytes per guest. What else do we need? $ codex "How much TCP connection takes?" Idle connection takes zero, while active connection consumes around 5kb Hereâs what we get if we assume that only 1M of connections are active at any given moment. 14M idle connections - 0 bytes Scheduling state for 15M guests - 220MB 1M active connections at 5kb each = 5GB Only half of our RAM budget, yay! I donât often exceed my own expectations. Letâs validate it: int main ( void ) { // Run 14M of idle connections - just listen and do nothing // SHOULD CONSUMER ZERO MEMORY! for ( int i = 0 ; i < 14_000_000 ; i ++ ) { int server = socket ( AF_INET , SOCK_STREAM , 0 ); listen ( server , 1 ) } } $ ./run_15m_idle_servers Out Of Memory $ dmesg | tail -n 1 'SHOULD CONSUMER ZERO MEMORY' - what are you, stupid? Looks like the kernel still has some leftover comments from Linus. Iâm not stupid, but I have to admit I was below average here. While an LLM is a significant boost for learning, itâs too easy to accept its answers without thinking critically and feel ashamed later on. But hey, embarrassment is a cost of entry - letâs dive into networking in the kernel. Networking in the kernel Remember when I said that our simple server uses only 5 syscalls? I missed one that was right in front of me. Let me highlight it: int main ( void ) { for ( int i = 0 ; i < 10_000_000 ; ++ i ) { socket ( AF_INET , SOCK_STREAM , 0 ); } } That code will OOM in a 10GB VM. The socket syscall allocates around 3300 bytes, whether the socket is active, listening, or doing nothing. Linux was clearly written at a time when RAM was big and cheap, sigh. Letâs ask AI where all the memory goes: Struct sizeof Description struct tcp_sock 2240B TCP state, queues, timers, sequence numbers, congestion control, retransmit and delivery bookkeeping struct socket_alloc 768B A 128-byte struct socket with an embedded wait queue, plus a 608-byte sockfs inode and padding struct file 184B Open-file operations, flags, credentials, reference count, and the pointer back to the socket struct dentry 192B The sockfs pseudo-name, inode pointer, and VFS lookup and lifetime bookkeeping Total 3384B Potato-potato, TLDR, the kernel uses that memory for many things. I was hoping to see some buffer: [u8; 3300] , but it doesnât look like we can optimise much without rewriting half the kernel. Itâs Sunday and I have few tokens left, so weâll have to think instead - how can we bypass the kernel? What are our options? Engineering wisdom tells us that if we canât solve a task, weâre working at the wrong level of abstraction. Hmâ¦ level, level, layer. Wait a minute! We started with HTTP and went level down to TCP/IP. That reminds me of something! Mom! Mom! Where are all my university books? I NEED THEM NOW! The OSI model isâ¦ umâ¦ something I studied at university. Yeah, thatâs a good definition. We started with our app and HTTP at the application layer, then went down to TCP/IP at the transport layer. There are three more layers below that. Can we go lower to get full control and solve our RAM problem? Oh yes, thatâs exactly what operating at the network and data link layers lets us do. What about going to the lowest? Clear. Each layer wraps the data from the layer above it. HTTP Application Â· L7 TCP Transport Â· L4 IP Network Â· L3 Ethernet Data link Â· L2 Physical L1 GET / Payload Payload Payload â¡ ð© Src port 50123 Dst port 80 Seq 1001 ACK 7001 Flags ACK Src IP 192.0. 2.10 Dst IP 198.51. 100.20 TTL 64 Protocol 6 (TCP) Dst MAC 02:00:00: 00:00:fe Src MAC 02:00:00: 00:00:01 EtherType 0x0800 (IPv4) FCS CRC TCP/IP is stateful, but everything below is stateless. None of the lower layers know or care about the payload, so nothing prevents us from sending new IP packets or even Ethernet frames with our own handcrafted binary data. We just need to reimplement the TCP and IP stack ourselves. Are there any examples? Embedded folks have solved this millions of times. The most extreme case is Adam Dunkelsâs Miniweb - it combines a custom TCP/IP implementation and an HTTP server that together need only 28 bytes (B-Y-T-E-S) to work. There are plenty of less extreme, more mature implementations, though: gVisor essentially reimplements the whole OS, including the network stack Seastar is a whole runtime with its own network stack from the amazing team behind ScyllaDB lwIP is a popular C implementation of TCP/IP F-Stack uses FreeBSDâs TCP/IP stack Go, C++, and C are nice languages (well, kinda), but theyâre nowhere near as nice as our beloved Rust. So weâll take smoltcp , which is purely amazing: >smoltcp is a standalone, event-driven TCP/IP stack that is designed for >bare-metal, real-time systems. smoltcp does not need heap allocation at all So, cargo add smoltcp and call it a day? Not so fast. smoltcp is essentially a smart parser and canât do I/O. How does it communicate with your network card? There are 3 ways: TUN is a virtual network interface that the kernel provides. It operates at the IP layer TAP is another kernel feature that operates one layer down, at the Ethernet layer DPDK lets you communicate directly with the network card using Ethernet frames, completely bypassing the kernel smoltcp is kind enough to provide the first two options out of the box, and theyâre easy to use. fn main () -> std :: io :: Result < () > { let ( mut device , config ) = match std :: env :: args () . nth ( 1 ) . as_deref () { Some ( "tun" ) => ( TunTapInterface :: new ( "smoltun" , Medium :: Ip ) ? , Config :: new ( HardwareAddress :: Ip ), ), Some ( "tap" ) => ( TunTapInterface :: new ( "smoltap" , Medium :: Ethernet ) ? , Config :: new ( EthernetAddress ([ 0x02 , 0 , 0 , 0 , 0 , 2 ]) . into ()), ), _ => panic! ( "pass tun or tap" ), }; let mut iface = Interface :: new ( config , & mut device , Instant :: now ()); iface . update_ip_addrs ( | addrs | { addrs . push ( IpCidr :: new ( IpAddress :: v4 ( 192 , 0 , 2 , 2 ), 24 )) . unwrap (); }); let mut sockets = SocketSet :: new ( Vec :: new ()); // Main network loop loop { let now = Instant :: now (); iface . poll ( now , & mut device , & mut sockets ); wait ( device . as_raw_fd (), iface . poll_delay ( now , & sockets )) ? ; } } But what about the third option, DPDK ? When you care about latency A LOT, every syscall is a bloody wound. The syscall itself might take 500ns, and copying data from the kernel to userspace might take another 1000ns, depending on the buffer size. That sounds tiny, but for perspective: itâs common for high-frequency trading firms to saturate 400Gbs network interfaces. That means processing up to 600 million packets per second, or roughly 1.7ns per packet. DPDK lets your program communicate directly with the hardware network card using Ethernet frames, bypassing the entire kernel network stack. You read from and write to a memory-mapped buffer without syscalls: when you want to send data - you simply write it to the buffer and youâre done; when you want to read what youâve received - itâs already there. Thereâs another, less obvious advantage - what happens when a new packet arrives at your network device? An interrupt fires, the CPU core stops executing your app, switches to the kernel, processes the interrupt, and then goes back to your app. Now imagine A LOT of incoming packets, so many that your app gets interrupted all the time. It has a beautiful name, livelock , and I guess debugging it in production is its own level of hell. DPDK lets you avoid all that, but thereâs a cost. DPDK works by running a busy loop that takes up an entire CPU core. It constantly moves data between memory and the network device in both directions, kinda like that: loop { send_from_app_memory_to_network (); receive_from_network_to_app_memory (); } Thereâs another, less obvious nuance. DPDK requires exclusive access to the network device because it uses a driver that operates at the hardware level - two drivers canât work with the same device at the same time. Once you enable the DPDK driver for your network interfaceâ¦ it disappears from the OS. Yep, nothing in ifconfig , if you enable it over SSH, youâll lose SSH access too. I can imagine a lot of funny stories coming out of that. Actually, thereâs a fourth option now - Linux now has an AF_XDP subsystem that does something similar. It lets you bypass the kernel network stack and uses the same idea of memory-mapped buffers to get zero-copy I/O in your app. The kernel still owns the device and interrupts still happen as usual. When a new packet arrives, the kernel runs a simple eBPF filter that decides whether to send it directly to the userspace buffer, bypassing the network stack, or process it normally. That means SSH still works. AF_XDP supports an alternative mode, SO_PREFER_BUSY_POLL , which is even closer to DPDK : you get a busy loop with no interrupts at the cost of a CPU core. DPDK still beats it because it bypasses the kernel completely, but AF_XDP is very close (and simply easier to manage). To support DPDK and AF_XDP in smoltcp , we only need to implement the Device trait with 3 methods if we want full control. Alternatively, we can use the existing crates rust-dpdk-net for DPDK and xsk-rs for AF_XDP to help us. Now the final flow is: The runtime loads 15M web server guests into its memory The runtime scheduler starts executing guests one by one Guest syscalls are intercepted by the runtime and replaced by the smoltcp network stack and its adapters All 15M guests start listening, each on its own address The scheduler polls for incoming data from smoltcp adapters, wakes up a guest, makes it process the data, and switches to the next And now we can finally finish the article. The kernel network stack uses up all the RAM at around 2.5M web servers, and RPS drops as we run more servers. With smoltcp , RAM usage grows slower - 620 bytes per idle server and around a kilobyte for an active one, we got to 16M of servers. DPDK is clearly the beast in this benchmark, with AF_XDP just behind it: Why is this so exciting? It means that by moving the network stack to userland, you can get full control on RAM usage and improve performance. And with custom runtime, you can simply run guests faster. Simply is a bit of a stretch - building a proof of concept is easy. Building a compatible Linux runtime and reimplementing all the syscalls with 100% POSIX compatibility take a bit more thought. And another article. title: Multiple vulnerabilities in Regexp and String case conversion
body_text: Security advisories: multiple vulnerabilities in Regexp and String case conversion | Ruby Ruby Install Docs Libraries Contribution Community News English ( en ) Български ( bg ) Deutsch ( de ) English ( en ) Español ( es ) Français ( fr ) Indonesia ( id ) Italiano ( it ) 日本語 ( ja ) 한국어 ( ko ) polski ( pl ) Português ( pt ) Русский ( ru ) Türkçe ( tr ) Українська ( uk ) Tiếng Việt ( vi ) 简体中文 ( zh_cn ) 繁體中文 ( zh_tw ) Install Docs Libraries Contribution Community News News News Security Recent News (RSS) News News Security Recent News (RSS) Table of Contents Table of Contents Security advisories: multiple vulnerabilities in Regexp and String case conversion Posted by mame on 18 Nov 2026 Seven vulnerabilities have been discovered in Ruby’s regular expression engine and in the case conversion of strings. We are aware of PoCs that prove some of them can be used to trigger remote code execution. We have released Ruby 4.0.10, 3.4.13 and 3.3.14 to fix them. We strongly recommend upgrading. CVE identifiers have been requested for these vulnerabilities but have not been assigned yet, so this advisory refers to them by their GitHub Security Advisory (GHSA) identifiers. GHSA-34m4-m9fh-gqp5 : Heap buffer overflow in case conversion of strings Ruby has a one-byte heap-based buffer overflow in the case conversion of strings. Changing the case of a crafted string may allow remote code execution. We are aware of PoCs that prove this flaw can be used to trigger RCE in some scenarios. GHSA-7x2q-68qv-6p8x : Double free in regular expression compilation Ruby has a double free in its regular expression engine. Compiling a crafted regular expression pattern may allow remote code execution in applications that compile attacker-controlled patterns. We are aware of PoCs that prove this flaw can be used to trigger RCE in some scenarios. GHSA-87fm-7w84-j2px : Integer overflow in case conversion of strings Ruby has an integer overflow in the case conversion of strings, which causes a heap-based buffer overflow. Changing the case of a crafted string may allow remote code execution. We are aware of PoCs that prove this flaw can be used to trigger RCE in some scenarios. GHSA-wpqw-5qxg-m68r : Out-of-bounds read in case-insensitive regular expression matching Ruby has an out-of-bounds read in its regular expression engine. Matching against a crafted regular expression pattern may allow remote code execution in applications that use attacker-controlled patterns. We are aware of PoCs that prove this flaw can lead to memory corruption in an attacker-controlled way. GHSA-3p8q-wmhx-vm2w : Heap buffer overflow in regular expression compilation Ruby has an integer overflow in its regular expression engine, which causes a heap-based buffer overflow. Compiling a crafted regular expression pattern may allow remote code execution in applications that compile attacker-controlled patterns. We are aware of PoCs that prove this flaw can be used to trigger RCE in some scenarios. GHSA-7whj-cfh7-xgm4 : Heap buffer overflow in Regexp#to_s Ruby has a heap-based buffer overflow in Regexp#to_s . Converting a crafted regular expression to a string may allow information disclosure or remote code execution in applications that compile attacker-controlled patterns. We are aware of PoCs that prove this flaw can be used to trigger RCE in some scenarios. GHSA-pvgc-g7gj-pv6h : Out-of-bounds read in case-insensitive backreference matching Ruby has an out-of-bounds read in its regular expression engine. Matching a crafted string may disclose memory contents or crash the process. Affected versions Ruby 3.3.13 and earlier Ruby 3.4.0 through 3.4.12 Ruby 4.0.0 through 4.0.9 Recommended action We strongly recommend upgrading to Ruby 4.0.10, 3.4.13 or 3.3.14. Ruby 3.3 is in the security maintenance phase. Ruby 3.2 and earlier have reached their end of life and will not receive these fixes. Estonia’s Digital Nomad Bet Pays Off As E-Residents Generate €125M All stories → More Latest Issue Culture Fintech Profiles European Business Magazine Awards 2026 About Executive Education Daily News Feed Media OutReach ACCESS Newswire Search Search European Business Magazine Search Home Business AI Agents Ask Better Questions Than KPMG Accountants in Landmark Audit Trial Business AI News AI Agents Ask Better Questions Than KPMG Accountants in Landmark Audit Trial By EBM Newsdesk November 18, 2026 1,807 views 0 comments LONDON, November 18, 2026 — Artificial intelligence has taken another significant step into the world of professional services after KPMG revealed that AI agents examining the accounts of a major UK-listed company sometimes investigated financial issues more deeply and asked better questions than its human audit team. The experiment, conducted by KPMG UK using more than 100 AI agents, marks an important development in the application of artificial intelligence to one of the most labour-intensive areas of the financial services industry. It also raises an uncomfortable question for the accountancy profession: if machines can increasingly perform the analytical work traditionally undertaken by highly trained professionals, how quickly will the economics of auditing change? According to the Financial Times , the project, codenamed Project Exponential, examined the financial statements of an unnamed FTSE 250 company. The AI agents worked alongside a conventional audit team, undertaking tasks across the audit process rather than simply assisting with isolated administrative functions. Join The European Business Briefing New subscribers this quarter are entered into a draw to win a Rolex Submariner. Join 40,000+ founders, investors and executives who read EBM every day. Subscribe KPMG UK head of audit Cath Burnet said the technology had, in several instances, gone considerably deeper into issues than the regular audit team, identifying areas requiring further investigation and asking questions that human auditors had not necessarily raised. The findings suggest that AI’s potential in professional services may extend well beyond improving productivity. It could fundamentally change how complex financial information is examined, interpreted and challenged. From supporting accountants to conducting audits Project Exponential represents a shift from using AI as a supporting tool towards deploying autonomous agents across an entire audit workflow. The agents collected information, analysed and documented data, developed draft conclusions and observations, and suggested subsequent steps. They were also able to work alongside one another, effectively dividing responsibilities and coordinating elements of the investigation. The technology was developed over approximately four months. However, KPMG was careful to distinguish the experiment from a formally approved statutory audit. Although an audit partner signed off on the experimental exercise, its findings were not used as the basis for formally approving the company’s accounts. Human oversight remained essential. During the trial, an auditor had to intervene when one AI agent failed to correctly match regulatory requirements with the company’s documentation. The episode illustrates both the capabilities and limitations of current AI systems when dealing with complex regulatory frameworks. KPMG plans to expand the initiative to as many as 20 larger audits, although the firm acknowledges that the technology is not yet sufficiently mature to be deployed across thousands of engagements. Data quality also remains a significant obstacle, with some businesses lacking the clean, structured information required for AI agents to operate effectively. A challenge to the Big Four business model? The implications for the accountancy industry could be substantial. Traditional auditing relies on large teams of junior accountants undertaking detailed and repetitive work, supervised by experienced managers and partners. AI agents potentially offer a different operating model, automating significant portions of data collection, analysis and documentation while allowing senior professionals to concentrate on complex judgements and exceptions. For firms such as KPMG, Deloitte, PwC and EY, the attraction is clear: faster audits, potentially lower operating costs and the ability to analyse much larger volumes of financial information. However, whether those savings will ultimately be passed on to clients remains uncertain. KPMG has acknowledged the potential for significant time savings but has not confirmed whether AI-driven efficiencies will translate into lower audit fees. Human judgement remains the final safeguard The transition also presents regulatory and professional challenges. The UK’s Financial Reporting Council has warned that the use of AI must not undermine auditor independence, integrity or professional scepticism. There are also concerns about data security, over-reliance on automated conclusions and the possibility of AI generating inaccurate or fabricated information. The fundamental responsibility for an audit opinion remains with the human auditor, regardless of the technology used. The KPMG experiment does not establish that AI can replace accountants or independently deliver a reliable statutory audit. It does, however, demonstrate that AI agents are beginning to challenge professionals in areas that were once considered dependent on human expertise. For the accountancy profession, the question is no longer simply whether AI will become part of the audit process. It is how much of that process will eventually be performed by machines — and what role human accountants will play when it does. & privacy Log out Off Accessibility Mode Seven new world-class models at scalable price-performance Nov 17, 2026 · Announcements · Ignite Back to news Share Share this article × LinkedIn (opens in a new tab) X (opens in a new tab) Facebook (opens in a new tab) Article link Copy link Share At MAI, our mission is to build you the very best models in the world and keep every developer and every enterprise at the frontier of capability. But as token spend skyrockets, we know that you also want models at a price point that lets you run agents 24/7 doing real engineering work. That’s why today we’re releasing a family of seven new world class models at a truly exceptional price-performance. Here’s the lineup: MAI Cyber 2 Flash beats GPT-6 Astra’s quality at less than 2% of the cost per task on the CyberGym-E2E benchmark. MAI Code 2 reaches 98% of the coding quality of GPT-6.1 Sol at about 40% of the price. And against Opus 5.5, it reaches 96% performance for just 5% of the price. MAI Code 2 Flash shows comparable performance GPT-6 Luna at 65% of the price, and Haiku 5.5 at 20% of the price. MAI Image 2.7 is #1 on Artificial Analysis image editing, outperforming GPT Image 2.6 Sunburst (max) at just one-fifth of the price. MAI Realtime 1 outperforms GPT-Realtime 2.1 and starts at just $0.01 per audio minute. Dragon Copilot Transcribe is built on MAI Transcribe 2, the world’s fastest and most accurate multilingual transcription model, and already powers 10 million patient encounters a month with multilingual error rates halved. Decision 1.1 is the latest decision model from Microsoft, 50x faster and 79x cheaper than GPT-6.1 Sol. Maia 200 , Microsoft’s second-generation AI accelerator, is now in production running our largest models, achieving 1.7x more tokens per watt.  Frontier cyber defense built to run 24/7 Security, alignment and containment are the most important priorities for agent development in 2027 and beyond. That’s our top priority. We need to run monitoring and control agents defending and patching live production systems 24/7. That’s why MAI Cyber 2 Flash was designed to deliver frontier intelligence at a fraction of the cost. Built with Microsoft’s decades of proprietary data and world-class security expertise, our models help defenders stay safe in this new era where attackers have cheap and abundant offensive tools. MAI Cyber 2 Flash builds on earlier MAI Cyber models that defenders already rely on. MAI Cyber accounts for almost 40% of scans in MDASH, and 90% of scans that started with MAI continued to use it. Our latest model is now priced 86% lower on output tokens than MAI Cyber 1.1 Flash, giving existing MDASH customers a stronger model at a lower price. Incredible coding performance at a fraction of the cost MAI Code 2 is built for the best price-performance for everyday enterprise coding tasks. Averaged over four widely used benchmarks that target the everyday enterprise coding tasks we see in GitHub Copilot (DeepSWE 1.1, Terminal Bench 2.1, SWE-Atlas and FrontierCode v1.1), MAI Code 2 gives you 98% of the performance of GPT-6.1 Sol at 40% of the price, and 96% of Claude Opus 5.5’s performance at just 5% of the price. We’ve built these models to prioritize the coding work our customers do every day. They’re explicitly not yet tuned for harder problems, like fundamental science research and very long horizon agentic work. MAI Code 2 also been tuned to generate great dashboards and visualizations. In a blind, side-by-side evaluation of frontend work, developers preferred MAI Code 2 over GPT-6 Sol 64% of the time. Try MAI Code 2 in GitHub Copilot today. Read more here . MAI Code 2 Flash is designed for high-volume, everyday tasks like code explanations, targeted edits, routine fixes, and rapid iterations, while bringing quality at a much lower cost. It performs comparably to GPT-6 Luna and Claude Haiku 5.5 at 65% and 20% of the price, respectively, across three coding benchmarks measuring day-to-day, high-volume routine coding tasks (DeepSWE 1.1, Terminal Bench 2.1 and SWE-Atlas). It’s available in GitHub Copilot and in a limited-access preview in Microsoft Foundry . The best image and transcription models in the world MAI Image 2.7 is the best image editing model in the world, taking the #1 spot on Artificial Analysis, outperforming GPT Image 2.6 Sunburst (max) at just one-fifth of the price. At text-to-image generation, our model is ranked #4, making us the second-best lab. And MAI Image 2.7 Flash brings world class image generation for high-volume scenarios at ~$10 per 1,000 images. Both are available in Microsoft Foundry here . MAI Realtime 1 is our first live speech-to-speech model, designed for natural, low-latency conversations. In our evaluations, it outperformed GPT-Realtime 2.1 across external and Dynamics 365 benchmarks. It’s priced for enterprise-scale use, starting at a budget-saving price of $0.01 per audio minute. You can try it out in MAI Labs and register your interest here . Dragon Copilot Transcribe , built on MAI Transcribe 2, is now live in Dragon Copilot, powering 100% of doctor–patient conversation transcriptions. It covers 10 million encounters a month, halves error rates in multilingual workflows, and is in the hands of a third of US physicians. The leading Decision model in the market Decision 1.1 provides model routing integrated right into your applications so that the bigger, pricier models are only used when you really need them. On the Artificial Analysis Decision Index Microsoft is ahead of Jev, Google and OpenAI, while being faster and cheaper. Used by 4,000 customers, it’s 50x faster and 79x cheaper than GPT-6.1 Sol. Customize models for your business We’ve heard again and again from leaders that no one wants to pour their IQ into someone else’s model. And if you build on open weights, can you really trust where they came from, or how they’ll behave when you use one as the foundation for your most valuable IP and data? We heard you. We started with Custom Models. AT&T developed an MAI custom model for 5G network operation analytics and it outperformed GPT-6.1 Sol at 1/50th of the cost. On complex scenarios, they found that Code 2 delivered frontier-level performance at a significantly lower price than alternatives. Today, we’re taking a big step forward with MAI Licensed Weights : models under your control. Take a frontier MAI model, customize it using your proprietary data if you want to. Then run it securely in your own Azure environment. You control who can access it. Your data and adaptations stay yours. And we’ll work with you through Frontier Company to deliver the custom model and embed it in your own products and agents. So that’s MAI, a family of world class models with exceptional price performance: the world’s best image editing model; the world’s best transcription model; frontier cyber defense at 2% of the cost; and world class everyday coding models at a price you can scale. And crucially all of it with Your IQ. Your agents. Your weights. All under your control. This is Frontier Intelligence you can trust, from the company you can trust. title: We need smart people who give a shit
body_text: 🧠 We Need Smart People Who Give a Shit • VioletPixel VioletPixel Justin Michael's notions and miscellanea Blog About Now Contact Feed Tuesday, November 17th, 2026 @ 7:01 PM PST 🧠 We Need Smart People Who Give a Shit Something I learned a long time ago, something that's been proven to me time and again, is that the world is held together by smart people who give a shit. This truth always comes into stark focus when I learn how a complex system functions—or, rather, how it barely functions. When I worked at Stripe I learned a lot about various banking and money movement systems, and it's terrifying how flawed and fragile these systems are. ACH is a great example. It's a complex system we rely on every day that is just barely good enough to function. It's old, riddled with flaws, and encumbered with legacy baggage. And yet, despite all of those problems, ACH usually works great and is generally considered to be safe, cheap, and reliable. The reason there's a mismatch between the technical reality of the ACH system and how it functions in practice is due to a single factor: smart people who give a shit. Every problem with ACH is fixed, patched, bypassed, overridden, routed around, or manually handled by people who have two things: Intimate knowledge of the system The drive and determination to force the system to work Those two things feed into each other. You have to care about a complex system to dive deep enough to learn how it works, and when you know a lot about how a complex system works you care more about it, especially if the system is important or critical infrastructure. Now, you can replace "ACH" above with a myriad of other complex systems—everything from huge infrastructure to nice-to-have apps—and everything I said remains true, both about the systems themselves and the people who keep them running. The world runs on these systems, and they depend on smart people who give a shit. Take those people away, and the systems collapse. And collapse is what we're starting to see. Some recent examples of various failures from just this past week or so: Microsoft 365 , Air Traffic Control , United Airlines' systems , the NSA's network , many major banks , Apple's systems , and more. We're told these failures and problems are not related. They're not the result of a cyberattack. They're not the fault of generative AI. I guess that depends on how you look at it. I don't have inside information about what's going on, but my experience dealing with complex systems tells me there's a common through line to all of these disruptions: there aren't enough smart people who give a shit. So where did they go? Capitalism has never been particularly kind to smart people who give a shit (or people in general... but I digress). Capitalism does, however begrudgingly, recognize that smart people who give a shit are required to build and maintain complex systems that serve capitalist goals. Thus, those people have been accommodated and incorporated into the system by virtue of their necessity and, in many cases, their rarity. Now, though, generative AI is here. To the people running the show—leadership and management—it seems like they can get the same or better value (and even more output!) from a machine. The machine is cheaper, works longer, doesn't take sick days or vacations, doesn't ask for any benefits, and never pushes back against a bad idea. People who don't do the actual work—the people who aren't in the trenches—have a hard time telling the difference between a flawed system held aloft by the drive and determination of smart people who give a shit and slop provided by generative AI. To them it's all just output: words you can read, code that runs, and pixels that look nice to their eye. It's all the same to them, so why does it matter where it comes from? It matters because generative AI isn't smart, and it doesn't give a shit. What seems like intelligence is an illusion propped up by a massive amount of data strip-mined from the commons with weights that nudge the output toward a generally desirable shape. What seems like care, concern, and attention is just generative AI doing what it's designed to do: telling you what you want to hear. The math and logic that power LLMs are as cold, unfeeling, and indifferent as the laws of physics. Smart people who give a shit notice things. They connect dots. They notice when things don't feel right. They know when something is about to go off the rails, and they know how to get things back on track. They know how to handle edge cases. They know how to manually handle a unique situation. They know what the right thing to do is, and they know when they need to put in extra effort or time to make something happen. Generative AI falls far short in these areas, but this is the glue that holds complex systems together. More prompting and more output isn't a substitute for this. It's hard for capitalist leadership to internalize any of that, though. It would be such a relief for them, such a burden lifted, to replace all those smart people who give a shit with generative AI. It would be so much easier to win at capitalism if generative AI lived up to the hype, and there's so much pressure for leadership and management to believe that the hype is real. Thus, a lot of the smart people who give a shit have been laid off, and the ones that remain are hollowed out. Telling people to stop doing the job they signed up for in favor of babysitting LLMs so they can do that job instead is a great way to make people less smart about the system they used to work on and give less of a shit about it. Every prompt moves them one step further away from the system they used to know inside and out. Every generated output that becomes part of the system means those people understand less about how the system actually works. Those people are robbed of the things that make them smart (the struggle of building and learning) and the things that made them gave a shit (a sense of ownership and close connection with the system). We've moved from a world dependent on complex and fragile systems held together by smart people who give a shit to a world of complex and fragile systems run by generative AI. The people running the generative AI are not as smart, nor do they give as much of a shit. There are, of course, exceptions (which is why a lot of things are still humming along), but we are on a course where the number of smart people who give a shit are decreasing, and that's a big problem. As long as the number continues to go down, more systems will fail. I think what we have here is a hot stove moment for capitalism. When you tell a young kid a stove is hot and they shouldn't touch it, you'll find there are two kinds of kids. For one kind of kid, the warning is the lesson, and they don't touch the stove. For the other kind of kid, the only lesson that works for them is being burned. They have to touch the stove at least once to learn the lesson. Capitalism was told the stove was hot, but their hand is on it right now. Unfortunately, we're all getting burned. ← 🛰️ Voyager 1: Almost One Light-Day Away 📊 NeatStats → VioletPixel : Justin Michael's notions and miscellanea Blog About Now Contact Feed This site is view source friendly!
