title: DNS resolvers are the wrong place to fight piracy
body_text: Quad9 Is Leaving France: Why DNS Resolvers Are the Wrong Place to Fight Piracy | Tech Stackups Skip to main content Tech Stackups Home Topics Comparisons Guides Articles AX Search Quad9 Is Leaving France: Why DNS Resolvers Are the Wrong Place to Fight Piracy November 18, 2026 Â· 30 min read Al Smith Technical writer On Tuesday, November 24, 2026, Quad9 will stop answering DNS queries from France. Quad9 is the Swiss non-profit behind the free 9.9.9.9 resolver, which blocks malware and phishing domains. It is not leaving because of costs or lack of users. It is leaving because a Paris court fined it for refusing to block a list of pirate sports-streaming domains on behalf of beIN Sports. With around 20 similar cases still pending in France, leaving the country is the only option Quad9 can afford. Cloudflare, which runs the competing 1.1.1.1 resolver, called the departure "a canary in the coal mine" , and the post reached the front page of Hacker News . In that thread, Quad9's CTO John Todd asked readers to write "a long-form, well-reasoned statement of why France is taking the wrong path", with plenty of sources, and to send it to policymakers. This is our attempt. Every claim below links to a primary document, a court ruling, or contemporaneous reporting. What Quad9 is, and why it matters â A DNS resolver turns a name like example.com into an IP address your computer can connect to. Most people use their ISP's resolver without knowing it. A public resolver is one anyone can point their device or network at instead, such as Google's 8.8.8.8, Cloudflare's 1.1.1.1, Cisco's OpenDNS, or Quad9's 9.9.9.9. Quad9 has a few properties that make it unusual: It is a non-profit. It was founded in 2017 by the Global Cyber Alliance, IBM, and Packet Clearing House , and moved its legal seat to ZÃ¼rich in 2021 , hosted by SWITCH, specifically so that its privacy promises would be backed by Swiss law. As John Todd put it at the time: "Privacy policies which are not backed by law are empty promises." Security filtering is its main purpose. Quad9 refuses to resolve domains that threat-intelligence feeds flag as malware, phishing, or botnet infrastructure. Its about page claims 670 million+ blocks a day across 230+ resolver clusters in over 110 countries . It keeps no user records. Quad9 does not know who its users are, and that is the point. Organisations have come to depend on it. Mullvad shut down its own public encrypted DNS service on November 2, 2026 and moved Mullvad Browser users with default settings to Quad9, funding Quad9 instead. (Mullvad Browser users in France will now be migrated to a resolver that disappears three weeks later.) Quad9's announcement lists dozens of French networks it sees traffic from, including the interministerial digital directorate DINUM, France Travail, CEA, Institut Pasteur, RENATER, EDF, SNCF, AP-HM hospitals in Marseille, France TÃ©lÃ©visions, Thales, and Airbus's Stormshield . Quad9 can't tell any of them it is leaving. As Cloudflare points out , when a resolver disappears, users don't see an error message. "Their Internet will simply stop working." How France got here â The law: Article L.333-10 of the Code du sport â The legal basis for all of this is Article L.333-10 of the French sports code . It was created by Law 2021-1382 of October 25, 2021 , the same law that merged HADOPI and the CSA into the new regulator Arcom . L.333-10 lets a sports rightsholder go to the president of the Paris judicial court and obtain "dynamic" blocking orders, meaning orders that cover sites already identified plus new mirror domains notified later through Arcom, against "toute personne susceptible de contribuer Ã y remÃ©dier" (any person able to help stop the infringement). That last phrase is what puts DNS resolvers in scope. In July 2026 , Parliament passed Law 2026-725 on professional sport , which amended L.333-10 and added an automated real-time blocking system run by Arcom. TorrentFreak reported that under the new system "ARCOM's agents no longer approve each block in advance." Quad9 called it "recklessly dangerous." The cases: from ISPs to everyone â The timeline shows how the circle of targets has widened: Date What happened Dec 2023 Canal+ sues Cloudflare, Google and Cisco under L.333-10 to force DNS blocking of football piracy sites. MayâJun 2024 The Paris court orders the three resolvers to block ~117 domains . Google complies. Cisco pulls OpenDNS out of France on June 28, 2024, citing a court order "issued under Article L.333-10 of the French Sport code" ( archived notice ). SepâOct 2024 New orders expand blocking by Google and Cloudflare. Dec 2024 Canal+ wins three orders against Quad9 and Vercara (Premier League, Champions League, Top 14 rugby). Because it can't geolocate users, Quad9 blocks the domains for the whole world : "we have to block these sites for all users, in all areas." May 2025 A beIN request against Google, Cloudflare and Quad9 is rejected for lack of evidence . Quad9 didn't defend that case at all, citing lack of resources. Mar 2026 The Paris Court of Appeal rejects five appeals by Google, Cloudflare and Cisco (RG 24/09372), the first appellate approval of DNS blocking under L.333-10: "Any filtering measure can be circumvented, and this possibility does not render the measures in question ineffective." The same month, the court issues simultaneous orders against 19 ISPs, Google, Cloudflare, Quad9 and VPN providers . Apr 2026 Canal+ obtains orders against Whalebone's EU-funded DNS4EU resolver , which complies by blocking "globally across our resolver tiers." May 13, 2026 beIN Sports obtains an order (RG 26/02207) requiring Quad9 to block IPTV sites showing the WTA women's tennis tour until the season ends on November 14. It starts with 6 domains and grows to 58 via Arcom notifications. Jul 2026 14 new Canal+ orders for the 2026/27 season target ISPs, Google, Quad9, DNS4EU, Cloudflare, VPNs, and Bing. Oct 7, 2026 The court refuses penalties against Cloudflare, NordVPN and Surfshark because each had made some effort to block. Cloudflare kept 1.1.1.1 out of it by acting through its CDN instead. Oct 21, 2026 The court imposes a â¬1,000/day penalty on Quad9 (RG 26/11882). Oct 22, 2026 Quad9 announces it will leave France on November 24. The ruling itself â The 21 October judgment is short and worth reading. A few details matter: The â¬580,000 figure was beIN's request, not the penalty. beIN asked for â¬10,000 per day per domain still reachable; across 58 domains that is â¬580,000 a day. The judge set â¬1,000 a day in total, running until the end of the WTA season on November 14. The judge used Quad9's malware filtering against it. Quad9 argued it could not implement geolocated blocking. The court (para. 16) replied that Quad9 "appears to contradict itself" because it already "applies automated filtering strictly limited to cybersecurity to neutralise malicious domains on a global scale." The fact that a resolver can drop a name for everyone was treated as proof it can drop a name for France. Refusing to try was enough. Paragraph 18: "Bound by an obligation of means, the Quad9 foundation states that it implements none in order to execute the decision. This circumstance alone justifies the imposition of a penalty." â¬1,000 a day for three weeks is survivable, about â¬24,000. Twenty more cases like it, each running for a full football season with ever-growing domain lists and Arcom's new automated system feeding them, is not. Quad9 says : "Quad9 cannot survive the accumulation of penalties yet to be assessed in 20 other pending cases." Why Quad9 can't just comply â Quad9 is often asked why it doesn't just block the domains. It has three options, and none of them work. 1. Block globally. This is what Quad9 did for Canal+ in December 2024 and what DNS4EU does today. It means a French court decides what a user in Brazil, Kenya or Germany can resolve, for the commercial benefit of one company. Quad9's announcement asks how France would react if other nations imposed their laws on French users through DNS. The answer is obvious, and the reverse should be too. Nothing limits this to sports either: once global blocking is accepted, every court in every country can add names to everyone's resolver. 2. Geo-block France. Quad9 has already tried this, in Germany. In the Sony Music v. Quad9 case , Quad9 used geoIP blocking for German users while the case continued. Sony's lawyers used a VPN to reach the content "from Germany" anyway, the court agreed this was non-compliance, and Quad9 was fined for contempt. GeoIP is a probabilistic guess about where an IP address is, not a legal fact about where a person is. A resolver that keeps no user records has no reliable way to define a "French user." As Quad9 told TorrentFreak : "There is no legally useful way for us to define a French user." Even the French order is geographically complicated: heise notes it covers the overseas departments and Saint-Pierre-et-Miquelon but excludes New Caledonia, Wallis and Futuna, and French Polynesia. 3. Pay and fight. Quad9 won in Germany. The Dresden Higher Regional Court held in December 2023 that DNS resolvers get the same liability privilege as access providers, and the German civil rights group GFF said "the judgement puts the onus on rights holders." But winning took "several years, six figures of cost to Quad9, and massive wasted time," and the opposition, in Quad9's words, "has more lawyers than we have money and time." As Quad9 wrote in 2025 , compliance costs that are routine overhead for Google are, "for small, mission-driven nonprofits like Quad9, â¦ an existential threat." That leaves leaving. Why DNS blocking doesn't work â The argument against resolver blocking isn't only about Quad9's survival. Even on its own terms, it does not do what the rightsholders want. It doesn't remove anything. The DNS only holds pointers. Quad9's Dresden write-up puts it this way: "The DNS does not contain content - it is a system designed for delivery only of pointers." The pirate server stays online and keeps serving everyone who reaches it some other way. The Internet Society's 2025 guide for legal professionals says the same thing. It takes seconds to bypass. Quad9 notes there are thousands of other open resolvers . Users can also run their own, or use encrypted DNS over HTTPS ( RFC 8484 ), which looks like ordinary web traffic. Arcom's own December 2025 study for the National Assembly says 20% of French internet users already use an alternative DNS resolver and 29% use a VPN. Quad9 compares DNS blocking to "holding a piece of newspaper in front of a stadium full of people to block the view of a concert." It is blunt. DNS works at the level of whole domains. A resolver can't block one infringing stream on a shared host without blocking everything else on that name. The IAB's RFC 7754 , the IETF's standard reference on blocking and filtering, says: "From a technical perspective, there are no perfect or even good solutions -- there is only least bad." ICANN's security committee revisited the question in SAC127, "DNS Blocking Revisited" (2025), warning implementers to minimise overblocking and avoid affecting users outside their jurisdiction. France's own registry operator, AFNIC, made the core point years ago in its scientific council's report on the consequences of DNS filtering : "Le DNS n'a pas Ã©tÃ© conÃ§u pour filtrer les contenus." (The DNS was not designed to filter content.) It is opaque. When a resolver is forced to lie, the user sees a site that doesn't load. They have no way to tell whether the site is down, their network is broken, or a court ordered the block. There is a standard for being honest about this: RFC 8914 Extended DNS Errors defines code 16, "Censored", for answers withheld "due to an external requirement imposed by an entity other than the operator." But nothing in the French orders requires resolvers to use it. Blocking at scale causes real collateral damage. France is not the only test case. Italy's Piracy Shield system blocked Google Drive for much of the country in October 2024 . A RIPE Labs study of Piracy Shield found more than 500 unrelated sites blocked and concluded that "IP-level blocking is an indiscriminate tool with consequences that outweigh its benefits." In Spain, LaLiga's IP blocking of shared Cloudflare addresses knocked innocent sites offline every match day, leading Cloudflare's CEO Matthew Prince to call the approach "bonkers" . The same RIPE study found most European piracy is hosted in Europe , which is where enforcement belongs: at the hosting provider. Measured by its own goals, the French system has a mixed record. Arcom reports 12,606 sports domains blocked since 2022, 6,496 of them in 2025 alone (up 71%), while piracy fell 4% in 2025 and 34% since 2021. The number of blocks is growing much faster than piracy is shrinking, and Arcom's figures don't separate the effect of resolver blocking from ISP blocking. Every one of those domains has to be found, blocked, and then found again when it reappears under a new name. OONI's 2025 measurement of French ISP blocking found that of 542 domains tested, 291 were blocked by at least one ISP but only 132 by all four. The European Commission's own 2025 assessment of its live-events piracy recommendation concluded the effects "have been limited and have not allowed to significantly curb the volume of online piracy of live events." What France loses â Driving Quad9 out of France doesn't hurt pirates at all. The people who lose are the ones who chose a resolver for security. French users lose a malware filter. Quad9 exists to stop people resolving phishing and malware domains. Users who move to an unfiltered resolver, or to their ISP's resolver, lose that protection. Users who move to an unknown free resolver may be trading it for one that sells their browsing data . As Cloudflare puts it, "Penalizing transparent services only pushes users toward less accountable corners of the web." Critical infrastructure may break silently. Hospitals, utilities and local authorities on Quad9's list will lose DNS if their IT teams miss the announcement. Embedded devices with 9.9.9.9 hard-coded may be hard to fix. The choice of resolvers shrinks. OpenDNS left France in 2024, and Quad9 leaves now. An Internet Society report cited by TorrentFreak warned that small and non-profit resolvers are the most likely to be pushed out, leaving the field to the largest companies, which can afford to fight or to build per-country infrastructure. Cloudflare can satisfy the court by blocking at its CDN; Quad9 has only a resolver. France's own digital sovereignty goals suffer. France promotes privacy-respecting European infrastructure, yet its courts are driving out a Swiss privacy-focused non-profit while US giants remain. How other countries block, and what is different about France â Governments have used DNS to block websites for years. What is new about the French sports cases is not the technique but who is ordered to carry it out, and how far the block reaches. Turkey: block at home, intercept the rest â In April 2017, Turkey's telecoms regulator BTK blocked all of Wikipedia under Article 8/A of Law 5651 , approved the same day by an Ankara criminal judgeship of peace. Turkish ISPs implemented it with DNS spoofing plus connection filtering . The regulator said blocking only the offending pages was "technically impossible", so it blocked the whole site. The Constitutional Court ruled 10â6 in December 2019 that the block violated freedom of expression, and access returned in January 2020. The more relevant precedent is Turkey's 2014 Twitter ban. It started as a DNS block on Turkish ISPs' resolvers, and people responded by spray-painting Google's DNS addresses on walls. Turkey did not ask Google to block anything. Instead, Google reported that "Google's Public DNS service has been intercepted by most Turkish ISPs", which had "set up servers that masquerade as Google's DNS service." When Cloudflare launched 1.1.1.1 in 2018, Turkish networks silently dropped its Wikipedia lookups the same way they did for Google and Quad9. Turkey's approach is heavy-handed, but it is domestic. The state makes its own ISPs tamper with traffic inside Turkey. France instead orders a foreign resolver to change the answers it gives, and because the resolver can't reliably tell who is French, the block either goes global or the resolver leaves. United States: take the domain away for everyone â The US does not block sites through ISPs or resolvers. It seizes the domain. A federal judge issues a forfeiture warrant (the banner above cites 18 U.S.C. Â§ 981(b) ), and the registry, such as Verisign for .com in Virginia, points the domain at government name servers . Z-Library's domains went this way in November 2022 . Operation In Our Sites seized 2,713 domains between 2010 and early 2014, and in July 2026 the Justice Department seized more than 1,000 World Cup streaming sites . A seizure is more drastic than anything France does: the domain stops working worldwide, for every resolver. But it acts on the alleged wrongdoer's own property, through the registry that holds the record, and it says so. Anyone who visits sees a banner naming the court, the agency and the statute. Nobody unconnected to the site is fined. The US has never had a court site-blocking regime. SOPA and PIPA were shelved in January 2012 after mass protests. In September 2026, two newer bills were merged into the DEFEND IP Act , which would cover ISPs and public DNS resolvers with more than $100 million in annual revenue. That threshold would leave a small non-profit like Quad9 out of scope. The bill has not had a committee vote and the EFF opposes it . United Kingdom: ISPs, and only ISPs â UK copyright blocking began with Newzbin2 in 2011 , when the High Court ordered BT to block the site using its Cleanfeed system, which the court described as "IP address re-routing and DPI-based URL blocking". In 2017 the Premier League won the first live blocking order against the six main ISPs. It blocks streaming servers only while matches are on, with the server list "re-set" each week. That is the same dynamic, match-day model France uses, but aimed only at the companies that connect UK customers. The UK's approach to pornography is different again. A plan to require age checks under the Digital Economy Act 2017 was dropped in 2019 . The Online Safety Act's age checks took effect on July 25, 2025, and Proton VPN saw UK sign-ups jump more than 1,400% . Ofcom enforces the rules against the sites themselves, with fines such as Â£1 million against AVS Group , and it fined one site that had geoblocked the UK . The Act lets Ofcom ask a court for an access restriction order binding ISPs, but as of November 2026 it has not sought one . Before either of those, ISPs switched on default "family filters" in 2013 and block the Internet Watch Foundation's child abuse list, with the IWF leaving each ISP to choose the method and recommending a splash page that tells users why. We found no UK order against a public DNS resolver. When Cloudflare started blocking pirate sites for UK users in 2025, it did so through its CDN with an HTTP 451 page, not through 1.1.1.1. France's other blocking regimes â France itself blocked through ISPs for a decade before the sports cases. Terrorism and child abuse. Since a 2015 decree , police keep a list of sites that ISPs must block within 24 hours, redirecting users to an Interior Ministry warning page. No judge is involved. In October 2016, a "human error" at Orange sent users of Google.fr and Wikipedia to that terrorism page. Copyright. Courts ordered six French ISPs to block the Allostreaming sites in 2013 , and four ISPs to block 57 Sci-Hub and LibGen domains in 2019 . OONI counts Arcom's mirror-site procedure "used 88 times in 2023 to block 549 domains", all through ISPs. TikTok in New Caledonia. In May 2024 the government had the territory's single ISP block TikTok during riots. The Conseil d'Ãtat later ruled that the open-ended block was a disproportionate interference. Pornography. Under the 2024 SREN law, Arcom can order blocking of porn sites without age checks, and the law names "fournisseurs de systÃ¨mes de rÃ©solution de noms de domaine" (DNS resolver providers) alongside ISPs. In March 2025, Arcom ordered Cloudflare to block camschat.net through its resolver within 48 hours. This was an administrative order with no judge, and the Paris administrative court rejected Cloudflare's challenge. Aylo pulled Pornhub out of France in June 2025 rather than comply. The porn case shows that resolvers are no longer a sports-only target in France. The resolver obligation is now written into a general law. Side by side â Case Who does the blocking Where it applies What the user sees Who decides Turkey, Wikipedia (2017) Turkish ISPs, intercepting foreign resolvers Turkey Errors Regulator, approved by a judge US domain seizures The domain registry Worldwide Seizure banner naming the court Federal judge (warrant) UK copyright UK ISPs UK Varies by ISP High Court UK Online Safety Act The site itself (fines) UK The site's own page Ofcom France, terrorism French ISPs France Interior Ministry page Police, no judge France, porn (SREN) ISPs and DNS resolvers France Arcom page Arcom, no judge France, sports (Quad9) Any resolver, foreign or not Worldwide, unless the resolver can geolocate Nothing; the site just fails Judge, plus Arcom adding domains What's the same, and what isn't â The similarities are real. Every one of these regimes uses lists that grow over time, every one hits legitimate content when it blocks a whole domain (Wikipedia in Turkey, Google.fr at Orange), and every DNS-based one is defeated by switching resolver or encrypting DNS. The differences explain why Quad9 is leaving: The target is a bystander. Turkey, the UK and earlier France order the user's own ISP. The US acts on the domain itself. The French sports orders go after a third party that neither connects the user nor hosts the site. The target is foreign and has no local network. An ISP knows its customers are in its country. A global resolver doesn't, so a national order turns into a global one by default. That gives a French judge something close to the worldwide reach of a US seizure, without the seizure's basis in the site's own wrongdoing. The user isn't told. The US shows a banner, French terrorism blocks show a ministry page, and Arcom's porn orders redirect to an Arcom page. The sports orders require none of this. The penalty falls on the intermediary. UK porn enforcement fines the site. The French sports regime fines the resolver, daily, for refusing to change answers about sites it has nothing to do with. Even Turkey, whose blocking record France would not want to be compared with, kept its blocking inside its own networks. It's not just France â Quad9 is the clearest casualty so far, but the same process is underway across Europe. Belgium: DAZN obtained an order against Cloudflare, Google and Cisco in March 2025, and OpenDNS left Belgium in April 2025 before returning when the order against Cisco was suspended. In August 2026, the Brussels business court upheld the core of the order , with fines of â¬100,000 per match day capped at â¬20 million per company. Cisco says its public DNS "does not allow for the implementation of selective, geolocated and dynamic blocking as required by the order." Cloudflare, Google and Cisco have appealed ahead of the January 2027 deadline. Italy: AGCOM fined Cloudflare â¬14.2 million in January 2026, 1% of its global revenue, for not blocking via 1.1.1.1. Prince threatened to pull servers and free services from Italy: "Play stupid games, win stupid prizes." Spain: A Barcelona court upheld LaLiga's right to block Cloudflare IP addresses. Germany is the counter-example. Courts there rejected resolver blocking for both Quad9 and Cloudflare . The EU level: A study commissioned by the European Parliament's legal affairs committee proposes a binding regulation that would require blocking within 30 minutes across DNS resolvers, VPNs and CDNs. John Todd's warning on Hacker News is that "the EU and EC are looking at this issue right now and I expect will look to France as a case study of how to do things for the rest of the region." That is why France matters beyond France. If its model becomes the EU template, every public resolver in Europe will face the choice Quad9 faced: lie to all users worldwide, build unreliable geolocation infrastructure, or leave. The counter-arguments â The Hacker News discussion wasn't one-sided, and the counter-arguments deserve answers. "Hosting providers are unreachable, so courts move up the chain." One commenter argued that pirate hosts are bulletproof and ignore courts, so going after the intermediaries is the only lever left. Another asked the Quad9 CTO directly where the problem should be attacked. This is the strongest point. But the RIPE data shows most of the hosting is in Europe and within reach of European courts, and the commenter's logic leads to blocking at the last link in the chain that cannot fight back. That is not the same as the link that can actually stop the infringement. "Friction works. Most people won't bother to switch." Some argued that DNS blocking is good because it nudges the majority while staying easy to bypass for those who know how. The Paris Court of Appeal used essentially this reasoning. But Arcom's numbers say a fifth of French users already use alternative DNS, the friction is gone the moment one person changes a router setting for a household, and the cost is paid by resolvers that never had anything to do with piracy. "Cloudflare is a hypocrite." Several commenters pointed out that Cloudflare's CDN fronts many pirate sites. That may be true, and it is an argument about Cloudflare's CDN, which French courts can already reach and have. It says nothing about whether a resolver should lie. "The yellow pages would be held responsible." One commenter asked whether we'd accept a phone directory that kept listing a drug dealer's new address. The analogy fails because a resolver is not a curated directory. It's closer to the operator who connects you to whatever number you dial. Quad9 has "no association with these domain names, nor with the operators of the websites." Making the operator liable for every number dialled is how you end up with no operator. What you can do â If you use Quad9 in France , check whether you do at on.quad9.net , and switch resolvers before November 24. Check routers, VPN configs, DHCP settings, Pi-hole upstreams, and any devices with 9.9.9.9 or 149.112.112.112 hard-coded. Whatever you switch to, read its privacy policy first. If you're in France or the EU , do what John Todd asked: write something long-form , ideally in French, make it indexable, and send it to your representatives. Quad9 specifically suggests telling Arcom that its mandate is to balance rightsholders' interests against citizens' digital rights, and that "balance cannot be claimed when the privacy and security of digital users are the collateral damage." If you work on infrastructure , push for transparency wherever blocking does happen. RFC 8914's "Censored" error code exists so users can tell a court-ordered block from a broken network. If you can afford it , Quad9 accepts donations for its legal defence. Its appeal against the May order is still pending at the Paris Court of Appeal. The canary â Quad9 put it this way : "Once the tools of censorship are built, they are rarely used sparingly or justly." The French system started with football. It now covers tennis, rugby, MotoGP and Formula 1, has expanded from ISPs to resolvers, VPNs, CDNs and search engines, and runs through an automated system in which no human approves each block. Each step was reasonable on its own. Together, they have pushed a non-profit security service out of the country while the piracy continues. The sports-rights industry has a real problem. DNS resolvers are the wrong place to solve it, and France is about to find out what the internet looks like when the trustworthy resolvers leave first. title: ID.me terms required for IRS sign-in
body_text: ID.me terms required for IRS sign-in - Consumer Rights Wiki Jump to content Main menu Consumer Rights Wiki Search Search Appearance Create account Log in Personal tools Create account Log in Main menu move to sidebar hide Navigation Main page Categories Random page Top Contributors Contribute Create a page How to help Wiki policy Article suggestion list Articles in need of work Projects hub Community Join the Zulip! Help Frequently asked questions Moderators' noticeboard Report a bug Browser Extension Install on Chrome Install on Firefox Contents move to sidebar hide Beginning 1 Background 2 Acceptance screen and continued-use rule 3 Privacy policy and terms clauses Toggle Privacy policy and terms clauses subsection 3.1 Marketing use 3.2 Corporate transactions 3.3 Arbitration and class-action waiver 3.4 Data kept after closing a wallet 3.5 2023 and 2026 versions 4 Government-verification carve-out 5 Login.gov and paying without signing in 6 TreasuryDirect move and Senate letter 7 References Toggle the table of contents ID.me terms required for IRS sign-in Page Discussion English Read Edit Edit source View history Give feedback Tools Tools move to sidebar hide Actions Read Edit Edit source View history Give feedback General What links here Related changes Printable version Permanent link Page information Cargo data Appearance move to sidebar hide From Consumer Rights Wiki Taxpayers who sign in to Internal Revenue Service (IRS) online services with ID.me , a private-sector sign-in provider, [ 1 ] [ 2 ] use it under ID.me's own Terms of Service, which send disputes outside small claims court to a neutral arbitrator instead of a judge or jury unless the user opts out within 30 days of accepting them. [ 3 ] ID.me's Privacy Policy says it "may use information for marketing purposes" & may transfer information in a sale, merger or other corporate transaction, [ 4 ] though it says information from state or federal government identity verification is not used for marketing for ID.me Shop, its shopping-discount site, unless the user consents or meets another listed exception. [ 4 ] [ 5 ] Login.gov , which the U.S. government maintains, also works for IRS sign-in, [ 2 ] & the IRS's Direct Pay service takes bank-account tax payments with "No sign-in required". [ 6 ] ID.me replaced the traditional login for Treasury 's savings-bond site TreasuryDirect on October 28, 2026, [ 7 ] & on October 29, 2026 senators Ron Wyden & Elizabeth Warren asked Treasury & the IRS to explain why they continue to use ID.me "instead of the government-run Login.gov platform". [ 8 ] Background [ edit | edit source ] The IRS describes ID.me as "a private sector sign-in provider for secure access to government and non-government websites". [ 2 ] ID.me's Terms of Service say the company provides "a level of assurance to businesses and government agencies" that a user's identity and attributes are verified "based upon widely-recognized standards", [ 3 ] & that "ID.me does not charge members any fees for registering and/or using the Service or Website." [ 3 ] The IRS sign-in page says taxpayers "need an ID.me or Login.gov account" to access tax information online. [ 1 ] The IRS says it uses these sign-in providers "to protect your privacy and data through identity verification". [ 2 ] One account covers the IRS online services: "Individual Online Account, Business Tax Account, Tax Pro Account, e‑Services and more". [ 1 ] ID.me's Privacy Policy says some partners, "such as the IRS", may require identity verification "to a higher level of certainty" under National Institute of Standards and Technology guidelines. [ 4 ] Treasury's savings-bond site TreasuryDirect says it uses ID.me because it "aligns with Treasury security requirements and those used by the Internal Revenue Service". [ 7 ] The IRS said on December 7, 2021 that it was "using ID.me to provide verification services". [ 9 ] It announced on February 7, 2022 that it would "transition away from using a third-party service for facial recognition", [ 10 ] & said on February 21, 2022 that taxpayers could still choose biometric verification "through ID.me’s self-assistance tool". [ 11 ] Acceptance screen and continued-use rule [ edit | edit source ] A user accepts ID.me's Terms of Service , with the Credential Policy made available at that time, by selecting "I agree" or "taking another affirmative action clearly identified as acceptance when these Terms are presented to you". [ 3 ] The Terms say ID.me's Credential Policy "gives further details of how we accomplish our identity proofing". [ 3 ] The Terms say the company keeps a wallet for each user "that contains your identity and group affiliation information". [ 3 ] ID.me's personal-information obligations are governed "at all times" by the Credential Policy & Privacy Policy. [ 3 ] A taxpayer emailed consumer advocate Louis Rossmann a screenshot of the "UPDATED TERMS & CONDITIONS" screen the taxpayer said they saw while signing in to IRS.gov through ID.me, showing ID.me & IRS logos and one button, "Accept Terms & Continue". ID.me's Privacy Policy dated November 2, 2026 says by using the platform "you agree that ID.me. determines how personal information may be used" for the user's wallet. [ 4 ] The policy's May 7, 2026 text lacked it. [ 12 ] The current Terms, Version 10.1.0 dated November 13, 2026, count continued use after revised Terms take effect as "acceptance of those changes", "Unless we expressly state otherwise"; a user who disagrees may stop using the Service & close the wallet first. [ 3 ] Version 10.0.3, dated March 3, 2023, said continuing use after notice "will indicate your agreement to all changes", "Unless otherwise noted by us". [ 13 ] The Credential Policy, Version 10.1, published July 1, 2024, requires users to reaffirm acceptance of "the prevailing Terms of Service, Privacy and other Policies and any other required agreements" "at least once every 5 years" or face credential suspension. [ 14 ] Public radio program Marketplace reported that Nancy Kim, a professor emerita at Illinois Tech's Chicago-Kent College of Law, said she found nothing reassuring in ID.me's terms, pointing out that although they state ID.me won't sell data, ID.me can change them. [ 15 ] Privacy policy and terms clauses [ edit | edit source ] Marketing use [ edit | edit source ] ID.me's Privacy Policy says: We may use information for marketing purposes. We may use your information to send promotional messages and newsletters via email, or otherwise alert you to products or Services we think might be of interest to you, including for ID.me Shop. [ 4 ] ID.me Shop, a page of deals & discounts, says it "is part of the Amazon Associates program and other affiliate programs" & "may earn money when you buy products through links on Shop". [ 5 ] Corporate transactions [ edit | edit source ] The policy also says: We may share your information in connection with a corporate transaction. We may disclose or transfer your information as part of, or during negotiations for, any purchase, sale, lease, merger, or any other type of acquisition, disposal, or financing involving our brands. [ 4 ] Arbitration and class-action waiver [ edit | edit source ] A capitalized notice atop ID.me's Terms of Service says they contain "A MUTUAL ARBITRATION PROVISION, JURY TRIAL WAIVER, AND CLASS-ACTION WAIVER" & that users may opt out "WITHIN THIRTY (30) DAYS OF ACCEPTING THESE TERMS". [ 3 ] Section 20 covers disputes "arising out of or relating to" the Terms, the Privacy Policy, the website or the service. [ 3 ] A dispute not resolved within 45 calendar days after the notice of dispute is received goes to arbitration , where "a neutral arbitrator will resolve all Disputes"; both sides give up suing before a judge or jury, individually or in a class action, except in small claims court. [ 3 ] Subject to an age exception, a valid opt-out & "nonwaivable statutory rights", disputes proceed "solely on an individual basis". [ 3 ] A user may opt out by emailing a notice titled "Opt-Out Notice" to [email protected] within 30 calendar days "after you first accept these Terms" or within 30 calendar days "after a material change to the Opt-Out Provisions takes effect". [ 3 ] Section 10 caps ID.me's aggregate liability at $1,000.00 "To the extent allowed by law". [ 3 ] Version 10.0.3, dated March 3, 2023, had the same cap, & its notice listed "A BINDING ARBITRATION CLAUSE AND A CLASS ACTION WAIVER" with no opt-out. [ 13 ] The opt-out appears in Version 10.1.0, in a copy last updated September 18, 2025 whose opt-out text matches the November 13, 2026 version. [ 16 ] [ 3 ] Data kept after closing a wallet [ edit | edit source ] Closing a wallet directs ID.me to deactivate the credential & "purge the associated data from active use", but ID.me "does retain" account & verification history "for up to three (3) years". [ 4 ] Use of the credential with state or federal government agencies "will be stopped" if the account is deleted. [ 4 ] Information given "in connection with a public sector agency" for verification "may be retained for up to three (3) years after wallet closure", "unless applicable regulations require a shorter retention period". [ 4 ] ID.me reserves the right to keep data from "certain high-risk transactions, particularly in government and healthcare settings", "exclusively for fraud prevention and government audit purposes". [ 4 ] The policy says biometric deletion requests "may be subject to an internal investigation prior to completion", "where determined as necessary to protect the platform against fraud", followed by "ID.me reserves the right to decline such requests". [ 4 ] Marketplace reported that Kim said ID.me can keep a user's data for up to three years even after a deletion request. [ 15 ] 2023 and 2026 versions [ edit | edit source ] ID.me Privacy Policy clauses, earlier and current Clause Earlier: Privacy Policy Version 7.1.5, dated December 1, 2023 [ 17 ] Current: Privacy Policy Version 7.1.8, dated November 2, 2026 [ 4 ] Marketing use of information Included [ 17 ] Included [ 4 ] Disclosure or transfer in a corporate transaction Included, in the same two sentences as the current text [ 17 ] Included [ 4 ] Government-verification carve-out [ edit | edit source ] ID.me's Privacy Policy adds after its marketing clause: Please note, if you are using ID.me Services in connection with legal identity verification for a state or federal government agency, or in association with Electronic Prescriptions for Controlled Substance Services, ID.me does not use any Personal Information provided as part of your verification for any type of marketing or promotional purposes related to ID.me Shop without your consent, or unless you otherwise use your ID.me credential for verification with any ID.me customer who is not a state or federal government agency customer, use your ID.me wallet in connection with ID.me Shop, ID.me Jobs, or ID.me Rx, or otherwise opt-in to receiving marketing communications from ID.me. [ 4 ] ID.me's policy says the company "may share" a user's name, date of birth & contact details for reporting with the government agency the user verifies for, & that verifying "constitutes consent" to it. [ 4 ] Terms of Service 10.1.0, dated September 18, 2025 & November 13, 2026, "do not provide consent to marketing calls or text messages". [ 16 ] [ 3 ] The August 18, 2026 IRS help page said ID.me "will not share, sell, rent or trade" personally identifiable information "with other parties, except to verify your identity and eligibility"; [ 18 ] the October 29, 2026 version points readers to "their privacy policies at Login.gov and IDMe". [ 2 ] Login.gov and paying without signing in [ edit | edit source ] The IRS help page last reviewed or updated on October 29, 2026 says that "The U.S. government maintains the Login.gov system", & that taxpayers who cannot verify their identity with one provider should "try the other provider". [ 2 ] The version last reviewed or updated on August 18, 2026 named only ID.me as the sign-in account. [ 18 ] The IRS sign-in page says to "choose ID.me" for anyone who does not have "an SSN, U.S. address, and smartphone, or tablet with a camera", SSN being a Social Security number. [ 1 ] Login.gov is provided by the federal General Services Administration (GSA). [ 19 ] Login.gov's privacy page says a user who creates an account & verifies their identity consents to Login.gov "collecting, using, keeping, and sharing your personal information" as its policies describe, "including to verify your identity and to help detect and prevent fraud". [ 20 ] Login.gov's Rules of Use say customer-support feedback may be used "for other purposes as we see fit, such as for marketing", though Login.gov "will not reveal your personal information outside of the Login.gov service" except "as required by applicable law or as stated elsewhere in these terms". [ 19 ] They also say disputes "shall be governed by federal law" & that no fees are charged for registering or using the service. [ 19 ] In a 2026 blog post, GSA wrote that Login.gov's privacy protections let people access government services "without their information being used for commercial purposes". [ 21 ] Direct Pay, the IRS service for paying taxes from a bank account, lists "No sign-in required"; people who have never filed, or who last filed over six years ago, are told they "can pay another way". [ 6 ] Taxpayers who cannot register online can have a tax return or tax account transcript mailed; the IRS lists "transcripts of past tax returns" & "tax account information" among their tax records. [ 22 ] TreasuryDirect move and Senate letter [ edit | edit source ] ID.me became available for TreasuryDirect logins on September 13, 2026 & replaced the traditional TreasuryDirect login on October 28, 2026. [ 7 ] TreasuryDirect says Login.gov "cannot be used to log in to your TreasuryDirect account", & a user who declines to let ID.me share their verified identity information cannot log in. [ 7 ] Its FAQ states neither TreasuryDirect nor ID.me "sells, rents, or shares your personal information with third parties for marketing or advertising purposes". [ 7 ] An ID.me spokesman wrote to Marketplace , "We do not sell, rent, or trade users’ personal information". [ 15 ] On October 29, 2026, Senate Finance Committee Ranking Member Ron Wyden, D-Ore., & Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee Ranking Member Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., demanded that Treasury halt "a rushed transition" to ID.me for Americans trying to access their savings bonds online. [ 8 ] The senators wrote: Americans should not have to provide sensitive personal information to ID.me as the price of accessing essential government services when a secure government-operated alternative is available [ 8 ] They asked the agencies to delay the ID.me requirement until after the 2027 tax filing deadline. [ 8 ] Their letter, dated October 27, 2026, said federal law requires agencies to implement "a single sign-on trusted identity platform" developed by the General Services Administration, citing 6 U.S.C. § 1523(b)(1)(D). [ 23 ] It said ID.me was awarded a five-year agreement with a ceiling of more than $1 billion for identity verification, authentication, and fraud prevention services. [ 23 ] The letter requested a response by November 9, 2026. [ 23 ] Trade publication Biometric Update reported that two Treasury orders for ID.me subscriptions were placed under "a five-year Treasury blanket purchase agreement for ID.me identity verification and authentication services" with "a ceiling of approximately $1.03 billion", and that "Federal procurement records show about $93 million obligated against the vehicle so far". [ 24 ] An August 31, 2026 memorandum from the Office of Management and Budget , M-26-18, says agencies offering other identity solutions must promote Login.gov as the default option for new account creation "for any user population that Login.gov is able to serve". [ 25 ] The IRS said in an emailed statement, quoted by news site FedScoop, that "Taxpayers can use Login.gov or ID.me" ahead of the 2027 filing season. title: Energy-Based Reasoners: 385x more efficient inference
body_text: Energy-Based Reasoners: Your Recurrent Reasoner Should Be an Energy-Based Model ⛰️ "> Energy-Based Reasoners : Your Recurrent Reasoner Should Be an Energy-Based Model William Chen 1 , Alexi Gladstone 2 , Zeyu Li 1 , Heng Ji 2 , Yilun Du 3 1 Duke University 2 UIUC 3 Harvard University arXiv Code TL;DR – We introduce Energy-Based Reasoners (EBRs) , reasoning models that learn an energy function over latent reasoning states and formulate looped updates as gradient descent on this energy. Its value scores candidate predictions without requiring an external verifier, while its gradient guides refinement and provides a natural signal for stopping. With only 1.8M parameters, EBRs achieve 99.9% accuracy on Sudoku-Extreme while using 345× less inference compute than the next-best model. On N-Queens and Graph Coloring, EBRs achieve state-of-the-art coverage while maintaining near-100% single-sample accuracy. Abstract Looping is a powerful inductive bias for reasoning. By repeatedly iterating a recurrent block, looped models can scale their effective depth and enable multi-step reasoning in latent space. However, existing looped models are not inherently guided by an explicit measure of progress, making it difficult to determine when to stop looping and how to improve upon the current state. To enable this, we introduce Energy-Based Reasoners ( EBRs ), which learn an energy function over latent reasoning states and formulate looped updates as gradient descent on this energy. The energy scores latent states, while its gradient guides refinement and provides a signal for stopping. To train EBRs effectively, we further introduce exploration-based training to discover additional modes and to better shape the energy landscape over a broader set of states. Across four algorithmic reasoning benchmarks, EBRs match or outperform prior recurrent reasoning models, achieving 99.9% accuracy on Sudoku-Extreme while using 345× less inference compute than the next-best model and maintaining comparable training compute. On all multi-solution benchmarks, EBRs achieve state-of-the-art coverage of distinct valid solutions while maintaining near-100% single-sample accuracy. These results suggest that energy-based models are a promising approach for strong reasoning performance. Why Energy? Existing looped reasoners update their latent state without any explicit assessment of it. An EBR learns an energy function that guides refinement, stopping and selection. E θ ​ ( z ; x ) ∈ R Score. The energy rates the compatibility between the reasoning state z and the initial board x . Lower means better compatibility. z t + 1 ​ = Π M ​ ( z t ​ − α ∇ z ​ E θ ​ ( z t ​ ; x ) ) Refine. The gradient turns the score into an improvement direction. ​ ∇ M ​ E θ ​ ( z ; x ) ​ < τ Stop. The state becomes stationary once the gradient is small, so the gradient acts as a stopping criterion. k ⋆ = ar g k min ​ E θ ​ ( z ( k ) ; x ) Select. Among multiple candidate solutions, we pick the one with the lowest energy. Correct solutions settle at low-energy stationary states. Energy, gradient norm and step size during descent on Sudoku-Extreme. Correct trajectories settle at low energy with small gradients, while wrong ones keep moving. Test-Time Scaling Running more descent steps refines each answer further, and running more trajectories gives the energy more candidates to choose the lowest-energy one from. EBRs reach EqR's best accuracy with 7× fewer iterations (left) and 43× fewer samples (right). GRAM and TRM from GRAM's paper; EqR from its released checkpoint. Mean ± SD over three seeds. Adaptive Stopping Each trajectory stops once its energy gradient falls below a threshold, so easy puzzles finish in a few steps and hard ones keep going. Method # Params Sudoku-Extreme ↑ Maze-Hard ↑ Single sample (%) TRM 5–7M 87.4 85.3 EqR 5–7M 93.0 – FPRM 7M 94.2 87.0 GRAM 10M 86.6 – Looped flows 5–7M 97.9 86.7 EBR Ours 1.8M 99.4 87.4 Multiple samples (%), number of samples N in parentheses PTRM 5–7M 98.8 (100) 86.7 (100) EqR 5–7M 99.8 (128) – GRAM 10M 96.1 (20) – Looped flows 5–7M 99.3 (5) 86.9 (5) EBR Ours 1.8M 99.9 (5) 88.3 (5) EBRs give the best single-sample accuracy among reasoning models. Within only 5 passes, they reach 99.9% and 88.3%, ahead of methods that draw up to 128. Stopping each trajectory once its energy gradient falls below a threshold keeps 99.9% accuracy with 10.9× fewer FLOPs than a fixed-depth EBR, allowing us to surpass EqR with 345× fewer FLOPs. Multiple Solutions EBR acts like stochastic gradient descent and can capture many different solutions. Coverage captures the share of each input's distinct valid solutions that 20 samples find. , Katie Bo Lillis , Sean Lyngaas , Davis Winkie , Zachary Cohen Updated Nov 17, 2026, 10:33 PM ET Published Nov 17, 2026, 10:31 AM ET Updated Nov 17, 2026, 10:33 PM ET PUBLISHED Nov 17, 2026, 10:31 AM ET The National Security Agency (NSA) headquarters at Fort Meade, Maryland, in 2010. Saul Loeb/AFP/Getty Images Federal agencies National security Digital security See all topics Facebook Tweet Email Link Threads Link Copied! Follow The highly classified network that the National Security Agency uses for its internal communications is down, according to six people familiar with the matter. The NSA closed its campus to most employees on Tuesday night, reverting to essential personnel only as it works to restore the network, according to a voicemail inbox used by NSA employees and a source familiar with the matter. The move to further restrict staffing levels came just hours after the NSA told employees they could return to work as normal. It is not clear what prompted the reversal. The agency had staggered employee arrivals earlier in the day as it worked to address the issue. The network, called NSANet, allows employees to communicate classified information internally. At this point there is no evidence of a cyberattack, sources said. “The National Security Agency experienced temporary degradation during scheduled routine maintenance,” the agency said in a statement on Tuesday afternoon. “While some internal systems were affected, mission-critical capabilities remain fully operational and our ability to defend national security continues. NSA’s infrastructure is designed with multiple layers of redundancy to maintain operations during planned maintenance or unexpected events.” A source familiar with the matter told CNN that restoration of the network was ongoing but not yet complete. Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said later Tuesday afternoon that the NSA outage was the result of the agency applying a software patch to address major software vulnerabilities that were discovered last month. “The patching that has gone on following that has caused some of these systems to not come back up when you patch them as expected,” Clayton said on Fox Business. “That is that is what has happened at the NSA today.” The vulnerabilities Clayton were referring to are in PHP, a programming language that powers about 70% of the world’s websites. AI tools helped researchers exploit them, setting off a scramble by government agencies and corporations around the world to address the issue in recent weeks. The NSA itself urged organizations to apply software patches. The flaws in PHP could allow hackers to break into websites and read memory that could contain sensitive information, like passwords. Clayton said there is no sign that any of the recent tech outages, including that affecting the NSA, were the result of a cyberattack. A current and a former US official said an outage at NSANet would not impact the agency’s ability to communicate urgent intelligence to President Donald Trump while he is traveling in Asia on Air Force One. Both sources described multiple redundancies and backup networks that the government could use to communicate securely with the president who is currently in the Philippines before heading to China tomorrow for talks with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin. NSANet is “more of a network of networks, and it’s unlikely that a full outage exists given the many redundancies in place,” a former senior NSA official told CNN. “It could impact analysis and reporting, but for highest priority requirements they would find a way to work those. So it is alarming, but likely not crippling.” A voicemail inbox recording for NSA employees on Tuesday morning described the situation as a “code yellow,” the second-highest in a system of three main levels that governs whether NSA employees report for work at the agency’s Fort Meade, Maryland, headquarters or not. The recording told non-emergency personnel to arrive for work in a staggered manner and for emergency personnel to arrive as usual. The New York Times first reported that detail. Sometime Tuesday evening, the inbox reverted to “code green,” instructing employees to report to work as scheduled. It was not immediately clear whether the outage was resolved. But later Tuesday night, the inbox moved to a “code orange,” closing the campus for most employees until further notice, according to the inbox recording and source familiar with the matter. The outage at America’s most powerful intelligence agency comes on the heels of multiple major tech glitches affecting airlines and other corporations around the country. All flights nationwide were grounded for hours on Friday after a massive systems failure, leading to thousands of flights being delayed or canceled. The Federal Aviation Administration traced the problem to a single router in Arkansas. Meanwhile, a massive outage last week affecting Microsoft products left people around the world unable to access Outlook email and Team meetings. And in recent weeks banks and other services have experienced outages, on Monday thousands of Chase Bank customers reported they had trouble using their online accounts. There is no indication that the NSA, FAA or Microsoft outages were caused by a cyberattack. But they are stark examples of how tech failures can roil markets and potentially threaten national security. The US shares intelligence with a group of countries in what is known as the Five Eyes intelligence-sharing alliance, which includes the US, UK, New Zealand, Australia and Canada. That intelligence sharing system has not been impacted as a result of the NSANet outage, according to a source from one of the countries and a former US intelligence official. Tuesday’s outage was not the first time the NSA’s internal computer networks have suffered significant disruption. In 2000, a tech failure at the agency downed computers for nearly three days and interrupted the processing of intelligence at Fort Meade, an agency spokesperson said at the time. title: What is w2rt6byl5nf1opmc-a.com?
body_text: What is w2rt6byl5nf1opmc-a.com? Jack.cab What is w2rt6byl5nf1opmc-a.com? Don't test in production. Published 11/15/2026 Iâm normal . This means I have a backlink monitor for this website. By pure chance, I was showcasing this to a friend when, suddenly, I got a new backlink: Backlinks APP 11/12/26, 2:37 PM New backlinks detected 1 new backlink detected: Most Popular Webpages In cab — siterate.org 11/12/26, 2:37 PM I tap in, 1 forgetting that 90% of backlinks I get are spam, and maybe this one could log my IP or even contain the 3-day 2 exploit chain of doom. Iâm greeted with this: Popular Webpages In *.cab Webpage Rank 23win.cab 110100 airports.cab 124393 pdf.cab 393627 hitclub.cab 422929 7m.cab 457524 max79.cab 712444 keonhacai5.cab 775520 jack.cab 783052 vic88.cab 856609 taixiuonline.cab 874131 Previous Next I sent an early draft of this article to another friend, who happens to be Vietnamese, and he told me thereâs five casino spam sites ahead of me, which I already knew because Iâm Faviconese. I have the most popular personal website on .cab, 3 but thatâs probably because I have the only personal website on .cab. I try some other TLDs. Rebane has the #1 .horse, synth.download is the 11th .download, whatever. Popular Webpages In *.net Webpage Rank sourceforge.net 83 cpanel.net 87 researchgate.net 103 php.net 106 launchpad.net 109 bugs.launchpad.net 128 cloudfront.net 152 behance.net 196 slideshare.net 204 themeforest.net 333 threads.net 388 w*****s.net 432 azurewebsites.net 532 doubleclick.net 579 earthlink.net 626 Previous Next page Redacted? I hover over it and discover it goes to windows.net.siterate.org . 4 Figuring out the pattern of redactions is not the topic of this article. I try .com. Popular Webpages In *.com Webpage Rank google.com 1 facebook.com 2 youtube.com 3 instagram.com 4 linkedin.com 5 twitter.com 6 apple.com 7 w2rt6byl5nf1opmc-a.com what the fuck 8 googletagmanager.com 9 microsoft.com 10 github.com 11 play.google.com 12 apps.apple.com 14 x.com 16 maps.google.com 21 Previous Next page What the fuck???? I visited this domain (two days after it was registered, more on that in a second) and Firefox gave me the error , dnsNotFound. To this day it doesnât resolve. I do a web search of âw2rt6byl5nf1opmc-a.comâ and I see references to the Majestic Million , a name I havenât heard in ages. Sure enough, thatâs what siterate.org uses: Position Domain Referring Subnets Referring IPs 1 google.com 504,763 61 2,177,943 673 2 facebook.com 463,877 178 2,143,213 1,688 3 youtube.com 421,041 31 1,760,838 1,323 4 instagram.com 392,625 92 1,739,231 1,295 5 linkedin.com 353,504 27 1,372,621 976 6 twitter.com 352,472 168 1,352,034 1,413 7 apple.com 283,697 290 845,882 607 8 w2rt6byl5nf1opmc-a.com 274,833 961 853,298 4,759 80 ailawandorder.com 72,898 34 154,976 66 The Majestic Million ranks domains based on the number of different subnets linking to them. 5 This domain is the fastest growing in the top 100. Another, maybe unrelated anomaly I saw is ailawandorder.com (registered in 2023) at rank 80, whose âAbout Usâ page says its CEO is serving as a Board Member at Majestic. This made me check rank 800 in case there was a pattern, and no, there isnât, thatâs nsw.gov.au. Before I got rate limited from Majestic, I opened Site Explorer, and it told me w2rt6byl5nf1opmc-a.com has 241,085,378 nofollow backlinks and 6 follow backlinks split across 5,163,708 referring domains. Checking Ahrefs, I see just 53 backlinks ; they read like the ones Iâve been getting since The Article fell off. All the backlinks on Majestic are âfreshâ, which means in the last 120 days. In fact, the domain was bought (not by me ð) for the first time (according to Certificate Transparency) on November 11, after most of the backlinks. I found an AI-generated PR from 2 weeks ago referencing the domain, and Tranco has data from October 5. Majestic has indexed 1,267 pages on this domain and crawled 27. The site isnât on the Wayback Machine so I canât collect its pages. In the Anchor Text table, the link count adds up to nine. There isnât an âotherâ section. Are the remaining 240 million links images? No, they arenât, it says the links are 100% TextLinks. Then I downloaded Majestic Million myself and searched for the domain. There were six subdomains. 5721d0cd26c13f745e1b368a2b5dfb0c.w2rt6byl5nf1opmc-a.com, rank 157 c0e3930fedc480e093a7bcad1a83c8a8.w2rt6byl5nf1opmc-a.com, rank 424 8628e302afeb346d191342ca114df068.w2rt6byl5nf1opmc-a.com, rank 554 2b1774347fbd085c628179dd339ddd26.w2rt6byl5nf1opmc-a.com, rank 822 e62f444581ce540d3cf5ac627b37c501.w2rt6byl5nf1opmc-a.com, rank 1,111 56aa73e7edd6f4e1fd3975b8b03761c0.w2rt6byl5nf1opmc-a.com, rank 36,933 For comparison, jack.cab, which youâve clearly heard of, is rank 804,163. What the fuck is going on? By the way, w2rt6byl5nf1opmc-a.com is at rank 38 on Tranco, which was designed to protect against this but still uses Majestic data. Theories I could probably figure out whatâs happening here in 30 seconds by buying a Majestic subscription but Iâm lazy. Copyright trap : maybe itâs fake, injected into the list by Majestic so they can discover whoâs using their list. Could w2rt6byl5nf1opmc-a.com and ailawandorder.com be in the top 100 for this reason? Probably not, because if they cared, theyâd relicense the list away from CC-BY. Also, the domains are ranking higher in Majestic over time instead of staying static. Majestic got hacked , and the hackers for some reason decided to tamper with the DB like this. No. Are you stupid, are you dumb, are you Dario Amodei, are you all three â½ Some loophole/gaming the rankings : Maybe âsubnetsâ is counted in a stupid way for IPv6 . Maybe the millions of domains are ip6.arpa. Majestic counts Class C subnets. A bunch of hacked websites linking to the domain : Seems unlikely, considering Iâm unable to find a single backlink in the wild that wouldnât be there for say, my website, and Ahrefs only has 53 backlinks for this domain. They could be cloaking . Update (November 16): Answer! Love the article! I work for Majestic Great spot. the answer: Some internal experimentation. Choose a domain, make it esoteric, do some experiments. However, looks like we forgot to add a filter to avoid reporting it. We will sort thatâ¦ â Steve Pitchford Moral of the story: donât test in production. AI disclosure All prose written by me, with no AI output, including but not limited to agents, chatbots, inline completions, or keyboard autocomplete. I choose not to be a meat proxy. I used a chatbot to convert four screenshots to HTML + CSS, to make the article responsive: Removed CSS from http://siterate.org/css/commons.css that wasnât being used in its tables . Then I handcrafted artisan jackslop: I copied and pasted the tables from the site, changed the [domain].siterank.org links to easter eggs since they donât resolve, and made the favicons have a stable size and load lazily. For the .com ranking, a friend gave me the idea of annotating the table, which I too implemented by hand. Generated a Discord message component from scratch, using the messageâs HTML and computed styles as context . Iâm not too satisfied with the result. Besides the corrections I made in the conversation, I wrapped it in a background, then manually added Discordâs .headerText { margin-inline-end: .25rem } , then changed the App tag from height: .9375em to height: 1.1em because it felt wrong. An early draft of this article joked about siterate.org being the first site I saw imitating Bootstrap without using Bootstrap, but during the embed process, the chatbot told me commons.css was actually bundled Bootstrap, so I removed that joke. Footnotes As opposed to clicking it, because I was on a phone at the time â© I forgot when I last updated Firefox. I mean, I know now because I updated it after I wrote this sentence. My phone hadnât done it automatically because I had low storage. â© On both Majestic and Tranco. â© Which doesnât resolve. â© Pretty sure ~20% of websites are behind the same set of Cloudflare IPs, so I donât know how well this works now. â© Reply on Bluesky Bluesky ! title: Harvard researchers find AI coding agents shifted the bottleneck to code review
body_text: Harvard researchers find AI coding agents shifted the bottleneck to code review Skip to content Antitrust Cyber Investments Markets Surveys Buyers Guide Geopolitics Newsletters Subscribe About Harvard researchers find AI coding agents shifted the bottleneck to code review Oct 13, 2026 Editor’s Note: Engineers at firms that adopted AI coding agents added about 30 percent more code, yet finished work did not measurably rise and getting code through review took 49 percent longer, according to a working paper by Harvard Ph.D. candidates Fiona Chen and James Stratton covering 718 firms. The paper, a job-market paper with no indication of completed peer review, measures what happens at the human checkpoint once drafting speeds up. Harvey’s motion-to-dismiss workflow and Cooley’s redaction agent, still in development with Google Cloud, both keep a lawyer at a comparable checkpoint, and neither announcement reports a measure of that review stage. For eDiscovery, privacy and compliance professionals, the study suggests a measurement approach for legal AI buyers: consider approved work product, revision rates and reviewer time alongside drafting output. It also shows that AI authorship can leave metadata in collaboration systems that records and legal hold programs may need to reach. Watch for a revised version of the paper and for any legal vendor that publishes review-stage figures, keeping in mind that the study examined software, not legal work. Content Assessment: Harvard researchers find AI coding agents shifted the bottleneck to code review Information - 92% Insight - 90% Relevance - 88% Objectivity - 90% Authority - 92% 90 % Excellent A short percentage-based assessment of the qualitative benefit expressed as a percentage of positive reception of the recent article from ComplexDiscovery OÜ titled, "Harvard researchers find AI coding agents shifted the bottleneck to code review." News Analysis – Artificial Intelligence Beat Harvard researchers find AI coding agents shifted the bottleneck to code review ComplexDiscovery OÜ Staff Engineers at firms that adopted AI coding agents added about 30 percent more code, but finished work did not measurably rise and getting code through review took 49 percent longer, a Harvard working paper found. In the study’s data, the extra coding produced no detectable rise in finished work, and code review became the bottleneck. Fiona Chen and James Stratton, both Ph.D. candidates at Harvard University, measured that pattern across 725,938 workers at 718 companies. Two legal AI announcements this month, Harvey’s motion-to-dismiss workflow and a court-filing redaction agent Cooley is developing with Google Cloud, place a lawyer at a comparable review step, and neither reports a measure of it. What the Harvard data measured How much weight that pattern can bear depends on where the numbers came from. Chen and Stratton built the study on data from Jellyfish, a company that sells an analytics platform tracking engineering activity, and joined it to LinkedIn employment records collected by Revelio Labs. The sample runs from January 2021 to March 2026 and covers Jellyfish client firms that consented to research use of their data. The paper’s tables list 68.3 million Jira issues, 200.9 million commits, 49.1 million pull requests and 21.3 million calendar events, though only 213 of the 718 firms supplied calendar data. The design is a staggered difference-in-differences comparison, which tracks month by month how outcomes changed at adopting firms against firms that had not yet adopted. A comparison like that is only as good as the reasons adoption dates differed, and here the authors point to a process legal and security teams will recognize, because they sit inside it. The paper says timing was shaped mainly by when firms learned about the tools and by how long procurement took, meaning sourcing, legal and security approvals and pilot programs. One interviewee’s firm approved a tool in about a day; another interviewee put the average approval time at six to 12 months. The authors call those procurement delays plausibly unrelated to how fast a firm was growing, which they argue supports comparing early and late adopters. They acknowledge one known imbalance, that larger firms adopted earlier, and they control for firm size. If some hidden difference remains, the authors say, it would more likely make AI look more productive than it is, not less. A bias in that direction would make the flat output result, if anything, generous to AI. The current version of the paper is dated Aug. 4, 2026, and the first was dated Jan. 7. Chen circulated it as her job-market paper, and nothing in the version reviewed for this article indicates journal acceptance or completed peer review. Her website lists coverage links to The Wall Street Journal and The Economist, and legal trade press picked it up this month, including an Oct. 12 eDiscovery Today post by Doug Austin that relayed an Ars Technica report. Drafts went up and finished issues did not With that provenance in view, the coding results are large. Lines of code added rose by 1,494 per worker-month against a baseline of 5,017, about 30 percent. Commits rose 20 percent, and pull requests, the bundles of code submitted for review, rose 23 percent. The authors note that these estimates capture the added effect of agents at firms that already had AI coding assistants, not the effect of AI from a standing start. Output is where the gain stops. The paper counts finished work as Jira issues resolved, and an issue counts as complete when its code is deployed to production. Agents moved that measure by 0.12 issues per worker-month on a 3.67 baseline, with a standard error of 0.17. That result is statistically indistinguishable from zero, and the 95 percent confidence interval rules out an increase above about 12 percent of the baseline, well short of the 30 percent rise in code written. The authors tested the obvious escape route. If engineers had shifted to larger tasks, a flat issue count would understate real output. So the researchers labeled a 0.5 percent sample of issues by size with GPT-4o and extended those labels to every issue with a text-embedding model. They found no shift in average issue size, and pull requests did not grow larger either, which the authors use to set aside the simplest explanation for what happened in review. Where the shortfall shows up: the review queue The paper locates the shortfall in code review. The time from pull request submission to merge rose 3.45 days on a 7.03-day baseline, a 49 percent increase. The share of pull requests receiving a formal change request increased by about 12 percentage points from a baseline of 13 percent, nearly doubling, and review comments per pull request rose 35 percent. The share of workers doing any code review rose 14 percent from a base of about 29 percent, while the share writing code showed no measurable change. AI review tools did not remove the bottleneck. By March 2026, nearly 80 percent of the firms had used one, yet AI generated only 23.3 percent of review comments, and only 10.8 percent of pull requests received even one AI comment. The authors write that the bottleneck persists after firms adopt such tools. The paper’s interviews show what that looks like on a team: a junior software engineer described a project where only one senior engineer could approve changes and could review the interviewee’s code only once a week. “After some outages that were caused by AI-generated commits, there were also new rules requiring senior engineer approval for AI-generated code, which created even more review bottlenecks,” the engineer said, in a quote the authors say they lightly edited for clarity. That account fits the model the authors use to explain their numbers, which has two channels. In the first, faster drafting sends more code to a fixed pool of reviewers, a problem that moving labor into review can largely relieve. In the second, the rise in change requests and comments, which faster drafting alone does not explain, reads through the model as a sign of lower-quality drafts. That problem, the authors say, would require better technology. Anyone buying an agent should care which channel dominates, because the two call for different spending. Employment did not move either Nor did the coding gains show up as job cuts. The estimates rule out a decline in overall employment larger than 2.9 percent. A noisier estimate rules out a decline in engineering employment larger than 13.8 percent. The authors caution that these are short-run effects measured in partial equilibrium, which could mask job losses at competing firms, and that the assistant estimate for engineering employment shows upward pre-trends that make it hard to read causally. Legal AI tools are designed around a similar checkpoint Those software results arrive as legal AI tools adopt a related design, and the Harvey and Cooley announcements both follow it: automate a first pass, then keep a lawyer at the checkpoint. Harvey’s workflow, co-developed with LexisNexis and announced Oct. 7, is the drafting case. Harvey says the multi-step process of reading the complaint, researching and drafting a motion to dismiss “commonly takes 40 to 50+ hours of work” and that its tool produces the research and a first draft “in a matter of hours.” The announcement describes “human checkpoints at the moments where a lawyer’s judgment matters most,” but it does not state how long lawyers spend at those checkpoints or how long it takes to reach a motion ready to file. Cooley’s Oct. 8 announcement applies the same posture to a different task, since its agent recommends redactions rather than drafting arguments. Cooley says the agent is still being developed and that attorneys make all redaction determinations before a filing goes to the court, which puts the human checkpoint at the last step before submission. As ComplexDiscovery reported Oct. 10, the announcement carries no error rate. For a motion filed in federal court, the checkpoint is a legal duty rather than a design choice. Under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 11(b), an attorney presenting a motion certifies several things about it to the best of the attorney’s knowledge, information and belief, “formed after an inquiry reasonable under the circumstances.” Its legal contentions must be “warranted by existing law or by a nonfrivolous argument for extending, modifying, or reversing existing law or for establishing new law.” Its factual contentions must have evidentiary support or, if specifically so identified, be likely to have it after a reasonable opportunity for further investigation or discovery. A first draft can arrive in hours, but that inquiry stays with the attorney, and the software evidence raises the possibility that review could absorb some of the drafting savings. The paper’s method carries a second lesson, this one for information governance teams. The researchers identified agent use partly from traces inside the firms’ own systems, including bot accounts tied to AI tools and signatures such as “Co-authored-by” lines in commit messages and pull request descriptions. AI authorship can leave its own metadata trail in collaboration systems. That trail is a record that a retention schedule and a legal hold may need to reach. None of this means legal work will behave like software, and the limits of the comparison matter. Document review is not code review, a production is not a pull request, and Chen and Stratton studied no legal work. A separate National Bureau of Economic Research working paper, revised in September 2026, reports a similar falloff using data on over 500,000 GitHub developers. Its authors, Mert Demirer, Leon Musolff and Liyuan Yang, found a 240 percent cumulative rise in commits from autonomous agents shrinking to 30 percent for actual releases. That paper carries its own disclosure: Demirer and Musolff each previously held a postdoctoral research position at Microsoft, which owns GitHub, and each now works as a paid research consultant for the company. Two software studies point to a pattern in software, not a finding about law firms. Document review offers a partial precedent Discovery practitioners have argued a version of this question before, and Austin’s post draws that comparison. He wrote that discovery has seen a similar debate over generative AI review, with some practitioners saying manual validation offsets the gains and others, including him, saying statistical sampling of the kind used in predictive coding is enough. For coding agents, though, he wrote that the extra review time may be warranted, since code that is 90 percent correct can still fail to run. His comparison suggests a useful split between two kinds of legal output. Population-level work such as first-pass relevance review can be validated by sampling. A single filing is different, because its citations, factual assertions and sensitive data generally need direct examination when one fabricated citation or one missed Social Security number is the failure. Buyers can turn that split into a test. Ask a vendor which kind of output its agent produces, then ask for the downstream measure rather than the drafting one: hours from upload to an approved work product, the share of drafts a reviewing attorney sent back and reviewer time per matter. Budget review capacity before scaling drafting volume, and log what reviewers change, because that log shows whether the bottleneck is volume or quality. Read the paper’s limits as closely as its findings Those questions apply to the paper’s own sourcing, too. The data partner has a commercial interest in the subject, and the relationship runs deeper than a data license. Jellyfish describes itself as an “AI Impact Platform,” and the authors have published on its blog: a Sept. 25, 2025, post by Chen and Stratton described itself as “part of our ongoing work with Jellyfish.” The paper thanks the Jellyfish team “for their partnership” and states that Jellyfish reviewed the manuscript only to check for proprietary disclosure, not for scientific content, and that the conclusions are the authors’. Its funders were the Stripe Economics of AI Fellowship, a Harvard Kennedy School program on wealth distribution and the Schmidt Sciences AI at Work Program. Jellyfish has also promoted an earlier version of the work. A Jan. 28 post on its blog by Nicholas Arcolano called it “a preliminary version of a new paper from our collaborators at Harvard Economics, Fiona Chen and James Stratton,” based on 100,000 software engineers across 500 companies. That post, and a March 17 Jellyfish press release after it, reported that AI was making coding faster and that “code quality doesn’t seem to be suffering.” The August version, built on a larger sample running through March 2026, reads the near-doubling in change requests through its model as a possible sign of lower draft quality. The two descriptions rest on different versions and samples, so they need not conflict, but a reader relying on Jellyfish’s summary would miss the quality question the current paper raises. The paper also carries small internal inconsistencies that do not touch the headline agent estimates. Its introduction rounds the sample to about 700 firms and 700,000 workers, and its main text describes 17 interviews where an appendix describes 21. Other limits are structural rather than clerical: the underlying data are proprietary, and use of AI tools through individual licenses goes unrecorded. None of those caveats overturns the central result, though the March 2026 data cutoff means a revision could move the figures. What the paper offers is a standard the two legal announcements discussed here do not meet: named authors, a disclosed method, a confidence interval and a measured checkpoint. If an agent cuts 40 hours of research and drafting to a few, how many of those hours reappear on the desk of the lawyer who signs the motion?
