[exclude_from_rss] [taq_review] [/exclude_from_rss] Industry News - Technology Beat Slush 2026 brings a smaller, sharper bet on European startups to Helsinki ComplexDiscovery Staff Finland marks the International Day for Failure today, a custom that began in 2010 when a student group at Aalto University proposed celebrating failure instead of lamenting it, Yle reported. Five weeks from now, a startup event that Aalto says its student community helped spark will test how far that appetite for risk can carry European technology. Slush 2026 runs Nov. 18 and 19 at Messukeskus, the Helsinki Expo and Convention Centre, with Investor Day and a founders' program on Nov. 17. The organizers have branded this edition a bet on Europe. The program published so far pairs that slogan with a sitting head of state, a European commissioner, a deliberately smaller crowd and a rebuilt startup competition. ComplexDiscovery will attend and report from Slush for the second consecutive year. A smaller crowd, by design Behind that program sits an unusual organizer. Slush is a not-for-profit owned by the Startup Foundation, a Finnish foundation that receives most of any profit the event makes, according to the organization's own description. It began in 2008 as a 250-person gathering. Its 2026 FAQ projects 5,800 startups and 3,300 investors, and its homepage advertises 12,000-plus attendees, 200-plus speakers and 600-plus side events across what Slush calls Slush Week. Students and recent graduates run the operation, supported by a volunteer corps that Slush's own pages put at between 1,600 and 1,800 people. Selectivity runs through the whole event. Slush says it does not pay speakers and speakers do not pay it, and every company seeking to attend must complete an application that the Slush team reviews personally. This year the headcount is smaller on purpose. When Slush named Noora Saksa chief executive on Jan. 27, it said the 2026 event would cut its audience by 10 percent to better serve its core of early-stage startups. Personal recommendations will tailor the experience to each company's growth stage, the announcement said. Saksa, who first joined Slush as a volunteer in 2021, framed the stakes in economic terms. "Startups are our best bet for GDP growth in Europe," she said in the announcement. She also set a goal there of at least two European technology companies in the global top 10 by market capitalization by 2050. Announcements that set the 2026 program The same rethinking reached Slush 100, the pitch competition whose earlier formats date to the event's 2008 founding year. This year's winner receives €500,000 with no equity taken, replacing the €1 million investment from venture firms that winners received from 2022 through 2025, according to Slush. "A flat €1M at a fixed valuation and standard terms no longer fits most startups," Saksa said. Dropping the investor-led model also opens the contest to founders from outside Europe and the U.S., Slush said. From over 1,400 applicants, Slush named 100 companies and then 20 semifinalists, who pitch on the Startup Stage on the first morning before three finalists compete for the prize. Slush also created Slush 20 Under 20, a program for builders who have not yet turned 20. The first list, published this month, names 20 people from over a dozen countries, the youngest of them 15, who together have raised over €10 million from venture investors, according to Slush. Anthropic, Index Ventures and Sifted support the program. "Europe's first €1T company could be founded by a teenager," Saksa said. Off the stage, Slush has changed address. Since July, it has worked from Kasvutalo, or Growth House, in Helsinki's Kamppi district. That is the new name Slush and the startup community Founders House gave to Sähkötalo, an Alvar Aalto building completed in 1973 as head office of the city's electricity utility. A Sept. 2 release counts about 50 companies and communities in the building, around 30 of them startups, investors and startup communities. "Every leading tech hub in Europe has its own startup district," Saksa said in the release. Who is on stage, and why practitioners should listen Those year-round moves feed a November program whose speakers are now partly public. Slush has published what it calls its first batch of 2026 speakers and says the stage program is full. The roster includes two officeholders, Alexander Stubb, Finland's 13th president, and Ekaterina Zaharieva, the European commissioner for startups, research and innovation. It also features Jessica Livingston, co-founder of Y Combinator; David Silver, former lead of DeepMind's reinforcement learning team and now chief executive of Ineffable Intelligence; and Matthew Prince, co-founder and chief executive of Cloudflare. Beyond Prince, cybersecurity professionals will find two security-company founders on the list. Eoin Hinchy ran security operations for 15 years at companies including eBay, PayPal and DocuSign before co-founding Tines, according to his Slush biography, and Madeline Lawrence is co-founder of Aikido Security. Legal technology arrives through Ross McNairn, whose company Wordsmith builds AI software for corporate legal departments. Paolo Fois of Lexroom is also listed, and his Slush biography says over 15 percent of Italian legal proceedings pass through Lexroom, without explaining how that share is measured. The third legal name is Joshua Browder of DoNotPay, whose speaker biography describes the service as "the world's first robot lawyer." That phrase has a regulatory history. In a September 2024 complaint, the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) alleged that DoNotPay did not test whether its AI lawyer service performed at the level of a human lawyer. The commission voted 5-0 on Jan. 16, 2025, to approve a final order, which the agency announced Feb. 11. The order requires DoNotPay to pay $193,000 and bars it from claiming its service performs like a real lawyer without sufficient evidence to back that up, according to the FTC. For eDiscovery and information governance teams weighing AI vendors, the lesson reaches beyond one company, because a federal regulator has already required one legal AI provider to support its performance claims with evidence. Every vendor claim heard in Helsinki deserves the same scrutiny. Company law has its own advocates on the program. Simon Schaefer, Iwona Anna Biernat and Vojtech Horna appear for EU-INC, a movement Schaefer co-founded in late 2024, according to his Slush biography. The European Commission has since proposed an EU-level company form under the EU Inc. name, which it describes as optional and digital by default. In its March 18 release presenting the proposed regulation, the Commission called on the European Parliament and the Council to agree on it by the end of 2026. In Parliament, the file has hit a delay: a vote in the legal affairs committee planned for Oct. 8 was postponed, with a new date around Oct. 19, Agence Europe and Table.Briefings reported. Attendees planning their days should know that Slush's public pages, as reviewed Oct. 13, list speakers and opening hours but not a session-by-session schedule. The media page says the agenda launches in the fall, and for 2025 Slush published its full stage agenda on the Slush Platform, the same online tool attendees use to book meetings. The main event opens with the Slush 2026 Opening Show at 10 a.m. Nov. 18. What Slush's own research claims, and what it cannot Whatever the final schedule, Slush's sales pitch rests on research it publishes itself. The Slush Startup Report 2026, released in May with data partner Dealroom, compared 2,108 European companies that first attended Slush in 2022, 2023 or 2024 with 229,866 European peers matched on founding year, country and growth stage. Every company in the Slush group was founded in 2016 or later and had not reached a Series B round when it first attended. After that first attendance, 26.4 percent of the Slush companies raised institutional capital, against 7.5 percent of benchmark peers measured over what the report calls the equivalent post-2022 period, which the report presents as a 3.5-times premium. On investor quality, 5.6 percent of the Slush companies were backed by a fund in the top 0.1 percent of Dealroom's global investor ranking, against 0.8 percent of peers. Readers should weigh those figures against the report's own caveats. The two groups start in different places. Nearly half the Slush companies, 48 percent, had no institutional backing when they first attended, while 89 percent of the benchmark companies were bootstrapped. The report acknowledges that already-backed companies raise money at higher rates in both groups, which is why its aggregate premium exceeds the premium within either subgroup. Among companies with no outside funding at first attendance, 17 percent of the Slush group raised venture capital afterward, against 5.6 percent of peers. Among those already backed, the rates were 35 percent and 23.2 percent. Its methodology also concedes that matching cannot account for how ambitious, well connected or ready to raise the attending companies already were. The findings are correlational, the report says, and its matching "cannot separate who attends from what attending does." The report closes by telling readers the data suggests the trip is worth taking, which marks it as research produced by the organization that sells the tickets. Two other Slush studies frame this year's message. In a February survey of 310 Finnish founders and operators, 53 percent of respondents said they were considering or actively planning to move business operations abroad, and 56 percent named general attitudes and culture as obstacles to growth. Slush says the respondents represent about 10 percent of Finland's active startups. It sent 10 reform proposals to Prime Minister Petteri Orpo, who said his government would review them in its April budget framework discussions. An October 2025 study with Dealroom and Accel found that 68 of 459 former full-time Slush staff members, or 15 percent, had gone on to found companies. Finland's stage carries geopolitical weight Slush makes its case for European founders from a city whose venues carry their own history. Investor Day on Nov. 17 takes place at Alvar Aalto's Finlandia Hall on Töölö Bay, where Slush's Investor Day page promises over 2,000 venture investors. Leaders of 35 states gathered there for the 1975 Conference on Security and Co-operation in Europe. They signed the Helsinki Final Act on the summit's last day, Aug. 1, 1975, according to the Finnish Heritage Agency and Switzerland's National Museum. Finland's own position has shifted since then. It became NATO's 31st member on April 4, 2023, and Stubb took office as president on March 1, 2024. Helsinki also hosts the European Centre of Excellence for Countering Hybrid Threats, which counts 35 participating states, all of them members of the EU or NATO. For security teams with Finnish operations, the country's Cybersecurity Act, which implements the EU's NIS 2 Directive, began phasing in obligations for covered entities on April 8, 2025, according to Traficom. Those entities then had until May 8 of that year to register and until July 8 to establish risk-management procedures, although public administration entities received no separate transition period for that risk-management obligation, the agency said. The technology record behind the event runs deep. Linus Torvalds, who enrolled at the University of Helsinki in 1988, started work on the kernel later named Linux in the fall of 1991, according to the Computer History Museum. Satellite company ICEYE, whose co-founder Rafal Modrzewski is on the 2026 speaker list, launched its technology in Finland and now serves defense clients worldwide, according to Slush's Helsinki page. What ComplexDiscovery will be watching ComplexDiscovery's coverage from Helsinki last year followed similar threads, examining how Harvey scaled domain-specific legal AI, how the BORDERLAND gathering approached dual-use defense technology, and what data provenance meant for information governance teams. Four threads stand out for 2026. The first is evidence: when legal AI founders cite adoption or accuracy figures on stage, record the claim and its basis, because statements made on stage can resurface in sales materials and procurement files. The second is corporate form: if EU Inc. advances, counterparties incorporated under a new EU-level form are likely to raise registry and records questions for diligence and discovery teams, in this publication's assessment. The third is resilience, because defense, space and infrastructure companies on the program, ICEYE among them, work in sectors where cybersecurity, export controls and data sovereignty overlap. The fourth is timing. Two of the 20 Slush 100 semifinalists build products around sensitive information: Foundation Clinic, which Slush lists as "the health-data platform for European healthcare," and GraceX, pitched as "your company's brain" with privacy built in. In this publication's assessment, companies at that stage are where security, information governance and discovery needs first take shape, which makes Slush a place for providers in those fields to see what early-stage clients will ask of them. The International Day for Failure, as Yle describes it, aims to take the stigma out of mistakes so that people feel free to create and innovate. For its Nov. 18 and 19 main event, organizers say they will trim the audience by 10 percent to better serve early-stage startups and award the Slush 100 winner €500,000 without taking equity. Finland's president, Alexander Stubb, and European Commissioner Ekaterina Zaharieva appear on the published speaker list. [exclude_from_rss] [taq_review] [/exclude_from_rss] Industry News - Technology Beat Slush 2026 brings a smaller, sharper bet on European startups to Helsinki ComplexDiscovery Staff Finland marks the International Day for Failure today, a custom that began in 2010 when a student group at Aalto University proposed celebrating failure instead of lamenting it, Yle reported. Five weeks from now, a startup event that Aalto says its student community helped spark will test how far that appetite for risk can carry European technology. Slush 2026 runs Nov. 18 and 19 at Messukeskus, the Helsinki Expo and Convention Centre, with Investor Day and a founders' program on Nov. 17. The organizers have branded this edition a bet on Europe. The program published so far pairs that slogan with a sitting head of state, a European commissioner, a deliberately smaller crowd and a rebuilt startup competition. ComplexDiscovery will attend and report from Slush for the second consecutive year. A smaller crowd, by design Behind that program sits an unusual organizer. Slush is a not-for-profit owned by the Startup Foundation, a Finnish foundation that receives most of any profit the event makes, according to the organization's own description. It began in 2008 as a 250-person gathering. Its 2026 FAQ projects 5,800 startups and 3,300 investors, and its homepage advertises 12,000-plus attendees, 200-plus speakers and 600-plus side events across what Slush calls Slush Week. Students and recent graduates run the operation, supported by a volunteer corps that Slush's own pages put at between 1,600 and 1,800 people. Selectivity runs through the whole event. Slush says it does not pay speakers and speakers do not pay it, and every company seeking to attend must complete an application that the Slush team reviews personally. This year the headcount is smaller on purpose. When Slush named Noora Saksa chief executive on Jan. 27, it said the 2026 event would cut its audience by 10 percent to better serve its core of early-stage startups. Personal recommendations will tailor the experience to each company's growth stage, the announcement said. Saksa, who first joined Slush as a volunteer in 2021, framed the stakes in economic terms. "Startups are our best bet for GDP growth in Europe," she said in the announcement. She also set a goal there of at least two European technology companies in the global top 10 by market capitalization by 2050. Announcements that set the 2026 program The same rethinking reached Slush 100, the pitch competition whose earlier formats date to the event's 2008 founding year. This year's winner receives €500,000 with no equity taken, replacing the €1 million investment from venture firms that winners received from 2022 through 2025, according to Slush. "A flat €1M at a fixed valuation and standard terms no longer fits most startups," Saksa said. Dropping the investor-led model also opens the contest to founders from outside Europe and the U.S., Slush said. From over 1,400 applicants, Slush named 100 companies and then 20 semifinalists, who pitch on the Startup Stage on the first morning before three finalists compete for the prize. Slush also created Slush 20 Under 20, a program for builders who have not yet turned 20. The first list, published this month, names 20 people from over a dozen countries, the youngest of them 15, who together have raised over €10 million from venture investors, according to Slush. Anthropic, Index Ventures and Sifted support the program. "Europe's first €1T company could be founded by a teenager," Saksa said. Off the stage, Slush has changed address. Since July, it has worked from Kasvutalo, or Growth House, in Helsinki's Kamppi district. That is the new name Slush and the startup community Founders House gave to Sähkötalo, an Alvar Aalto building completed in 1973 as head office of the city's electricity utility. A Sept. 2 release counts about 50 companies and communities in the building, around 30 of them startups, investors and startup communities. "Every leading tech hub in Europe has its own startup district," Saksa said in the release. Who is on stage, and why practitioners should listen Those year-round moves feed a November program whose speakers are now partly public. Slush has published what it calls its first batch of 2026 speakers and says the stage program is full. The roster includes two officeholders, Alexander Stubb, Finland's 13th president, and Ekaterina Zaharieva, the European commissioner for startups, research and innovation. It also features Jessica Livingston, co-founder of Y Combinator; David Silver, former lead of DeepMind's reinforcement learning team and now chief executive of Ineffable Intelligence; and Matthew Prince, co-founder and chief executive of Cloudflare. Beyond Prince, cybersecurity professionals will find two security-company founders on the list. Eoin Hinchy ran security operations for 15 years at companies including eBay, PayPal and DocuSign before co-founding Tines, according to his Slush biography, and Madeline Lawrence is co-founder of Aikido Security. Legal technology arrives through Ross McNairn, whose company Wordsmith builds AI software for corporate legal departments. Paolo Fois of Lexroom is also listed, and his Slush biography says over 15 percent of Italian legal proceedings pass through Lexroom, without explaining how that share is measured. The third legal name is Joshua Browder of DoNotPay, whose speaker biography describes the service as "the world's first robot lawyer." That phrase has a regulatory history. In a September 2024 complaint, the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) alleged that DoNotPay did not test whether its AI lawyer service performed at the level of a human lawyer. The commission voted 5-0 on Jan. 16, 2025, to approve a final order, which the agency announced Feb. 11. The order requires DoNotPay to pay $193,000 and bars it from claiming its service performs like a real lawyer without sufficient evidence to back that up, according to the FTC. For eDiscovery and information governance teams weighing AI vendors, the lesson reaches beyond one company, because a federal regulator has already required one legal AI provider to support its performance claims with evidence. Every vendor claim heard in Helsinki deserves the same scrutiny. Company law has its own advocates on the program. Simon Schaefer, Iwona Anna Biernat and Vojtech Horna appear for EU-INC, a movement Schaefer co-founded in late 2024, according to his Slush biography. The European Commission has since proposed an EU-level company form under the EU Inc. name, which it describes as optional and digital by default. In its March 18 release presenting the proposed regulation, the Commission called on the European Parliament and the Council to agree on it by the end of 2026. In Parliament, the file has hit a delay: a vote in the legal affairs committee planned for Oct. 8 was postponed, with a new date around Oct. 19, Agence Europe and Table.Briefings reported. Attendees planning their days should know that Slush's public pages, as reviewed Oct. 13, list speakers and opening hours but not a session-by-session schedule. The media page says the agenda launches in the fall, and for 2025 Slush published its full stage agenda on the Slush Platform, the same online tool attendees use to book meetings. The main event opens with the Slush 2026 Opening Show at 10 a.m. Nov. 18. What Slush's own research claims, and what it cannot Whatever the final schedule, Slush's sales pitch rests on research it publishes itself. The Slush Startup Report 2026, released in May with data partner Dealroom, compared 2,108 European companies that first attended Slush in 2022, 2023 or 2024 with 229,866 European peers matched on founding year, country and growth stage. Every company in the Slush group was founded in 2016 or later and had not reached a Series B round when it first attended. After that first attendance, 26.4 percent of the Slush companies raised institutional capital, against 7.5 percent of benchmark peers measured over what the report calls the equivalent post-2022 period, which the report presents as a 3.5-times premium. On investor quality, 5.6 percent of the Slush companies were backed by a fund in the top 0.1 percent of Dealroom's global investor ranking, against 0.8 percent of peers. Readers should weigh those figures against the report's own caveats. The two groups start in different places. Nearly half the Slush companies, 48 percent, had no institutional backing when they first attended, while 89 percent of the benchmark companies were bootstrapped. The report acknowledges that already-backed companies raise money at higher rates in both groups, which is why its aggregate premium exceeds the premium within either subgroup. Among companies with no outside funding at first attendance, 17 percent of the Slush group raised venture capital afterward, against 5.6 percent of peers. Among those already backed, the rates were 35 percent and 23.2 percent. Its methodology also concedes that matching cannot account for how ambitious, well connected or ready to raise the attending companies already were. The findings are correlational, the report says, and its matching "cannot separate who attends from what attending does." The report closes by telling readers the data suggests the trip is worth taking, which marks it as research produced by the organization that sells the tickets. Two other Slush studies frame this year's message. In a February survey of 310 Finnish founders and operators, 53 percent of respondents said they were considering or actively planning to move business operations abroad, and 56 percent named general attitudes and culture as obstacles to growth. Slush says the respondents represent about 10 percent of Finland's active startups. It sent 10 reform proposals to Prime Minister Petteri Orpo, who said his government would review them in its April budget framework discussions. An October 2025 study with Dealroom and Accel found that 68 of 459 former full-time Slush staff members, or 15 percent, had gone on to found companies. Finland's stage carries geopolitical weight Slush makes its case for European founders from a city whose venues carry their own history. Investor Day on Nov. 17 takes place at Alvar Aalto's Finlandia Hall on Töölö Bay, where Slush's Investor Day page promises over 2,000 venture investors. Leaders of 35 states gathered there for the 1975 Conference on Security and Co-operation in Europe. They signed the Helsinki Final Act on the summit's last day, Aug. 1, 1975, according to the Finnish Heritage Agency and Switzerland's National Museum. Finland's own position has shifted since then. It became NATO's 31st member on April 4, 2023, and Stubb took office as president on March 1, 2024. Helsinki also hosts the European Centre of Excellence for Countering Hybrid Threats, which counts 35 participating states, all of them members of the EU or NATO. For security teams with Finnish operations, the country's Cybersecurity Act, which implements the EU's NIS 2 Directive, began phasing in obligations for covered entities on April 8, 2025, according to Traficom. Those entities then had until May 8 of that year to register and until July 8 to establish risk-management procedures, although public administration entities received no separate transition period for that risk-management obligation, the agency said. The technology record behind the event runs deep. Linus Torvalds, who enrolled at the University of Helsinki in 1988, started work on the kernel later named Linux in the fall of 1991, according to the Computer History Museum. Satellite company ICEYE, whose co-founder Rafal Modrzewski is on the 2026 speaker list, launched its technology in Finland and now serves defense clients worldwide, according to Slush's Helsinki page. What ComplexDiscovery will be watching ComplexDiscovery's coverage from Helsinki last year followed similar threads, examining how Harvey scaled domain-specific legal AI, how the BORDERLAND gathering approached dual-use defense technology, and what data provenance meant for information governance teams. Four threads stand out for 2026. The first is evidence: when legal AI founders cite adoption or accuracy figures on stage, record the claim and its basis, because statements made on stage can resurface in sales materials and procurement files. The second is corporate form: if EU Inc. advances, counterparties incorporated under a new EU-level form are likely to raise registry and records questions for diligence and discovery teams, in this publication's assessment. The third is resilience, because defense, space and infrastructure companies on the program, ICEYE among them, work in sectors where cybersecurity, export controls and data sovereignty overlap. The fourth is timing. Two of the 20 Slush 100 semifinalists build products around sensitive information: Foundation Clinic, which Slush lists as "the health-data platform for European healthcare," and GraceX, pitched as "your company's brain" with privacy built in. In this publication's assessment, companies at that stage are where security, information governance and discovery needs first take shape, which makes Slush a place for providers in those fields to see what early-stage clients will ask of them. The International Day for Failure, as Yle describes it, aims to take the stigma out of mistakes so that people feel free to create and innovate. Slush is now asking Europe to place a larger bet on its own builders, while its own research concedes it cannot separate the founders who walk in from what the room itself does for them. Which claims made on Helsinki's stages next month will your organization be ready to verify before it relies on them? This early outlook from ComplexDiscovery provides a strategic reference point for identifying where eDiscovery, AI, and European innovation will intersect over the coming year. [exclude_from_rss] [taq_review] [/exclude_from_rss] Event Calendar The 2026 Event Horizon: Early Outlook for eDiscovery, AI, and European Innovation ComplexDiscovery Staff As the professional landscape for data discovery and legal technology continues to evolve, the 2026 event calendar offers early evidence of an accelerating convergence between eDiscovery, artificial intelligence, and Europe’s leadership in digital governance. While this preview is not exhaustive, it provides a practical point of reference for professionals engaged in law, technology, and information management as they assess their strategic priorities and learning opportunities for the year ahead. The Shifting Center: eDiscovery Meets AI Across continents, the pipeline of 2026 conferences and summits points to one clear trend: artificial intelligence is rapidly reshaping the conversation, from automated review and advanced analytics to risk management, data strategy, and legal innovation. Traditional benchmarks such as Legalweek in New York, ILTACON in Nashville, and Relativity Fest in Chicago remain anchor points for eDiscovery practitioners in North America, serving as forums for technology launches, best practices, and discussions on the shifting regulatory landscape. At the same time, U.S. cyber risk series such as the NetDiligence Cyber Risk Summits—scheduled for Miami Beach, Toronto, San Diego, and Philadelphia—continue to support lawyers and technologists at the frontline of incident response, insurance, and digital forensics. Europe: At the Forefront of AI and Legal Innovation For professionals seeking global perspectives and direct connection to the heart of regulatory change, the 2026 calendar’s European segment is especially compelling. A suite of focused programs—spanning the Nordics, Baltics, Western Europe, and key legal and digital hubs—demonstrates the region’s expanding influence over the future of law and technology: Latitude59 (Tallinn, Estonia): Ground zero for Baltic innovation, with deep dives into startup ecosystems and legal tech. CyCon (Tallinn, Estonia): A critical juncture for cyber conflict, AI-aided defense strategies, and transatlantic security. Slush 2026 (Helsinki, Finland): Europe’s flagship for startup culture, technology ventures, and the frontiers of AI and governance.
